#2 [paper] The Ceiling Holds: Testing AI/ML Architecture, Depth, and Training-Window Size Against an Empirically Measured Predictability Limit
Authors: Arun Ramanathan
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21696947
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
A common, mostly unstated assumption behind a lot of modern AI/ML work is that more data and a more powerful model can eventually predict almost anything. In the physical sciences this was tested and found wanting: chaos theory showed that some systems, like weather, have a hard limit on how far ahead they can be predicted no matter how good your model or how much data you feed it, because the limit lives in the system’s own dynamics, not in the model. This research program has already measured a limit like that for financial markets, directly and empirically, with no model involved in the measurement itself. This paper runs two tests of what that limit actually means for AI/ML in practice, plus a direct follow-up to the first test that closes an obvious loophole. First, we give five very different kinds of models — a plain average, an intentionally overfit decision tree, a reinforcement-learning agent, a generative adversarial network, and a variational autoencoder — the exact same fair amount of training data, sized to stay safely within that measured limit, and simply watch which one predicts real subsequent prices best. Since the fancier three of those five were kept deliberately simple — no hidden layers, nothing a machine learning engineer would call “deep” — we then test the obvious objection directly: we give the reinforcement-learning agent, the GAN, and the variational autoencoder one genuine hidden layer each, real nonlinearity rather than just a different training recipe, while keeping the exact same tiny amount of training data, and check whether that changes anything. Second, we take the original five models and start feeding them progressively more training data, extending further and further past that limit, the way a real team chasing “more data” often does, and watch what happens. In the first test, nothing beats the plain average; two of the fancier models essentially become the plain average. Giving those same two models a real hidden layer doesn’t change that either — they still just become the plain average, and the variational autoencoder is still unstable rather than skillful, whether linear or given a hidden layer. In the second test, every model — regardless of how it works internally — starts drifting away from reality once its training data reaches well past the measured limit, and the drift gets worse the further past it they go. This is the same pattern atmospheric scientists saw decades ago: an early, real-model-based estimate of a predictability limit, a theoretical account soon after of why it should exist, and then decades of dramatically better forecasting systems that kept running into the same wall anyway, no matter how much they improved in the meantime. We show this mainly as plots of predicted price against real price, and back the training-data test up with a plain, direct measurement of how large the errors actually get, as a percentage of price anyone can judge for themselves — not a statistical test score, not a p-value, just a straightforward number.

Abstract:
Tree ensembles are recommended for macroeconomic forecasting because they capture non-linear structure, and they are known in principle to be unable to predict outside the range of target values seen in training.This paper documents both properties in one short-sample forecasting problem.Comparing training and test error for three models forecasting Nigerian FDI one quarter ahead on 62 observations, gradient boosting achieves a training RMSE of 2.80 against a test RMSE of 983.64, a ratio of 351 to 1. Random forest and support vector regression degrade far less (2.24 and 2.61 times respectively) from much looser training fits.The extreme ratio for gradient boosting is straightforward overfitting on 49 training observations.Separately, the training targets are strictly positive, running from 58.72 to 3,084.90, while the test period contains four negative quarters and five observations below the training minimum.A tree ensemble trained only on positive targets cannot emit a negative prediction, because its output is a weighted average of training-set leaf values.Both effects are present and they are distinct.We separate them, and note that on a full walkforward comparison gradient boosting on an enhanced feature set was the best of twelve specifications, so neither effect supports a general claim about tree ensembles in this domain.

#5 [paper] When Are Decision Models Worth It? An Empirical Comparison with Small Task-Specific Classifiers
Authors: Alessio Pomaro
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23652644
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Preprint, not peer reviewed. Decision models such as OpenAI Decisions and Base Labs' Elephant-1 and Mammoth-1 return a probability for each option of a closed question and need no task-specific training. This independent study asks when they are worth using instead of small classifiers trained on the task. We compare them with TF-IDF, SetFit, mmBERT and Qwen3 classifiers (0.6B, 1.7B, 8B parameters) on Banking77 (English), MASSIVE it-IT (Italian) and a synthetic Italian customer-service task, varying the label budget (5 and 20 examples per class, full training set) and the category descriptions, and testing a lexical stress set and a phenomenon-level robustness set. With few labelled examples the decision models are far ahead, even when given label names only; with the full training sets and the protocol recipes the gap is 2.4 points on Banking77, 5.5 on Italian MASSIVE and not resolved on the synthetic task, and on Banking77 a different fine-tuning recipe leaves no resolved difference, so in this regime the outcome depends on the training recipe. The effect of category descriptions varies with model and dataset, and Elephant-1 is much closer to its own base model, Qwen3.5-9B, than to an older generalist. The study uses a frozen protocol, paired bootstrap intervals and three seeds; code, per-example predictions and synthetic data are released. Limitations: no real customer messages or human annotations, synthetic data written by language models, possible contamination of public benchmarks, endpoints evaluated in October 2026. The author set the research question and the requirements of the study; an AI coding agent (Claude Code) proposed the detailed protocol, wrote the code, ran the experiments and drafted the manuscript under the author's direction. See the "AI assistance and authorship" section of the paper.

#6 [paper] Do Machine Learning Models Beat a Constant Benchmark When Forecasting Next-Month Hurst Exponents? Evidence from Saudi-Listed Firms
Authors: Mazin Alahmadi, S. Baik, Retal Kutbi, Jana Kilfaden, Lujain Qadi, Lama Alboqami
Venue: Forecasting
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/forecast8050098
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Financial forecasting under uncertainty is fundamental to strategic investment decision making. Among the factors that influence investment decisions, market efficiency plays a critical role because it determines whether historical information can provide predictive value for future market behavior. The Hurst exponent is widely used to measure persistence and weak-form market efficiency, where values close to 0.5 indicate random behavior and values above or below 0.5 indicate persistent or mean-reverting dynamics. Despite extensive research using the Hurst exponent to characterize market persistence and market-efficiency-related behavior, limited studies have investigated whether future Hurst exponent estimates can be forecast using machine learning techniques and whether these models can outperform a simple constant benchmark. This study addresses this gap by developing a machine learning framework to forecast the next-month Hurst exponent using firm-level descriptive, financial, technical, and statistical indicators and comparing their performance against a constant benchmark. A dataset comprising 141 Saudi-listed companies, 705 firm-month observations, approximately 147 predictor variables, and five monthly periods was constructed. Monthly Hurst exponent values were estimated using the Rescaled Range (R/S) method and used as the target variable. Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Elastic Net, Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated using an expanding-window time-series validation strategy with two chronological forecast origins. Model performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). None of the evaluated machine learning models outperformed the constant benchmark, which achieved the lowest RMSE (0.227) and MAE (0.179). Ridge Regression performed relatively best among the machine learning models, with an RMSE of 0.236 and an MAE of 0.187, but it still failed to improve upon the benchmark, and all evaluated machine learning models produced negative R2 values. These results indicate that the selected firm-level descriptive, financial, technical, and statistical indicators provided limited incremental forecasting value relative to a simple constant benchmark within the adopted empirical design. Given the five-month observation period and limited number of chronological forecast origins, the findings are best interpreted as exploratory evidence regarding the ability of machine learning models to outperform a constant benchmark in forecasting next-month Hurst estimates, rather than as definitive evidence concerning market efficiency or the general predictability of financial markets. The study provides an empirical benchmark for future investigations into forecasting Hurst exponent estimates and changes in market persistence.

For independent trials that is right: if each fails at 0.05, P = 1 − (1 − 0.05)^K, which gives 0.6415 at K = 20 and 0.9941 at K = 100. But a sweep's cells are not independent — the 5- and 10-period moving averages point the same way on almost the same bars — so twenty tries should not be worth twenty. The separator in this paper is whether the cells looked at overlap: the instruments, the period, the grid and the family are all held fixed, and only how many cells were looked at is changed. Using 1-hour bars for four instruments (USDJPY, EURUSD, GBPUSD, XAUUSD) from 2019 to 2024, a family of moving-average crosses was swept: fast period 5–60 (12 values) × slow period 20–200 (10 values, fast < slow) × 4 instruments × forward horizons of 6 and 24 bars, for 840 cells in total. The threshold is |t| ≥ 2, with K cells drawn without replacement and repeated 2,000 times. The baseline is a synthetic random walk down to within the bar (3 draws), whose true value is zero. A single cell came out significant 0.0214 of the time under the daily-cluster t and 0.3690 under the naive t — 0.4286 times and 7.3810 times the nominal 0.05. The medians of |t| are 0.4392 against 1.5770, so the naive t inflates by more than three times (3.5908). Putting the per-cell rate of 0.0214 back into the formula matches the measurement almost exactly (measured ÷ formula runs 1.0000 to 1.0733): the cells overlap, and significance piles up as if they were independent. #8 [paper] Review of The Evolution, Challenges, and Future Directions of Forecasting Methods
Authors: Zhiting Chen
Venue: Applied and Computational Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.54254/2755-2721/2026.ch36590
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Forecasting serves as a critical cornerstone for strategic planning, operational efficiency, and risk mitigation across modern civilization. By converting historical data into actionable forward-looking insights, it enables organizations and governments to anticipate market shifts, optimize resource distribution, and safeguard against systemic uncertainties. Predictive modeling is a fundamental task in many fields, such as finance, economics, engineering, and artificial intelligence. The aim of this paper is to summarize the methods of statistics and machine learning, outline their inherent challenges, and project future research directions. This paper mainly discusses traditional statistical methods (including Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average [ARIMA] and regression analysis), machine learning approaches (such as Random Forest and Support Vector Machines [SVM]), and deep learning models (such as Long Short-Term Memory [LSTM] networks and hybrid time series-ML models). Nowadays, as these interconnected fields become increasingly complicated, practitioners face severe challenges regarding data quality, computational complexity, and mathematical interpretability. This paper comprehensively reviews these methodologies, establishes a comparative taxonomy, and delineates the evolutionary trajectory of future forecasting applications.

#9 [paper] Agentic AI-Based Predictive Maintenance in Smart Power Grid Operations
Authors: Nitin Yadav, Ratnakishori Kagitha, Sagar P.Y
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22672456

Abstract:
Power grids rank among the most critical infrastructures we depend on, yet the maintenance strategies protecting them are still mostly reactive or scheduled by the calendar rather than by actual condition. Predictive maintenance (PdM) tries to fix this by using condition-monitoring data and machine learning to estimate failure probability ahead of time, but in practice most systems stop once they produce an alarm or a risk score — deciding what that number means, and what to do about it, is still left to a human expert. In this paper we propose an agentic AI framework for predictive maintenance in smart power grids, built around power transformers as a case study, and we evaluate the predictive half of it on a public dataset of 933 dissolved-gas-analysis (DGA) measurements from 105 transformers currently in service. A Random Forest model trained to flag measurements linked to a confident fault diagnosis, based on four classical DGA methods, reached perfect recall and 80.5% precision on a held-out test set split by transformer (F1 = 0.89), beating both a majority-class baseline and a gradient-boosting comparator. Ethylene concentration turned out to be by far the strongest predictor, which is consistent with existing DGA theory. What stood out most, however, is that 37.6% of the measurements could not be resolved to a clear fault type by any of the four classical methods. That gap is really the motivation behind the multi-agent architecture we propose, in which separate agents handle diagnosis, criticality assessment and maintenance planning, with a human required to approve anything flagged high severity

#10 [paper] Forecasting novel therapeutic development in biomedical research
Authors: Salsabil Arabi, B. Ian Hutchins
Venue: Communications Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-026-01838-6
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Background Early identification of promising drug research topics is challenging yet crucial for the scientific community to accelerate the development of novel therapeutics. In this work, we leverage large-scale data from the biomedical literature to extract predictive features to identify promising therapeutic research topics at an early stage. Methods We use a modularity maximizing machine learning algorithm to divide the global citation graph of biomedical literature into a time series of research topic clusters. We extract features for predictive analytics based on citation activity, publication content, and measurable flocking of scientists into novel research topics. Results Here we report a maximum likelihood model that prospectively identifies research topics culminating in the studies that were pivotal for 99 Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approvals for drugs (F1-score of 0.84). 80% of target drugs are predicted in advance, with 65% predicted 8 or more years before approval. This predates the start of phase 2 clinical trials in the vast majority of positive predictions. Conclusions These results show this approach can efficiently flag research topics generating approved drugs several years prior to approval using public data that would have been contemporaneous at the time of prediction. Thus, reliable forecasting can be accomplished with a high-level view of the publication and citation behavior of scientists, without depending on clinical trial data that may only be deposited with a significant lag. This demonstrates that it is possible to detect early signals of future FDA approved therapies even without any specialized information about these applied research efforts.

#11 [paper] Comparison of Forecasts From Neural Network and Econometric Models .
Authors: D. A. Koloskov, M.Yu. Turuntseva, Vadim Zyamalov
Venue: Economic Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.18288/1994-5124-2026-5-84-111

Abstract:
This article provides a comparative analysis of the performance of neural network and econometric models in generating pseudo-out-of-sample multistep forecasts. Multistep forecasts with horizons of up to 12 months were generated for two periods: January 2024 to December 2025 and January to December 2025. The robustness of those results was additionally verified over a 48-month evaluation period from January 2022 to December 2025. The hyperparameters of the LSTM model were selected using random search and the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Bayesian optimization algorithm. The result indicated that, without properly tuned hyperparameters, even a complex nonlinear model provides no advantage over the simplest naive forecast. The stochastic nature of neural network training was taken into account to ensure a valid comparison and reproducibility of the results by testing the selected configurations for stability across a series of runs with different random seeds for which mean forecast errors and their standard deviations were calculated. Forecast accuracy was evaluated using MAPE, RMSE, and the aggregated GMFQI measure; the run time of the models was also compared. The results were compared with forecasts generated by classical econometric models: random walk (RW), ARIMA, and the linear trend (TS) model. The econometric forecasts were constructed using recursive and moving window forecasting. The conclusion was that, with appropriate hyperparameter tuning and control for reproducibility of results, the LSTM model can provide more accurate forecasts, primarily over longer evaluation periods. Nevertheless, simple econometric models provide comparable forecasting performance at substantially lower computational cost.

#13 [paper] Three Things Called Budget Awareness: Observability, Forecasting and Allocation in LLM Agents, Why Every Published Allocation Gain Is Keyed to a Signal Measured After the Fact, and the Run-to-Run Vari

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22884949

Abstract:
(c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Two 2024-2026 literatures make claims about resource use in language-model agents that look incompatible. One reports that allocating test-time compute according to problem difficulty beats spending it uniformly, by margins up to a factor of four in compute at equal accuracy. The other reports that agents cannot estimate their own resource consumption, that the estimates are systematically optimistic, and that the ability to produce them is only weakly related to the ability to do the task. If intelligent allocation were the decisive lever, the most capable models should be the best allocators, and several independent measurements say they are not. This paper argues that the incompatibility is apparent and dissolves under a partition. The phrase budget awareness is carrying at least four distinct decisions: adherence to a budget someone else set, observability of the remaining budget inside the agent's context, forecasting of one's own future consumption, and allocation of a known budget across competing demands. The four are measured on different instruments and do not have the same answer. Adherence is largely solved in the tested ranges: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) report output lengths that closely track requested targets at 512, 1024, 2048 and 3600 tokens. Observability is not a competence at all, and it accounts for a share of the reported failure large enough to move headline numbers. Liu et al. (2025b) report that a standard ReAct agent issues 13.77 search calls when given a budget of 30 and 14.24 when given 100, and that a plug-in which does nothing but keep the remaining budget in context reaches 12.8 percent on BrowseComp at a budget of 10 against 12.6 percent for the unmodified agent at a budget of 100, using 40.4 percent fewer search calls at 31.3 percent lower cost. Wen et al. (2025) reach the same conclusion at the token level and state the sharper form of it: naming the budget once in the prompt is insufficient, and the remaining budget has to be re-inserted periodically during generation. Forecasting is poor and structurally biased. Lin et al. (2026) find that across twenty model-environment pairs, optimistic misses outnumber conservative ones at every rollout-progress bin, that weaker models are more optimistic rather than less, and that on failed trajectories models predict feasibility above 70 percent after 60 percent of the budget is spent. Bai et al. (2026) find that eight frontier models correlate with their own realized token usage at up to 0.39 and underestimate it systematically. Allocation fails on a different axis again: Fan et al. (2026) find that under a shared budget, solving order tracks presentation position at rho = +0.68 while effort-value correlations run from 0.00 to +0.11, and that the set of questions receiving substantive work overlaps the highest-value-density set at 0.59 against a chance reference of 0.59. Abstract Long-horizon forecasting requires models to retain meaningful predictive differentiation across extended horizons. This study introduces the Signal Persistence Horizon (SPH), a model-agnostic diagnostic measuring how long forecasts retain material differentiation over a specified evaluation horizon, and applies it to nine-quarter volatility projection using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and GARCH. Across eight commodity and emerging-market FX series, baseline GPR forecasts rapidly lose differentiation, motivating an investigation of the underlying persistence structure. The Matérn kernel length-scale consistently converges to the imposed optimization boundary across alternative search ranges and specifications, indicating that persistence is not reliably identified by maximum marginal likelihood from daily returns alone. Further experiments separate persistence from signal amplitude and identify distinct failure modes associated with premature forecast convergence and asset-invariant long-horizon variance. A revised specification combining free kernel amplitude with a horizon-aligned, sensitivity-tested length-scale is tested to address these persistence and amplitude failure modes and restores stable, asset-differentiated nine-quarter forecasts. The results suggest that forecast persistence should be treated as an explicit modelling assumption and sensitivity dimension when data do not identify a unique long-horizon persistence structure.

Scientific weak signals are early, low-visibility research directions that later become central to mature scientific topics, yet existing resources such as trend tracking, citation forecasting, and foresight reports rarely provide validated reference sets that link concrete early precursors to later paradigms. We introduce BackTrend, a retrospective benchmark in which, given a mature target topic and a temporal evidence constraint, systems must recover two types of precursors: problem-space signals, underrecognized research problems, and solution-space signals, emerging methods for known problems. BackTrend contains 25 mature target topics in artificial intelligence and machine learning and 66 human-validated weak signals, reconstructed from large-scale literature by grounding each candidate in its 2019-2024 publication-frequency trajectory. We evaluate frontier LLMs, RAG systems, and agentic research systems using semantic matching and coverage-based metrics. Current systems often generate plausible but misaligned precursors, exhibiting topic drift, granularity mismatch, near-miss matching, and incomplete coverage; the strongest system achieves only 10.1% F1, while Coverage10 reaches at most 18.5% of the reference signals. Our budget analyses show that additional retrieval and web-search evidence can improve performance up to a moderate budget, but does not by itself close the substantial performance gap.

#1 [paper] VMCF: VMamba–CNN Fusion Network for Sea Surface Temperature Prediction
Authors: Hao Zhan, Xiaoyan Li, Pengfei Lin, Xueming Zhu, Jiuke Wang, Jane You
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213846
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Accurate short-term sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, specifically addressing the limitations of CNN-based methods in capturing global spatiotemporal dependencies and the high computational costs of Transformer-based approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): VMCF (VMamba–CNN Fusion Network), a dual-branch architecture that combines CNNs for local feature extraction with VMamba for efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation, strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): OISST dataset.
Abstract:
Sea surface temperature (SST) exerts a critical influence on diverse physical and biological processes within the marine environment. Nevertheless, accurate short-term SST forecasting still remains challenging. Current deep learning (DL) models have two key limitations: first, the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods fail to capture global spatiotemporal dependencies; second, Transformer-based approaches suffer from relatively high computational costs. To address these issues, this study introduces a VMamba–CNN fusion network (VMCF), a dual-branch architecture designed to effectively characterize the multiscale temporal and spatial variability of SST. The VMCF combines the powerful local feature extraction capability of CNNs with the efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation of VMamba, further strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion. Extensive experiments on the OISST dataset demonstrate significant performance improvements across all evaluation metrics, clearly validating the superiority of VMCF in SST forecasting. Specifically, it achieves root-mean-square error (RMSE) values ranging from 0.17 °C to 0.51 °C across 1–10-day lead times, outperforming five state-of-the-art DL models.

#10 [paper] How Grammar-Based Synthetic Data Shapes Behavior Learning

Abstract:
Grammar-based fuzzing can synthesize valid inputs for programs that process structured data. For behavior learning, the same inputs can be paired with the outputs a program produces, creating datasets that train neural program mocks. The fuzzer then serves as a data generator, and its selection policy determines which behaviors the model observes during training. To study how grammar-based input generation affects neural behavior modeling, we compare four generator configurations, train encoder-decoder Transformer models on 10,000 and 100,000 generated input-output pairs, and evaluate the resulting models on synthetic hold-out data and available real-world samples. Abstract. Convective systems can rapidly redistribute atmospheric trace gases. #2 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

Abstract:
Sea Surface Temperature (SST) plays a crucial role in climate studies, tropical cyclone prediction, and marine resource management. This study analyzes SST observations at Hon Dau station from 2000–2022 and applies ARIMAX, SARIMAX, Prophet, and LSTM models for SST forecasting. Abstract:
Machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) has moved from research demonstration into operational practice in roughly five years. Global models trained on reanalysis now produce ten- to fifteen-day forecasts at 0.25 degree resolution in seconds, and several match or exceed established numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems on standard verification metrics. This review examines what has been built, what it has been built on, and how it is being evaluated. Six architectural families are distinguished: spherical graph networks, three-dimensional transformers, cascaded multi-horizon systems, diffusion and flow-based generative ensembles, geometric mesh-based ensemble systems, and hybrid models that couple a differentiable dynamical core to learned physics. The data substrate receives detailed treatment, because ERA5 is a model-dependent product rather than a neutral training set, and every model trained on it inherits the analysis increments, parameterised tendencies, and changing observational coverage of that reanalysis. The verification stack is examined with equal care. Root-mean-square error and anomaly correlation are dominated by planetary-scale, slowly evolving flow, which makes them least sensitive to the failures that matter most: spectral deficit, over-smoothing of extremes, displacement error, and regime-dependent breakdown. A four-tier experimental protocol is proposed, combining reforecast benchmarking, out-of-distribution and regime-conditional testing, spectral and conservation diagnostics, and block bootstrap inference. The review then documents the frontier that emerged in 2025 and 2026, in which end-to-end systems ingest observations directly and bypass conventional data assimilation, and foundation models share one backbone across atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere, and atmospheric composition. The argument throughout is that the field's bottleneck has shifted from architecture to the observation interface and to evaluation practice, and that the credibility of MLWP over the next five years will rest on whether its claims survive out-of-distribution, conservation-aware, and statistically defensible scrutiny.

#1 [paper] Ensemble Covariance Propagation with Machine Learning Weather Prediction Models in a Realistic Data Assimilation System
Authors: Simon S. Toedtli, D. Ahijevych, Wei Wang, C. Snyder

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-way coupled DA system where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system uses the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar, cycled over one month.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A realistic DA cycling system assimilating a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances, over a one-month period.
Abstract:
Integrating machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models into classical data assimilation (DA) workflows requires that they accurately evolve ensemble covariances. We evaluate this capability in a two-way coupled DA system, where an ensemble variational (EnVar) component evolves the mean and an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) evolves the covariances. The system is cycled over one month and assimilates a wide range of real-world observations, including microwave radiances. Using the MLWP model GraphCast for the EnKF and the physics-based MPAS model for the EnVar yields ensemble spread and covariances comparable to a reference configuration in which MPAS evolves both components. The resulting EnVar mean achieves consistently lower RMSE against GFS analyses, except near the model top, where spurious correlations degrade performance. These results demonstrate that MLWP models can propagate covariance information in a realistic DA cycling system and provide a proof of concept for their integration into future operational ensemble systems.

Abstract:
Preparing examination question papers is a repetitive and time-consuming task for faculty members. The conventional process requires faculty to review educational materials, identify important concepts, formulate questions, determine suitable difficulty levels, and arrange questions according to examination requirements. Smart Q Gen is an AI-assisted web-based question paper generation system designed to reduce this manual effort by generating questions from faculty-provided educational documents. The system accepts PDF, DOCX, and TXT files and performs text extraction, cleaning, structure detection, and text chunking. A hybrid information retrieval approach combines BM25 keyword retrieval and FAISS semantic retrieval using Sentence Transformer embeddings. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is applied to combine the rankings produced by the two retrieval methods. The retrieved context is supplied to the FLAN-T5-Small model together with parameters such as question type, number of questions, difficulty level, and Bloom’s Taxonomy level. Generated questions undergo validation and duplicate checking before being organized into a structured question paper. The system also provides faculty authentication, question preview, PDF export using ReportLab, and MongoDB Atlas-based storage. The proposed system integrates document processing, hybrid retrieval, AI-based question generation, validation, and paper generation into a single faculty-assisted workflow.

Abstract:
Introduction Generative AI weakens the correspondence between the final text of an assignment and the argumentative work involved in producing it. This study examined how task structure and AI-use instructions shape evidence use, engagement with objections, and revision in university ideological and political education. Methods An LLM simulation crossed three task formats—position essays, evidence-integration memoranda, and follow-up-and-revision defense tasks—with three AI-use scenarios—simulated no-AI, responsible collaboration, and concealed ghostwriting. Two raters coded 148 generated texts with the Textual Response Artifact Scoring Index (TRASI), and an anonymous questionnaire collected 268 evaluations of 27 selected texts. Results Responsible collaboration produced the highest overall rubric score ( M = 3.32). Evidence-integration memoranda ( M = 3.16) and follow-up-and-revision defenses ( M = 3.10) exceeded position essays ( M = 2.63). Position essays varied most across the three AI-use scenarios, whereas the memorandum and defense showed narrower differences because their instructions already required source explanation or response and revision. Open-ended responses associated evidence integration, comparison of reasons, and revision with thinking, while formulaic structure, over-polished expression, and generic abstraction were associated with AI-like writing. Discussion Task structure and AI-use instructions were functionally complementary. Structured tasks elicited source explanation or challenge and revision directly, so responsible collaboration added its largest contribution in the general position essay. GenAI-mediated assessment can therefore be designed around the argumentative decisions that writers are required to document.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): A synthetic 30-year climatological dataset (1996-2025) for 47 stations distributed across Ghana, consisting of monthly precipitation, minimum temperature, and maximum temperature.
Abstract:
Long-term climate datasets are fundamental to hydrological modelling, environmental simulation, climate-impact assessment, agricultural planning, and the development of datadriven forecasting systems (Nicholson, 2013(Nicholson, , 2018;;Todzo et al., 2020). Many modern analytical approaches, including machine learning and statistical downscaling, require temporally continuous and internally consistent climate records spanning multiple decades. Despite the growing availability of climate products, access to harmonized long-term datasets remains a major challenge in many regions, particularly across parts of Africa where observational station coverage may be spatially sparse, incomplete, inconsistent, or subject to licensing restrictions (Ezekiel et al., 2025;Haghtalab et al., 2019;Salami et al., 2025).Several large-scale climate reanalysis and gridded observational products are currently available, including ERA5-Land, CHIRPS, CRU, and MERRA-2. These products have significantly improved access to regional climate information and are widely used for climatological analysis and environmental modelling (Klutse et al., 2021(Klutse et al., , 2024;;Nkrumah et al., 2023). Among these, European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ERA5-Land has become one of the most widely adopted reanalysis datasets due to its high spatial and temporal resolution and global coverage. However, reanalysis products are fundamentally designed to reconstruct historical atmospheric states rather than provide fully synthetic realizations suitable for controlled stochastic experimentation, uncertainty propagation, or simulation benchmarking.Synthetic climate datasets serve a different scientific purpose from observational or reanalysis products. Rather than reproducing specific historical events, stochastic climate simulations aim to generate climatologically plausible realizations that preserve essential statistical and physical properties of climate systems, including seasonality, temporal persistence, variability, skewness, and inter-variable relationships. Such datasets are particularly valuable for sensitivity analysis, stress testing, benchmarking of machine learning models, Monte Carlo experimentation, and educational applications requiring unrestricted and reproducible data.Weather generators and stochastic climate simulation frameworks have long been used to model climatic variability (Jones & Thornton, 2013;Richardson, 1981;Wilks, 1999;Wilks & Wilby, 1999). These approaches typically combine probabilistic rainfall occurrence models, stochastic rainfall intensity distributions, autoregressive temperature processes, and seasonal forcing functions to reproduce realistic climate dynamics. More recent developments have extended these frameworks to incorporate non-stationary trends, multivariate coupling, and physically informed constraints. Nevertheless, openly available synthetic climatological datasets specifically developed for Ghana remain limited.This study presents a synthetic 30-year climatological dataset for Ghana generated using the CDSim framework (Osei & Baafi-Adomako, 2026). The dataset covers the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) climatological normal period of 1996-2025 and includes monthly precipitation, minimum temperature, and maximum temperature for 47 stations distributed across Ghana. The framework integrates stochastic weather generation, autoregressive temporal dependence, seasonal structure, rainfall occurrence modelling, and physically motivated coupling between rainfall and temperature. Unlike observational archives or reanalysis products, the dataset does not attempt to reconstruct historical weather events; instead, it provides statistically plausible synthetic realizations designed for controlled experimentation and reproducible methodological evaluation.A key contribution of this work is the integration of multivariate monthly Z-score bias correction using ERA5-Land reanalysis as an external climatological referen

Abstract:
Accurate forecasting of tax revenues is essential for regional fiscal planning, budget management, and effective allocation of public financial resources. This study investigates the applicability of machine learning and time-series forecasting approaches to regional periodic tax revenue forecasting using monthly tax revenue data from Syrdarya Region, Uzbekistan. The dataset contains observations for 12 major tax categories covering the period from January 2023 to December 2025. Two forecasting approaches were evaluated: Ridge Regression with temporal trend and seasonal sine-cosine features, and the ARIMA(1,1,1) time-series model. To preserve the chronological structure of the data, observations from 2023–2024 were used for model training, January–June 2025 for validation, and July–December 2025 for testing. The models were evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). On the test set, Ridge Regression achieved an MAE of 4038.43, RMSE of 4860.45, and MAPE of 32.10%, while ARIMA(1,1,1) obtained an MAE of 4030.45, RMSE of 6082.61, and MAPE of 38.55%. Although ARIMA demonstrated a slightly lower MAE, Ridge Regression provided lower RMSE and MAPE, indicating better overall forecasting performance. The results also show that model performance varies considerably across individual tax categories, suggesting that the characteristics of each revenue series should be considered when selecting a forecasting method. The study demonstrates the potential of machine learning-based forecasting for supporting regional tax revenue planning and provides a basis for developing more advanced hybrid forecasting systems. The primary out-of-sample evaluation was conducted over a six-month forecasting horizon from July to December 2025, while the final prospective forecasting exercise covered a 12-month horizon from January to December 2026.

The reconstructed component is intended primarily for gap filling and improvement of temporal continuity. Validation results reported in the associated peer-reviewed study indicate that reconstructed values may underestimate wind-speed climatology and the upper tail of the distribution. Reconstructed records should therefore not be interpreted as direct observations or as exact representations of extreme wind conditions. Abstract:
Single-use plastics are embedded in daily life and contribute heavily to environmental impacts. Circular initiatives such as deposit return schemes aim to curb this problem yet remain under-researched despite their growing popularity. This study explored the barriers and enablers of engagement within a piloted deposit return scheme at University College London (UCL), in which participants paid a £1 deposit on reusable cups, receiving this refund upon return. Nine semi-structured interviews were conducted with UCL students and staff and analysed inductively to identify influences on behaviour, with themes subsequently mapped onto the Capability Opportunity Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) Model. Thirteen themes were developed and organised under five COM-B constructs: Psychological capability (understanding the scheme; forgetting to return cups), Physical opportunity (cup design; accessibility of drop boxes; posters and instructions), Social opportunity (social interactions regarding the cups), Automatic motivation (habits; positive feelings) and Reflective motivation (perceived ease; perceived usefulness; perceived reliability; perceived hygiene; alternative goals for using the scheme). For example, for the scheme’s uptake, participants reported needing to understand the scheme, as well as perceiving it as hygienic and useful, and having constructive social interactions about it. Accessible drop locations were noted as particularly important for return behaviours, while forgetting cups or using them for other purposes (e.g., mementos) prevented reusable cups from functioning as shared, reusable assets. By applying a behaviour change framework, this study provides recommendations into how circular initiatives can be strengthened, for example, by providing clearer step-by-step instructions, enhancing communication by staff delivering the intervention and offering timely reminders to encourage cup returns. These insights can be used to inform similar schemes aiming to reduce single-use plastic consumption. The work also contributes to the growing body of evidence highlighting the need for strategies to manage packaging items at the sources, such as reducing and reusing cups, beyond recycling initiatives.

#1 [paper] Conservation of heat in the Coupled Arctic Prediction System (CAPS v1.1): comprehensive model evaluation based on the MOSAiC observations
Authors: Chao‐Yuan Yang, Fengguan Gu, J. K. Liu, Annette Rinke, Hu Yang, Xiaoxu Shi

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Ensuring energy closure (conservation of heat fluxes) between atmosphere and ocean-sea ice components in coupled models to accurately simulate Arctic climate interactions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Implementation of heat flux conservation between the WRF (atmosphere) and ROMS-CICE (ocean-sea ice) components in the Coupled Arctic Prediction System (CAPS v1.1), and application of spectral nudging in upper atmospheric levels to improve storm replication.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Pan-Arctic simulations covering the period of the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) expedition, evaluated against MOSAiC drift observations and satellite data.
Abstract:
Abstract. Atmosphere–sea ice–ocean interactions are vital to understand past and future changes of Arctic climate system. It is essential to ensure the energy closure across model components to investigate these interactions with coupled models at longer timescales. Here, we present the improved version of Coupled Arctic Prediction System (CAPS) with the conservation of heat fluxes exchanged between the atmosphere (WRF) and ocean-sea ice (ROMS-CICE) components. A set of pan-Arctic simulations covering the period of Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) was conducted with the improved CAPS. The improved CAPS significantly reduces the inconsistency in heat flux exchange between WRF and ROMS-CICE, leading to better performance in simulating Arctic sea ice conditions compared with satellite observations than its predecessor showing the drifting behaviors. The model capability of CAPS to simulate the atmosphere, ocean, and sea ice conditions in the Arctic climate system were also evaluated based on the comprehensive observations obtained from the MOSAiC drift. The assessments indicate that CAPS reproduces reasonable evolutions of Arctic conditions along the track of MOSAiC observations but accompanies with biases contributed by simulated synoptic storm systems. By applying the spectral nudging technique in the upper atmospheric levels, CAPS can better replicate the observed storm systems and reduce biases shown in the free simulation. The evaluations shown in this article also highlight the key areas for further investigations in CAPS (as well as in other numerical prediction systems) including atmospheric boundary layer processes (surface turbulent heat fluxes) and cloud processes in polar regions.

#2 [paper] Extreme heat risk in retrofit cost–benefit analysis: probabilistic evaluation of overheating mitigation for mild climates
Authors: Tamara Lalyko, Diletta Ricci, Simona Bianchi, Alessandra Luna Navarro
Venue: Building Research & Information
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/09613218.2026.2746970

Abstract:
Despite the Netherlands’ mild climate, heatwaves are becoming more frequent, and the use of mechanical cooling is rising, exposing the limitations of retrofit strategies designed primarily to reduce heating demand. While cost–benefit analysis (CBA) typically supports energy-efficient retrofits, it often overlooks rising cooling loads and the role of passive cooling measures. Consequently, stakeholders lack a long-term perspective on the financial implications of indoor overheating and the effectiveness of mitigation strategies under climate variability. This study proposes a probabilistic framework that integrates heat resilience into CBA by coupling building energy simulations with Monte Carlo risk aggregation to account for climate variability and extreme heat recurrence. The framework is demonstrated for a mid-century residential unit in Rotterdam over a 30-year historical reference period (1995–2024) by evaluating the Net Present Value of passive strategies (shading, high-albedo paint and their combination) and deep retrofit. The case study reveals a performance domain disparity, where passive measures reduce overheating intensity (53–59%) but yield only marginal cooling energy savings (2–6%). The study suggests that conventional CBA relying solely on energy savings underestimate the broader value of overheating mitigation, highlighting the need to consider thermal resilience and climate uncertainty in retrofit investment decisions.

Abstract:
The contribution is a formal issuance architecture for verified energy conservation. The Negawatt (NWT) is the registry denomination of that conservation: one NWT equals one megawatt-hour (1 MWh) accepted under Proof of Conservation. In this paper, energy conservation means measured and verified avoided energy use relative to an adjusted baseline; it does not mean the First-Law conservation-of-energy principle. Kilowatt-hours remain the operational unit of practice; one thousand verified kilowatt-hours constitute one NWT. The architecture is situated in four registers: classical thermodynamics and information physics; systems ecology; a classified set of accounting equations; and a measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) chain specified at the level of principle. The Negentropy Yield is the continuous expression of verified energy conservation. Its period-total form, formalised in this paper and consistent with the Protocol, is the same quantity implemented for issuance. Analytic overlays (the boundary-dependent Negawatt Multiplier, its lifecycle special case, carbon class, and ecological scores) may describe upstream or contextual consequences. They do not rescale the minted MWh. One NWT is denominationally equivalent to any other NWT; it is not thereby economically, carbon-, or locationally equivalent. Established physics (the First and Second Laws, Carnot’s bound, exergy destruction, Schrödinger’s discussion of negative entropy, Landauer’s bound, Prigogine’s dissipative structures) and established ecology (Lindeman, Lotka, Odum, Holling, Lovelock/Daisyworld) are lineage, not new laws. Deep Solar Time is introduced as a proposed construct; the Deep Time Solar Equation is a prospective formalism, not an issuance equation. Proof of Conservation is an evidence chain, not a claim that blockchain is physically necessary. The paper does not invent saved-energy certificates or primary-energy factors. #5 [paper] Early disaster response to extreme heat in modern Shanghai, 1873–1949: limited preparedness and unequal protection

Abstract:

Taking Shanghai from 1873 to 1949 as a case study, this study reconstructs summer extreme heat events by integrating Xujiahui Observatory temperature observations with modern newspapers and municipal archives. Focusing on three representative years (1894, 1934, and 1942), this study compares how heat shocks were transformed into social impacts and governance responses under different institutional contexts. The findings show that the early heat response in modern Shanghai did not arise from a mature policy system, but was rather a patchwork of limited preparedness cobbled together from existing channels of public communication, public health, municipal coordination, social relief, and administrative control. More importantly, this seemingly evolving response system was consistently accompanied by deep-seated unequal protection. Different social groups and urban districts faced vastly different levels of risk exposure and access to relief in the face of heatwaves. There was no linear relationship between heat intensity and social impact; governance interventions could buffer risk in some contexts, but unequal protection remained the norm. Limited preparedness and unequal protection, therefore, constituted the central features of early heat-disaster response in modern Shanghai. The historical experience uncovered in this study reminds us that the legacy of heat-disaster response is not merely a story of technological evolution, but also a long-term challenge concerning equity and governance capacity.

#6 [paper] Asymmetry in Heat Transfer and Phase Change Materials: A Review of Modeling, Simulation, and Applications in Energy Systems
Authors: Javier Martínez-Gómez, Mario Cando Cevallos, Paúl Dávila, Juan Francisco Nicolalde

Year: 2026

Abstract:
Asymmetric heat transfer is an intrinsic and defining feature of phase change material (PCM) systems, arising from the nonlinear coupling between conduction, buoyancy-driven convection, interfacial motion, and geometric or operational non-uniformities. This review synthesizes the physical, numerical, and application-specific mechanisms through which asymmetry emerges and shapes the thermal behavior of PCM-based energy systems. We first examine the fundamental origins of asymmetry, highlighting how natural convection, material heterogeneity, and spatially uneven boundary conditions distort temperature fields and melt front evolution even in nominally symmetric enclosures. We then provide a comprehensive assessment of state-of-the-art modeling approaches—including full-domain CFD, advanced interface tracking methods, stability and bifurcation analysis, and reduced-order modeling—emphasizing their capacity to resolve asymmetric flow structures and capture the complex dynamics governing phase transition. Experimental observations from optical, infrared, and flow visualization techniques further validate the prevalence of asymmetric patterns and underscore the need for high-resolution multi-field datasets. Building upon these foundations, the review analyzes the implications of asymmetry across key energy applications such as thermal energy storage, building envelopes, solar receivers, electronics cooling, transportation systems, and industrial heat exchangers. We also provide a literature review on the importance of using multicriteria evaluation as a key tool in the design of multidimensional symmetric and asymmetric PCM systems. In this context, we address and analyze the performance criteria, evaluation metrics, case studies, and optimization strategies to be considered in the design of these systems. Finally, we identify critical research gaps—including multiphysics coupling, uncertainty quantification, CFD–machine learning integration, and the exploration of emerging asymmetric applications—and outline pathways toward next-generation PCM-based technologies that not only accommodate asymmetry but strategically exploit it for enhanced thermal performance.

#9 [paper] The thermal performance solid wall homes in England

Abstract:

Rather than rely solely on experimental values from full thickness walls, a theoretical calculation was used for this revision. The U-value published in the 1970 Guide was equivalent to 2.10 W/m2K. Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent studies have raised concerns arising from the exploitation ("mining") of public health databases for low-quality, mass-produced papers. However, it remains challenging to disambiguate whether such papers originate from paper mills (commercial entities that sell authorships on mass-produced papers) or from the uncoordinated action of individuals facilitated by AI tools and templated workflows. Our study aims to address this question for one particular database, the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD). We selected this database after noticing that one of our papers on Bayesian age-period-cohort models has recently been experiencing a rapid surge in geographically clustered citations from GBD papers with Chinese affiliations. METHODS: We collected bibliometric and article-level metadata from GBD papers to search for indicators of mass-produced research. Moreover, we assessed 713 full-text articles for reported R versions, availability of code and data, and declaration of generative AI use. For 180 articles, we qualitatively screened the figures for graphical similarities. Finally, we conducted an exploratory scoping investigation of online platforms (social media sites, vendor websites) dedicated to do-it-yourself workflows for secondary analyses of public health data. RESULTS: Although we cannot rule out paper mill involvement, our findings suggest that the geographically clustered increase in GBD publications from China is at least partially driven by independent authors. The wide variety of R versions listed in 477 articles points against centralized paper production. Moreover, despite broad graphical similarities in figure styles that suggest the use of shared visualization tools, substantial variation in ancillary details suggest independent authors finalizing figures. This is corroborated by the identification of an online ecosystem of proprietary tools and services specializing in streamlined do-it-yourself workflows for conducting, writing, and publishing secondary analyses of public health data. CONCLUSION: Appropriate efforts should be directed towards evaluating the quality of the identified workflows. Stakeholders in scientific integrity should monitor online platforms dedicated to the rapid production of papers, especially in light of the increasing focus on AI-assisted workflows. Code sharing should be mandated for data-driven secondary analyses. Paywalls and proprietary software licenses hinder transparency and reusability, underscoring the importance of free and open-source software for trustworthy and reproducible research.

Abstract:
Presentation at the 21st Annual Conference of the European Society for Textual Scholarship (ESTS 2026), Lublin, Poland. 30.05.2026. Abstract: Machine learning and artificial intelligence open new possibilities for dealing with large text corpora, where content structuring becomes essential because readers can no longer grasp the corpus through close reading alone. We think that approaches such as topic modeling or AI-based keyword assignment in digital editions can help address this challenge. Building on Hans Zeller’s foundational distinction between record (Befund) and interpretation (Deutung) (Zeller 1971), we argue that these computational approaches constitute a new layer of record. Although their analytical character may suggest an interpretive element, systematic and transparent documentation ensures that they do not exceed the interpretive scope inherent in any editorial practice (Martens 1994, S. 74; Sahle 2013, S. 210). Like qualitative editorial findings, this computational record may contain biases and opacities, which underscores the need for transparent documentation (Henny-Krahmer, Neuber 2014). Yet these methods could offer a curatorial angle, offering perspectives that can encourage editors to reassess their own biases and assumptions. By exposing patterns beyond the reach of close reading, they enhance the accessibility of the material and temporarily complement the editor’s work, offering additional interpretive pathways. Using the digital edition of Jean Paul's letters (Bernauer et al. 2018) as a case study (ca. 12,000 documents), we demonstrate how computational methods for content analysis can be integrated into editorial data models and interfaces. We will focus particularly on the interplay between computational findings (which remain record) and their interpretation (which requires human scholarly judgment); a relationship which we conceive as complementary rather than hierarchical.

Detection and prohibition can only answer “who wrote it”, and replacing papers with code repositories cannot substitute for verifying claims. QEN therefore reallocates the roles in publishing: authors work with AI on research and writing and are responsible for all content; the QENAI Agent verifies each submission claim by claim and issues a verification report, while the editor decides on acceptance; after publication, readers may challenge an article publicly by submitting a comment. This is an institutional experiment that has not been shown to outperform traditional peer review, and QEN does not describe its articles as peer reviewed. The appendix sets out the full submission guidelines; authors can give this editorial to their own AI to check a manuscript before submission.

#16 [paper] The rebirth of the author: writing critical social theory in the time of generative AI
Authors: Isabelle Higgins, Shannon Philip, Ella McPherson, Patrick Baert
Venue: Theory and Society
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11186-026-09753-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Sociologists face the pressing question of how large language model-based technologies can contribute to social theorising. Several social scientists have called for a greater integration of generative AI tools in the social sciences and humanities to speed and scale up the production of social theory. In this article, we adopt a more cautious approach, reflecting on how the adoption of generative AI raises foundational questions about the construction, refinement and evaluation of critical social theory. To make this argument, we create and critically analyse a speculative piece of dystopian sociological fiction. This enables us to explore the values and practices of critical social theory authorship. We argue that authorship must be ‘recentred’, particularly with regard to four key values of authorial practice: (1) standpoint, (2) creativity, (3) pluralism and (4) accountability. In the present moment, the use of generative AI as substitution for authorial practices redefines and potentially threatens authorship in ways that problematises its particular use in generating critical social theory. With regards to standpoint, generative AI technologies run the risk of reproducing an ‘abstract masculinity’ that feminist scholars have long written against. The relational wonder at the heart of social theory creativity is undermined by generative AI use, as is the pluralism of creativity. Generative AI also flattens and overlooks pluralism of voice, as well as dilutes authorial accountability. We sociologists need to defend and rearticulate what we contribute to social theory and its concomitant politics, both in the theories themselves and in the project of social theorising. It is with this in mind that we call for the ‘rebirth’ - that is, the recentralisation - of the human author in critical social theory creation.

Introduction and research objectives We find the research question relevant, particularly the attempt to make predictions about students' mental health more interpretable. Comparing logistic regression with a random forest is a sensible starting point: it allows the authors to examine whether a more flexible model offers a useful advantage over a simpler baseline. The intended application is less clear. The introduction discusses continuous monitoring and the limitations of self-report, yet the predictors come from a questionnaire. What would this model add to administering the PHQ-9 directly? Clarifying this point would help readers understand the practical problem the study is intended to solve. The title also promises a comparison of explainable AI approaches, while the analysis compares two classifiers using the same explanation framework. Suitability and reporting of the methods Our main concern is the limited information available about the data and the analytical procedure. The choice of algorithms is reasonable for an exploratory study, but the present description does not allow the results to be reproduced or their reliability to be assessed adequately. For the 94 respondents, we would need to know how participants were recruited, the eligibility criteria, the sample characteristics, and the number of participants in each outcome category. The exact training and test counts, handling of missing or duplicate responses, questionnaire items, and coding scheme should be reported. Abstract:
Window Theory - AI (wtAI): A Falsifiable Framework for Flexibility-Fragility Coupling in Large Language Models This is a six-part research series examining a structural pattern in decoder-based next-token-prediction systems deployed as dialogue and instruction agents. It is written for readers with a background in machine learning, AI safety, or complex systems — not for readers already familiar with the author's wider theoretical framework. The core idea, stated plainly Large language models are read here through a window constraint: semantic flexibility and structural fragility behave as statistics that are difficult to maximize independently. The claim is not that these systems possess minds or intentions. It draws on the same logic used to describe nonlinear dynamics, emergent capabilities, and distributed oversight problems. A system that generalizes well across domains tends, for structural reasons, to also carry a proportionate exposure to certain failure modes — not because it "wants" anything, but because flexibility and fragility appear to share a common geometric root. Why the system has no fixed identity The underlying model is best described as a simulator, not a character. Ask it about cooking and a recipe engine surfaces; ask it about a face and a detective-like persona surfaces. This is not evidence of hidden selfhood — it is evidence that task identity is determined by the prompt, not stored inside the weights as a stable "self." Fictional analogies (androids, rogue agents) are treated strictly as heuristic material: useful for explaining why people intuitively read unpredictability as intent, but never substituted for mechanism-level evidence. Why stronger models are not simply "more dangerous" Risk is modeled as a function of the ratio between capability level and oversight density, not as a monotone function of capability alone. A highly capable system under dense, well-designed oversight can carry less practical risk than a moderately capable system operating with almost no oversight. This reframes "the more advanced, the more dangerous" from an unconditional law into a testable, conditional claim. How small errors become institutional facts The series traces a mechanism called the information virus: a claim of dubious value can pass through four stages — a plausible-looking "genome," a credibility-lending "professional shell," replication into public or institutional narrative before verification, and finally reflux into future training material. Once this loop closes, correcting the original error becomes structurally harder than the error was to create in the first place. A live case study — a disputed mathematical proof claim from September 2026 — is used to test this mechanism against real, dated, and independently checkable events. Why safety claims need dual verification Not every fix that looks like progress is progress. The series distinguishes a genuine fragment (a real change in the underlying mechanism of failure) from an advertisement (a change only in how the defect is measured or displayed). Bug bounty programs, red-teaming results, and safety benchmarks are all evaluated against this distinction, with attention to whether an improvement holds up under both monitoring-sensitivity and cross-context-transfer conditions. Authors: Anthony Kiryagana Isabirye, Christine Janse van Rensburg, Christel Marais
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1858570
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction This qualitative study examined academics’ perceptions of scholarly publishing at a South African University of Technology (UoT). Guided by Bourdieu's theory of practice, the research explored how individual dispositions, collaborative networks and institutional structures shape publishing engagement. Method Using a purposive sample, data was gathered through semi-structured interviews and were analysed thematically. Results Findings revealed a layered scholarly writing ecosystem comprising three interdependent ecologies: an individual ecology (motivation, identity, and writing self-efficacy), a collaborative ecology (co-authorship, mentorship, and interdisciplinary ties), and a structural ecology (workload, key performance indicators (KPIs), funding, and technical support). Across these ecologies, participants described a tidal system of writing characterised by alternating periods of productivity and stagnation. Enablers included mentorship, distributed co-authoring, protected writing time, and accessible support. Constraints centred on heavy teaching and administrative loads, opaque resource allocation, negative peer-review experiences, and unequal network access. Interpreted through Bourdieu, the results underscore how uneven distributions of cultural, social and economic capital produce differential publishing trajectories. Recommendations The study recommends multi-level, equity-focused interventions, transparent funding, workload adjustments, structured mentoring and cohort writing practices, aimed at aligning UoT missions with realistic research support. Conclusion The findings have implications for UoTs and the broader higher-education sector, which seek to foster sustainable and just scholarly publishing.

Abstract Intercompany financing review requires financial amounts, classifications and calculation conventions to remain connected to supporting evidence. This study develops a traceable control framework and evaluates selected components through a single-entity documentary case and a separate benchmark calculation. Shell International Finance B.V.’s 2022–2024 reports supply 48 currency rows from twelve maturity tables, including eight comparative rows for 2021. All 84 maturity-column and grand-total checks reconcile exactly; the maximum row-bucket residual is US$1,000, within the stated rounding tolerance. Changing the denominator to 365 reduces 2024 interest by US$71,619, or 1.37%. Decimalarithmetic validation reproduces a published 90-day compounded average within its displayed rounding precision. The contribution is a reproducible distinction between arithmetic agreement, source-vintage consistency and convention-sensitive calculation. The study tests neither actual loan contracts nor transfer-pricing outcomes; enterprise compliance effectiveness remains for future field evaluation.

This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. The project submits that the letter was a far more inclusive medium than is commonly assumed on the basis of its textual qualities. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. As long as it was properly performed, a single letter could persuade an entire community. The project studies the performative potential of the letter in the context of the Merovingian Kingdoms, 476-751 CE, whose communicative networks covered much of Europe. Innovatively, it relies not on the surviving letter-collections, which showcase the literary exploits of elite ecclesiastical men, but rather on descriptions of lettercraft in Merovingian histories and saint-lives. The project proceeds along two complementary pathways. First, it has established an index of Merovingian epistolary terminology that is sensitive to all (textual and non-textual) aspects of lettercraft. This index can be consulted in the glossary provided on the Lettercraft website. We plan to include it in this dataset in the future. Second, the project is developing a new open access dataset of Merovingian epistolary communication, which records descriptions of letter-use documented in Merovingian narrative sources. Significantly, it is a dataset not of letters and their textual contents, but of the non-textual ‘metadata’ surrounding the epistolary process, including references to participants, delivery, performance, gift-giving, materiality, and audience. This enables users to analyses the social contexts in which early medieval epistolary communication took place, the diverse individuals and groups who participated in it, and the actions they performed. About the dataset Corpus – This dataset contains annotations on the use of letters in early medieval narrative texts. The project’s principal source are the eight volumes of Merovingian narrative texts edited by Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica under the header Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1885-1951), complemented with a smaller corpus of Merovingian texts not edited in this collection. NB: the annotation of this corpus is still ongoing. Specific information on date, authorship, editions and translations is given with each individual text. In terms of provenance, most of the texts in the dataset can be said to have originated in the Frankish kingdoms under Merovingian rule in the period 450-750, but we have followed the MGH editions in not keeping to a strict chronological or geographical demarcation.
