Abstract:
Associate Professor, Department of Government The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in many consolidated democracies today poses a unique challenge. Political parties and leaders who enjoy popular support risk tearing apart the democratic fabric through tactics that appear lawful and are often invisible. What options do democracies have to defend themselves against such actors? Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. Political parties may exclude antidemocratic parties from coalitions, or they may choose to include them while seeking to moderate their positions. Alternatively, they may focus on expanding social protections in order to address the structural injustices that antidemocratic actors exploit. Such choices raise difficult normative questions. This book offers conceptual tools for making these choices intelligible and brings to light the principles that animate them. Political theorists addressing these issues have paid a great deal of attention to justifying repressive measures. Militant democracy, which includes the pre-emptive restriction of political and civil rights, has received so much attention in the past decade that one would be forgiven for thinking there is no alternative. This book is partly a reaction to this one-sided engagement with repressive measures. It examines less-known approaches to democratic self-defence that prioritise toleration and social integration respectively, strategies that are used as much, if not more, than militant restrictions. The three rationales of democratic self-defence that emerge –militant, tolerant, and social– are presented as ideal types. Unlike much theorising on democratic self-defence, which is prescriptive and advances a single normative framework, this book adopts a deliberately comparative approach that examines the strengths and weaknesses of each ideal type, as well as their connections and contrasts. It proposes conceptual definitions and analyses the normative justifications underpinning each type. The aim is to clarify the principles embodied in practices of democratic self-defence, enabling actors to better understand the normative commitments behind their choices and to make decisions that are ethically justified, democratically legitimate, and consistent with the values they seek to defend. The book also seeks to move the discussion beyond legal instruments and state responses by bringing broader societal and public actors into view. At the same time, it remains focused on agency: on both defenders of democracy and those who seek to undermine it. In doing so, it resists the tendency to portray democracy as a quasi-natural system whose resilience must simply be enhanced. Unlike many studies framed around the concept of democratic resilience, this book foregrounds human agency and the diverse actors who actively defend democracy across multiple spheres. Decisions about whether and how to confront antidemocratic actors do not fall exclusively on any single category of actor. They concern government authorities, courts, state agencies, municipal leaders, business actors, journalists, academics, and others. Democratic self-defence should therefore be understood as a form of agency distributed across a variety of actors. Abstract:
The Marine Geology and Geophysics Core Program supports research on all aspects of the geology and geophysics of the present ocean basins and margins, as well as those of the Great Lakes.

The Program supports science that includes:

- Structure, composition, tectonics, and evolution of the oceanic lithosphere

- Paleoceanography, paleoclimate, and sea level change

- Submarine volcanology, petrology and geochemistry of the oceanic crust and upper mantle lithosphere

- Marine hydrogeology, water-rock interaction, seeps and gas hydrates

- Hydrothermal venting and in situ fluid processes, and associated geochemistry

- Geochemical indicators of life operating below the seafloor

- Marine sedimentology, stratigraphy, sediment transport, and diagenesis

- Mid-ocean ridge spreading, back-arc rifting, transform processes, and ocean island/seamount formation and evolution

- Submarine components of subduction zone systems and passive margins

- Marine geohazards (e.g., earthquakes, faulting, mass wasting, geological aspects of tsunamis)

- Coastal processes (e.g., geological aspects of hurricanes, sea-level change, erosion, offshore deposition)

The Marine Geology and Geophysics Program supports acquisition of new field data and the leveraging of and/or synthesis of existing data. The program supports analytical and laboratory experimental projects, methods development, and modeling. All activities should have relevance to and advance the understanding of marine geoscience processes. The Program interfaces with NSF programs across the Geosciences and across the Agency. For proposals that cross between Programs, proposers should contact the relevant Programs to seek guidance on submission.

#2 [paper] HOMEROS seismology notebook - 'Project funded by OSCARS - HOMEROS'
Authors: Vasilis Anagnostou, Eleftheria E. Papadimitriou, V. Karakostas
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22745992
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
An open, end-to-end Jupyter notebook that builds an earthquake catalogue from continuous seismic waveforms using machine-learning phase picking. Starting from nothing but a station list and a date range, it downloads open FDSN data, picks P and S arrivals with a neural network, associates them into events, estimates local magnitudes, and exports a catalogue, a map, and a phase file ready for double-difference relocation. The demo region is the central Ionian Islands and western mainland Greece, one of the study areas of the HOMEROS project (Harmonising Observations from Multi-hazard Environments in Research for Open Science). Nothing in the workflow is specific to that region: the search area, station list, and date range are all parameters in a single configuration cell. What the notebook does The workflow is organised as a daily batch pipeline, so it scales to long time spans without running out of memory. Each stage corresponds to a section of the notebook. Station metadata. A response-level StationXML inventory is requested from the configured FDSN providers (NOA, with EIDA as fallback). Wildcard channel requests are expanded against the inventory into exact three-component triplets, so only channels that actually exist are requested. The inventory is cached and reused on later runs. Daily waveform download. For each day, one folder is created and filled with one full-day (86 400 s) MiniSEED file per component. Each trace is merged, padded, resampled to a common sampling rate, detrended, and instrument-response-corrected at download time. Downloads run in a thread pool, fall back across providers, skip files already present, and record the outcome of every request in a per-day JSON manifest. Phase picking. PhaseNet is applied through SeisBench using the pre-trained INSTANCE weights. The network outputs continuous P and S probability traces, converted to discrete picks at a configurable threshold. A CUDA device is used automatically when available. Association. Picks are grouped into events with PyOcto, using 4D space–time partitioning over the configured latitude, longitude and depth volume with a homogeneous velocity model. Association runs day by day on a station table filtered to the stations that produced picks that day. Local magnitude. For each event, the horizontal components of each contributing station are simulated to a Wood–Anderson instrument, the peak amplitude is measured in a 3 s window anchored on the S pick, and a station ML is computed with a standard distance correction. The event magnitude is the median of the station values. Figures and export. The notebook maps epicentres and stations, plots associated picks per station, and writes a hypoDD-format phase file ready for double-difference relocation. Demo run The notebook is archived with the outputs of a two-day run over 23 requested stations from networks HT, HL, HP and HA, covering 1–2 March 2026: 3 494 PhaseNet picks, 28 associated events, and a local magnitude for every event. Two days is a demonstration size; the same notebook runs unchanged over months of data by changing a single parameter, since the per-day loop releases waveform memory and clears the GPU cache between days. Outputs Per-day and merged pick tables, pick-to-event assignment tables, and an event catalogue in CSV, with one row per event giving origin time (UTC), latitude, longitude, depth, ML, and the number of stations used. Per-day download manifests and a processing summary recording traces, picks and events per day. An epicentre and station map, a picks-per-station figure, and a hypoDD-format phase file. Scope and caveats This is a teaching and demonstration workflow, not a production catalogue pipeline. Hypocentres are association-grade: they come from a homogeneous velocity model and are meant to be good enough to group picks, not to be final, which is why a hypoDD phase file is exported. Magnitudes are approximate, using a non-local distance correction with no station correct

#3 [paper] A novel approach for evaluating scientific productivity and visibility of FP7 projects: the complementarity of reported publications and funding acknowledgement
Authors: Niliek Silva Alés, Antonio Perianes‐Rodríguez
Venue: Revista española de Documentación Científica
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3989/redc.2026.3.1905
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Research funding is crucial for fostering scientific collaboration, ensuring that the objectives defined in scientific policies are met and determining the influence of research within the scientific community. The Seventh Framework Programme (FP7) was the European Union’s main funding instrument for the 2007-2013 period. This macro programme was structured into specific schemes to strengthen European economic growth, sustainability and global leadership. The main goal of this study is to analyse European funding and its scientific productivity based on funded projects and publications. The metadata on funding required thorough data cleaning, and the three open sources used‒CORDIS, Open Funder Registry (OFR) and Research Organisation Registry (ROR)‒had to be standardised. The FP7 project list was imported into a relational database, and the EurSciVoc taxonomy was used to evaluate the data by discipline areas. More than two out of three projects were funded under three schemes: FP7-PEOPLE, FP7-IDEAS-ERC and FP7-ICT. One third of the projects with funding acknowledgements in OFR had no publications reported in CORDIS. These new unreported publications had a significant influence on their scientific fields, adding another 60% to the tallies of projects, publications and funding. The results confirm the advantages of evaluating funding activities using several open data sources.

#4 [paper] The MESOSCAN Dataset: A Collection of Mesofauna Images from UK Forest and Peatland Soils

Abstract:
A UK forest and peatland soil mesofauna image dataset collected by Forest Research from 2024 to 2025 onwards. Mesofauna are arthropods that live in the soil ranging from approximately 2mm down to 0.2mm in size. Their biodiversity is a key indicator to the health and sustainability of the soil. This dataset is a systematic attempt at collecting and curating valuable images that can be used to help recognise specimens, and to provide training data to machine learning systems that can substantially automate identification and make monitoring more scalable. An example, baseline, machine learning model is provided to validate the data and to illustrate how it can be used - see the ./notebooks folder for this. Highlights: Currently 2600+ training images across 35 taxa each 1600x1600 pixels. Samples were currated from 21 sites across the UK with specimens taxonmically identified prior to imaging. Emphasis has been on creating a varied and extensive range of views for a number of specimens. A selection of realistic and independent test image are provided from cluttered assemblages. Structure The dataset is principally focused on mites (Acari) and springtails (Collembola) which together make up of the majority of mesofauna biomass of soil samples. Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals should demonstrate the following expected outcomes:

- A sound understanding of the specific needs of industrial users (including but not limited to innovative SMEs, startups and scaleups) for Technology infrastructure services in specific priority areas including but not limited to advanced materials, clean energy, or health and biotechnology;

- Increased opportunities for industrial users for development, testing, up-scaling and deployment of new technologies via the use of services offered by Technology Infrastructures;

- Strengthened innovation and technology development capacity of European SMEs, startups and scaleups via improved access to Technology Infrastructures;

- Attractiveness and effectiveness of the developed access schemes for broadening the range of Technology Infrastructures users, especially for startups and scaleups, including with transnational access.

Scope:

Startups, scaleups and other innovative SMEs require access to state-of-the-art research and technology facilities, equipment and expertise to test, upscale, validate new products and technologies, shortening the time-to-market and increasing the chances for a successful commercialisation. Access mechanisms to Technology Infrastructures as well as access contracts and collaboration or service provision agreements are often complex, while the costs of using such infrastructures can significantly surpass the financial capacities of growing innovative companies.

The action will develop and test pilot multi-site access schemes for startups, scaleups and other innovative SMEs, involving a critical mass of Technology Infrastructures operators and users in priority areas (including but not limited to advanced materials, clean energy, or health and biotechnology). It should build on existing initiatives with already developed single access points to a comprehensive set of facilities and services in a selected technology area, like for example Open Innovation Test Beds or other integrated networks, that allow for a quick deployment of a common access scheme.

The action should include setting-up a pilot centrally managed and funded access programme, allowing companies quick access to the needed services, with simplified and standardised access conditions applicable across the EU, to be coordinated and in line with the work on the envisaged European Charter of access for industrial users to research and technology infrastructures. While the focus shall be the provision of access and support services to companies, the action can also include enhancing the accessibility and usability of technology infrastructure services to ensure that they meet the evolving needs of users.

The action should aim at significant broadening of the user base of the technology infrastructures to address the needs of startups and scaleups that do not have access to such facilities in their local ecosystems. To this end, proposals should include the development and implementation of activities to increase the visibility and promote and demonstrate the uptake of technology infrastructures services provided to users across the EU.

Furthermore, proposals should aim to enhance transnational and multisite collaboration among Technology Infrastructures fostering the building of technology infrastructures ecosystems, the sharing of experience, resources, and best practices in management, service offer, staff exchange and networking. Proposals may also benefit, especially for communication and dissemination activities, from sharing best practices and taking stock of what other relevant projects are developing in the field of Technology Infrastructures.

#7 [paper] doi:10.70132/j7356948637
Venue: Insights into Regional Development
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.70132/j7356948637
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Africa's development financing has been shaped by traditional international institutions such as the Bretton Woods Institutions (BWIs) and newer entities, such as the New Development Bank (NDB), established by the BRICS countries.The BWIs, particularly the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, have provided critical financial support.Still, they are often criticised for their rigid conditionalities, which limit African countries' autonomy in development planning.In contrast, the NDB offers a more flexible, partnership-driven approach despite facing governance and institutional capacity challenges.The study explores the feasibility and challenges of collaboration between BWIs and the NDB to fund development projects in Africa.Addressing a gap in the literature, the research investigates how these institutions can work together to create a more balanced and effective development model that prioritises both economic growth and social development.The problem lies in the stark differences between the BWIs' conditionality-driven model and the NDB's evolving governance structures, which present challenges to achieving sustainable development in Africa.Utilising a qualitative research design, the study gathered data through semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders, including policymakers and development experts, and document analysis of institutional reports.Findings indicate that while BWIs' strict conditionalities promote fiscal discipline, they often undermine social development by prioritising short-term economic goals.Conversely, the NDB's flexibility supports greater local ownership but struggles with governance and accountability issues.Both institutions are influenced by the geopolitical interests of their dominant member states, complicating their effectiveness in promoting Africa's long-term development.Recommendations include creating a hybrid financing model that combines the financial discipline of BWIs with the flexibility of the NDB, strengthening governance through joint capacity-building initiatives to address institutional capacity gaps, and ensuring that development projects align with Africa's long-term strategic goals.Future research should focus on longitudinal studies to assess the lasting impacts of these institutions on sustainable development outcomes in Africa.

#8 [paper] The nature and evolution of EU funds for migration and asylum: introducing the MigFund dataset 2000–2023
Authors: Federica Zardo
Venue: European Political Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s168209832610068x
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract This article introduces the MigFund dataset, a comprehensive resource that traces the European Union’s financial commitments to migration and asylum from 2000 to 2023. Developed in response to long-standing calls to ‘follow the money’ in EU migration governance, the dataset records over 1,700 funding measures across internal and external programmes, disaggregated by sub-policy area, target group, geographic scope, and degree of restrictiveness. Drawing on the literature on policy tools, the article conceptualises EU funding as an expression of institutional preferences, bureaucratic negotiation and strategic framing, shaping and shaped by evolving policy priorities. A key contribution of the dataset is its coding of each measure along a restrictive-to-open continuum, enabling researchers to assess how EU financial tools promote either mobility and protection or containment and control. The article details the dataset’s structure and coding logic and presents key descriptive findings on the evolution of EU funding, showing a steady expansion of resources and increasing complexity in the programming landscape. Through this empirical lens, the article invites a reconsideration of financial instruments as autonomous policy tools, capable of reinforcing, offsetting or reconfiguring broader migration policy logics. MigFund thus provides a basis for macro- and meso-level analyses of funds in EU studies, migration studies and public policy more broadly.

#10 [paper] From financial autonomy to performance-based funding for sustainable development financing of higher education institutions in Uzbekistan
Authors: Ziyodakhon Abdualimova, Rakhmatilla Kholmuradov, Sharifa Hamroyeva, Hilola Yusupova, Nilufar Valiyeva
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1920875
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The expansion of HEIs in Uzbekistan has generated a new finance problem: universities must expand access, develop research capacity and modernise infrastructure with still-constrained public budgets. This paper presents a policy-oriented model relating financial autonomy to sustainable development funding of HEIs during Uzbekistan's shift from cost-based to rating-linked performance funding. The study presents the Financial Autonomy and Development Capacity Index (FADCI), combining revenue autonomy, expenditure flexibility, research financing, infrastructure capacity and governance readiness, corroborated by expert AHP weighting and piloted on six HEIs. The analysis suggests that performance-based funding from 2027 is likely to promote sustainable development financing only if autonomy is combined with transparent data, equalisation, internal audit capacity and mission-sensitive metrics. The methodology can be replicated by emerging higher education systems moving from budget dependence to accountable financial autonomy.

Abstract:
Paediatric HIV outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) have significantly improved over the past two decades, largely due to donor-funded programmes that promote early infant diagnosis (EID), antiretroviral therapy (ART), and community-based service delivery. Despite these achievements, many countries in the region remain highly dependent on external donor financing, raising concerns about the sustainability of paediatric HIV services during periods of funding uncertainty. Transition frameworks should prioritise paediatric service continuity, strengthen health-system resilience, and align financing responsibilities between donors and governments to reduce preventable child morbidity and mortality.

Abstract:
The Graduate College's Dissertation Completion Fellowships help outstanding Illinois graduate students complete the doctoral degree by providing a 9-month* stipend of $25,000 along with waivers of tuition, service fee, health service fee, AFMFA fee, library/IT fee. In addition, the fellow will receive partial payment of the graduate student health insurance fee per semester as well as basic dental and vision coverage. The number of awards offered will depend on the level of funding available. *Note that, starting in 2026-27, the standard duration of the fellowship period will shift from 12 months to 9 months. If, however, an awardee wishes for funds to be disbursed over 12 months, that is allowable. Should the awardee end up depositing before the end of the 12 month period, though, any remaining funds will be forfeited. The intent of the fellowship is to help students complete their dissertations. Accordingly, awardees are discouraged from holding multiple waiver-generating appointments. The criteria used in making the awards include the significance of the research, as reflected in the nominee’s proposal and the letters of support, the student's productivity and efficient progress toward the degree as shown in the academic record, and the likelihood that the student will defend and deposit the dissertation by August 2028. Departmental distribution of awards will also be taken into account. The fellowship period runs August 16, 2027 to May 15, 2028.

Abstract:
The Fulbright-Hays DDRA Fellowship Program, funded by the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and administered by the International and Foreign Language Education (IFLE) Office, provides opportunities for graduate students to conduct full-time dissertation research abroad in modern foreign languages and area studies. ED defines "area studies" as a "program of comprehensive study of the aspects of a society or societies, including the study of their geography, history, culture, economy, politics, international relations, and languages." Eligible Regions and Countries: Allowable projects are those that focus on one or more of the following geographic areas: Africa, East Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands, South Asia, the Near East, Central and Eastern Europe and Eurasia, and the Western Hemisphere (excluding the United States and its territories). Projects Not Allowable: Applications for research focused on the following countries are not eligible: Andorra, Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, San Marino, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, and Vatican City. Note that it may be possible to conduct research in Western Europe, provided the project itself is focused on another world region. Projects in countries designated as "closed" by Fulbright-Hays are ineligible. See the "Maintenance Allowances" section in the FY 2025 DDRA Application Instructions for details. Applications for projects in countries currently designated by the Department of State with a Level 4 travel advisory may be submitted, but awardees may end up having their travel plans delayed or canceled due to travel restrictions. Applicants may propose research projects lasting from 6 to 12 consecutive months. Projects may begin as early as January 1, 2026 and must end by March 31, 2027. Students do not apply directly to the Department of Education for these awards. Instead, applications must be submitted on behalf of the applicant by the student's institution of higher education (IHE). Students must therefore work closely with their IHE for an application to be submitted successfully.

Abstract:
The Graduate College's Dean’s Doctoral Fellowship (DDF) supports the recruitment of academically talented students whose educational pathways and experiences may include financial, institutional, or other barriers to graduate education. The fellowship reflects the Graduate College’s commitment to expanding access to graduate education and strengthening the Illinois graduate community by recruiting students from many educational, geographic, and familial backgrounds. The DDF provides financial support to students who demonstrate strong potential for success in graduate study and whose pathways to graduate education reflect significant barriers or nontraditional routes. Through this recruitment fellowship, the Graduate College seeks to expand opportunities for talented students to pursue doctoral education at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and to connect fellowship recipients with programs and resources that support their transition to and success in graduate education. Eligibility and Selection Criteria DDFs are intended as recruitment fellowships. To that end, only those students who are seeking admission to a doctoral program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (Illinois) are eligible. #20 [paper] The need for, feasibility of, and barriers to implementation of a trauma traveling fellowship: a survey of ESTES members
Authors: Jared M. Wohlgemut, S.C. Gupta, Stefano P. B. Cioffi, Heura Llaquet Bayo, Helen S. Wohlgemut, Jonathan Hobby, Shahin Mohseni, Diego Mariani
Venue: European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-026-03321-2
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Purpose Many European surgeons lack access to high-volume trauma training. A Trauma Traveling Fellowship, supported by the European Society of Trauma and Emergency Surgery (ESTES), could broaden educational and clinical exposure to trauma care, but feasibility and implementation factors are unclear. The aims of this survey are to assess the aspirations, expectations, and perceived challenges of prospective fellows and host centres for an ESTES Trauma Traveling Fellowship. Methods A cross-sectional, web-based survey was distributed to all ESTES members, capturing demographics, fellowship aspirations, perceived barriers, and host centre capacities. The survey incorporated Likert scales, free-text responses, and was guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) and the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance / Practical Robust Implementation and Sustainability Model (RE-AIM/PRISM). Results Of 903 invited, 210 responses (23.3%) were analysed. The median age was 38 years; 71% were consultants, and 29% were residents. Most (71%) would consider applying for a Fellowship, and 47% stated their centre could host Fellows. Only 23% currently access funded fellowships. Key aspirations included hands-on participation in trauma care, although hosts could more often only guarantee observational roles. Major barriers included funding and institutional permissions. Most respondents supported implementing the fellowship as it was perceived to align with ESTES priorities. Conclusions There is strong support among European trauma surgeons for an ESTES Trauma Traveling Fellowship, recognising both its potential value and practical impediments. Addressing funding and regulatory barriers will be crucial. A structured and adaptable implementation approach, combined with ongoing evaluation, may help ensure long-term success.

The scope of the call explicitly requires advancing the knowledge of Southern Ocean dynamics and sea ice dynamics, including the distribution, underlying mechanisms, and impacts of changes to reduce uncertainties in projected future changes #1. It specifically calls for understanding abrupt, irreversible change, tipping elements and thresholds, and the future dynamics of oceanic carbon pools #1. The call also seeks to explore the vulnerability of Southern Ocean ecosystems to climate change and anthropogenic activities #1. While the call does not use the specific term "marine heatwave," it addresses the broader physical and biological consequences of thermal extremes and ocean warming in the Southern Ocean, which aligns with the goals of a marine heatwave early warning project #1. The expected outcomes include improved multidisciplinary scientific understanding of the Southern Ocean and contributions to key ocean and climate monitoring indicators #1. Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#4 [paper] Performance of the Heatwave ED Forecast Tool in the Emergency Department Network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland
Authors: Matteo Paganini, Ilaria Costantini, Ilenia Mascherona, Simone Cosci, Laura Di Domenico, Ana Maria Vicedo-Cabrera, Roberta Petrino
Venue: medRxiv
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.11.26365239
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives: Heatwaves drive surges in acute care demand, yet heat-health action plans (HHAPs) lack tools to scale emergency care responses. This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave-related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. Methods: This retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. The model was trained on summers (June-August) 2016-2024 and tested on summer 2025, defining heatwaves as daily mean temperature >25 °C for ≥3 consecutive days. Results: A non-linear temperature-demand association was shown across the clusters, with ED visits increasing at higher temperatures. Model fit varied across clusters (R 2 0.389–0.672), and the reference model consistently outperformed naïve baselines. During two heatwaves in 2025, prediction errors remained within acceptable ranges. Baseline demand, heatwave occurrence, and model performance varied substantially within the canton. Conclusions: These findings have implications for the design of HHAPs, suggesting that emergency care preparedness should rely on locally calibrated demand forecast rather than standardized activation protocols.

#5 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#6 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#8 [paper] Marine Heatwave Detection and Dynamics in the Indonesian Seas under ENSO and Indian Ocean Dipole Forcing
Authors: Qurnia Wulan Sari

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Detection and analysis of Marine Heatwaves (MHWs) in the Indonesian seas, specifically examining their relationship with El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) forcing.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A reproducible Python workflow that acquires and preprocesses Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) data, detects MHWs, acquires ENSO and IOD climate indices, and performs statistical summaries, sensitivity assessments on climatological baselines, and spatial composite analyses.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Indonesian seas, using OISST sea surface temperature observations and climate indices for ENSO and IOD.
Abstract:
This repository contains a collection of Python scripts for detecting, quantifying, and analyzing Marine Heatwaves (MHWs) in the Indonesian seas, with particular emphasis on their relationship with large-scale climate variability associated with the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD). The scripts provide a reproducible workflow for examining the spatial and temporal characteristics of marine heatwaves, including their frequency, duration, intensity, cumulative intensity, and spatial distribution. The workflow integrates sea surface temperature (SST) observations from the Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) dataset with climate indices representing ENSO and IOD variability. The repository includes the following components: 1. OISST data acquisition and preprocessing. 2. Marine heatwave detection and event characterization. 3. Acquisition and processing of ENSO and IOD climate indices. 4. Statistical summaries, figures, and tables of MHW characteristics. 5. Comparison of alternative climatological baselines and sensitivity assessments. 6. Analysis of MHW temporal dynamics and long-term variability. 7. Investigation of regional climate drivers and sensitivity to ENSO and IOD conditions. 8. Spatial composite analysis to identify regional patterns and climate-related MHW responses. The scripts are designed to support reproducible climate-ocean research and provide a framework for understanding how large-scale climate modes influence marine heatwave variability across the Indonesian seas. This repository is intended for researchers, oceanographers, climate scientists, and students working on marine climate variability, ocean warming, extreme ocean events, and tropical ocean-atmosphere interactions. The code can be adapted to other marine regions and extended with additional oceanographic datasets and climate indices.

#9 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#10 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#11 [paper] Day-to-day atmospheric circulation modulated the impact of marine heatwaves on heatstroke risk in Hokkaido in August 2023
Authors: Takehiro Morioka, Tomonori Sato
Venue: SOLA
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44393-026-00038-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Extreme high temperature and humidity threaten high-latitude regions that are less adapted to such conditions. While marine heatwaves (MHWs) can contribute to hot and humid conditions over land, the modulation of these impacts by the day-to-day atmospheric circulation remains poorly understood. This study focused on Hokkaido, the northernmost prefecture in Japan, to investigate how the daily atmospheric circulation regulated the distribution and intensity of MHW-related heatstroke risk during August 2023. Regional atmospheric model simulations indicated that the MHWs that developed south of Hokkaido increased the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) by approximately 2°C in southern coastal areas. Backward trajectory analysis showed that the intensity of MHW-induced heatstroke risk was governed by the daily atmospheric circulation. On days when MHWs substantially impacted the WBGT in the southeastern coastal region, air parcels passed over regions with high sea surface temperatures (SSTs). Conversely, when trajectories bypassed these MHW areas, the impact remained low. These results demonstrate that the daily atmospheric circulation can determine the magnitude of heatstroke risk over land. Our findings suggest that the relative positioning of airflow pathways and the SST distribution should be considered to improve heatstroke risk prediction in coastal regions.

#12 [paper] cSINGV v1.0: development and evaluation of a 1.5 km coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling system for the Western Maritime Continent
Authors: Rajesh Kumar, Claudio Sánchez, Juan Manuel Castillo, Jian‐Guo Li, Bijoy Thompson, Pratiman Patel, Alvin Ng, Kaushik Sasmal
Venue: Geoscientific model development
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-19-10479-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Development and evaluation of a high-resolution coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling system for the Western Maritime Continent (WMC).
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a convection-permitting atmospheric model (SINGV) with ocean (NEMO) and wave (WAVEWATCH III) components using the Regional Coupled Suite and OASIS3-MCT coupler. The system was evaluated via a six-month simulation (Jan–Jun 2019) against observational/reanalysis datasets, comparing cou…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Western Maritime Continent (WMC), characterized by complex coastlines, shallow seas, and strong air–sea interactions.
Abstract:
Abstract. This study presents cSINGV v1.0, a high-resolution (1.5 km) regional coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling system developed for the Western Maritime Continent (WMC). The system integrates a convection-permitting atmospheric model (SINGV) with newly configured ocean (NEMO) and wave (WAVEWATCH III) components within a unified coupling framework based on the Regional Coupled Suite and OASIS3-MCT coupler. The primary contribution of this work lies in the development of a fully coupled system enabling two-way interactions between atmosphere, ocean, and waves at kilometre scale. The ocean and wave components are specifically configured and optimised for the WMC, a region characterised by complex coastlines, shallow seas, and strong air–sea interactions. The model is evaluated using a six-month simulation (January–June 2019) against multiple observational and reanalysis datasets. The ocean and wave components show good agreement with reference datasets, with sea surface temperature errors generally below 0.5 °C and significant wave height errors around 0.2 m. The influence of coupling is assessed by comparing the coupled and uncoupled atmospheric configurations. Results show that coupling improves the spatial organisation of precipitation, the diurnal cycle over the ocean, and the offshore propagation of convection, while differences in near-surface atmospheric variables remain modest. Process-based analysis indicates that these improvements are primarily linked to enhanced latent heat flux driven by thermodynamic air–sea feedbacks associated with sea surface temperature variability. Case studies of Sumatra squall events further indicate that coupling can influence the organisation and persistence of eastward-propagating convection, with the magnitude of this impact depending on the dominant convective regime. Overall, cSINGV provides a physically consistent framework for representing coupled processes in the WMC and offers a useful platform for investigating air–sea–wave interactions at convection-permitting scales.

#13 [paper] Mitigating Summertime Marine Heatwaves via Targeted Marine Cloud Brightening
Authors: Matthew T. Luongo, Edward Blanchard‐Wrigglesworth, Kyle Armour, Haruki Hirasawa, Jacob Cohen, Aaron Donohoe
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5kv4t
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. Initiating MCB in May 2019 mitigates important negative consequences of the event, substantially reducing the MHW magnitude and limiting associated declines in surface oxygen. The impacts of this intervention are mostly local and limited to summer, even when MCB is extended into winter, with nonlocal climate effects smaller than internal variability. By demonstrating local efficacy and minor remote impacts for mitigating the Blob 2.0, this work motivates further study of whether localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs.

#14 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#15 [paper] Developing a coastal hazard prediction system in ice-infested waters – Part 1: High-resolution regional wave modeling in the Estuary and Gulf of St. Lawrence
Authors: Jérémy Baudry, Dany Dumont, David Didier, Pascal Bernatchez, Sebastien Dugas
Venue: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-26-4231-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. This study is the first of a two-part paper that summarizes the development of a prototype coastal hazard prediction system providing short-term (+48 h) forecasts of the total water level (TWL) at 50 m resolution for the province of Quebec, Eastern Canada. In this first part, the implementation of the offshore wave model component of the system, which is a regional 1 km-resolution WAVEWATCH III™(WW3) configuration for the Estuary and Gulf of St. Lawrence (EGSL), is presented and discussed. The configuration is forced by high resolution atmosphere, ocean and sea ice forecasts provided by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) and includes a state-of-the-art parameterization of wave propagation and attenuation in sea ice that has been tuned with observations from the EGSL. Performances are assessed against wave data collected over a two-year period during which the forecasting system was running operationally, and against historical storm data using a model hindcast. Results demonstrate reasonable forecast skills both for normal and extreme wave conditions during ice-free periods with errors ranging from 15 % to 31 % of the mean wave height. However, when sea ice is present, performances are drastically reduced, primarily due to inaccuracies in the predicted ice fields at spatial scales over which wave energy typically dissipates in sea ice.

#16 [paper] Seasonal Predictability of Summer Hazards Over the Korean Peninsula and Implications for Hazard Response
Authors: Seokhwan Hwang
Venue: Korean Society of Hazard Mitigation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.9798/kosham.2026.26.4.241
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Summer heat and monsoon rainfall in Korea are closely linked to the phase of quasi-stationary Rossby waves along the meandering upper-level jet. This study evaluates the seasonal predictability of individual summer hazards and examines response strategies for hazards that remain beyond the reach of seasonal forecasting. The upper-level ridge phase is diagnosed using hot-minus-cool composites and Takaya-Nakamura wave-activity flux. A pre-season probabilistic forecast is then developed from slow spring boundary forcing, with cross-validation designed to exclude information from the verification year. Four hazard indices—heat wave days, summer rainfall, SPI drought, and soil moisture—are each decomposed into a predictable component and a synoptic-scale residual. Validation with ERA5 (1979-2024) shows that significant skill is confined to the upper-level circulation and seasonal-mean temperature (Western Pacific Subtropical High r = 0.76; mean temperature r = 0.43). The four hazard indices exhibit very weak correlations with the predictable component (|r| < 0.05) and are strongly correlated only with the synoptic-scale residual. Although the number of heatwave days is strongly correlated with seasonal-mean temperature (0.79), the seasonal predictability of the mean temperature does not translate into predictive skill for heatwave days. All four hazard indices ae significantly associated with the same synoptic-scale residual, suggesting that heat and dryness can co-exist in years that are not predictable in advance. Seasonal forecasting is therefore best used within the limits of a probabilistic tilt of the seasonal mean, while the four hazard indices should be addressed through short-range forecasting and real-time monitoring. Response systems should be reviewed to accommodate the range of variability observed in the record.

#19 [paper] Multi-season evaluation of temperature and wind in the marine boundary layer along the United States northeast coast in the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model
Authors: Bianca Adler, Laura Bianco, David D. Turner, Joseph Olson, Xia Sun, Joshua Gebauer, Nicola Bodini, Stefano Letizia
Venue: Geoscientific model development
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-19-8627-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) model is run operationally by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to provide high-resolution short-range forecasts for the continental United States. The evaluation of the HRRR model off of the United States coasts has been challenged by the lack of suitable continuous profile observations in the marine boundary layer in the past. State-of-the art remote sensing instruments were recently deployed along the coast of New England in the northeastern United States for the multi-year Third Wind Forecast Improvement Project and provide a unique opportunity for the evaluation of temperature and wind in the marine boundary layer in the HRRR model. We used 1 year of data at three sites, two of which were on islands, to document the seasonal characteristics of the marine boundary layer and its representation in the HRRR model for different forecast hours. Overall, the HRRR model captured the seasonal and diurnal evolution of temperature and wind very well. However, low-level horizontal wind shear and static stability were too weak in the model, especially during the warmer months. At certain sites, these biases were accompanied by errors in sea surface temperature, suggesting a potential, though localized, link. Low-level jets (LLJs) occurred in approximately 20 % of the hourly profiles with a maximum frequency during spring and summer. Up to 60 % of the LLJ profiles during peak seasons were correctly predicted, using the critical success index as a measure. Abstract:

These optimized and interpretable decomposed signals are then used as inputs to standalone forecasting models, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), deep Random Vector Functional Link (RVFL), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). These optimized and interpretable decomposed signals are then used as inputs to the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), deep Random Vector Functional Link (RVFL), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models to forecast. Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. However, surface anomalies cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the surface. #2 [paper] Alternative futures for laboratory medicine in 2050: scenarios and signposts for diagnostic capability contraction.
Authors: Yuji, Koichiro, Yuji, Wakako, Ohnishi, Hiroaki
Venue: Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42723619/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Laboratory medicine has begun to describe its own future, and the images it produces are almost uniformly expansionary. What they rarely contain is a collapse scenario: a future in which the field delivers less than today. A profession planning for 2050 needs one. CONTENT: We summarise what structured foresight offers a clinical readership, entering through the threats quadrant of a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis, and treat the standard taxonomy of futures as a lens, not a required method. We define diagnostic capability contraction as progressive degradation rather than catastrophic disappearance, distinct from retiring tests that add nothing. Six drivers are specified: loss of laboratory-developed tests, reduced test availability, workforce attrition, supplier dependency, geographical access and payment. Evidence comes from three jurisdictions, including Japan, where one regulatory driver produced different outcomes in the same period. We set out four scenarios for 2050, one per generic image, and propose signposts as early-warning indicators, with action thresholds, for the contraction scenario. Estimates of likelihood attach to the indicators, not the futures. SUMMARY: The evidence base is uneven across drivers, and informatively so: what is not anticipated is not measured. The argument applies to our own prior work, expansionary in the same way. OUTLOOK: A set containing a contraction branch gives laboratory leadership what an expansionary set cannot: what to watch for, and when to act. A preferred future chosen without it comes from a shorter list than the field faces. Building a balanced set is work that no small group of authors can do alone.

#20 [paper] ISO 15189:2022 in Clinical Biochemistry Laboratories: A Practical Review for Quality Improvement
Authors: Mrs. Varsha Vivek Gharat and Mr. Vivek Keshav Gharat
Venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.48175/ijarsct-38436
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: ISO 15189:2022 is the latest international standard that defines the requirements for quality and competence in medical laboratories. Compared with previous editions, it places greater emphasis on patient safety, risk-based thinking, impartiality, digitalization, personnel competence, and continual quality improvement. Clinical biochemistry laboratories play a vital role in patient diagnosis and treatment; therefore, effective implementation of ISO 15189:2022 is essential to ensure reliable, accurate, and timely laboratory services. Objective: This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the requirements of ISO 15189:2022 and their practical implementation in clinical biochemistry laboratories. It highlights the major changes introduced in the 2022 edition and discusses their significance in improving laboratory quality management systems. Methods: This review is based on an analysis of ISO 15189:2022 requirements, relevant CLSI guidelines, NABL accreditation criteria, and published scientific literature related to laboratory quality management and clinical biochemistry practice. Results: The review summarizes key aspects of laboratory organization, personnel competence, equipment management, reagent control, sample management, method verification and validation, measurement uncertainty, internal quality control, external quality assessment, risk management, document control, internal audits, management review, and continual improvement. Practical examples relevant to routine clinical biochemistry laboratories are included to facilitate effective implementation.

#21 [paper] Bridging laboratory and clinical practice: timelines and challenges in wet lab research
Authors: Nisreen Mohammed Al-Namnam, Steph Collishaw, Melanie Wheeldon
Venue: Bone and Joint Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1302/2046-3758.1511.bjr-2026-0221.r1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
For surgical trainees embarking on a period of laboratory research, the transition from operating theatre to bench science can be both rewarding and disorienting. This annotation is written specifically for clinicians entering a wet laboratory environment, typically on an out-of-programme research placement, who may be unfamiliar with the realities of experimental science. Drawing on the first-hand experiences of a multidisciplinary orthopaedic research team, it explains why laboratory timelines are often longer than expected, and offers practical guidance for working effectively alongside PhD-level scientists, postdoctoral researchers, research technicians, and their trainees - collaborators whose technical expertise is indispensable to experimental success. Wet lab work involves complex protocols, tissue handling, assay optimization, and regulatory approvals, all of which can significantly extend project timelines. Effective communication, realistic planning, and mutual respect are crucial to manage unforeseen challenges and ensure that experiments are reliable, reproducible, and clinically meaningful.

final_text: The paper that matters most for the Plastic pathways project is #20, titled "Defining the Sustainability Threshold of Circularity: A Comparative Assessment of Plastic Recycling Pathways" #20. This study is the most relevant because it directly examines the potential conflict between increasing plastic recycling rates and achieving global carbon reduction targets #20. It provides a comparative environmental assessment of different waste management methods, ranging from mechanical recycling to chemical and advanced recycling, to determine their energy requirements and lifecycle carbon emissions #20. By identifying the "sustainability threshold" at which recycling becomes more carbon-intensive than virgin plastic production, the paper offers a practical framework for selecting recycling technologies based on national energy-system characteristics #20. This evidence-based guidance is critical for aligning circular economy strategies with climate mitigation objectives, ensuring that resource recovery does not compromise global decarbonization #20.

#1 [paper] Microplastic contamination in agricultural systems: impacts on plant productivity, economic losses, and supply chain resilience.
Authors: Xu, Tong
Venue: Frontiers in plant science
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42920819/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Microplastics (MPs) have transitioned from a predominantly marine concern to a defining threat facing terrestrial agroecosystems, where croplands now function as one of the largest global reservoirs of plastic particles. This review synthesizes evidence to construct an integrated narrative that links the entry of MPs into farmland with declining plant productivity, quantifiable economic losses, and the erosion of agricultural supply chain resilience. The synthesis is based on a documented search of Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar covering January 2018 to March 2026, with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria reported in Section 1.1. Sources, fate and soil-phase processes are treated in condensed form, because they are already covered comprehensively elsewhere; we retain only the evidence that propagates into crop, economic and supply-chain outcomes. Building on these soil-level disturbances, we evaluate the phytotoxic consequences for crops, spanning inhibited germination, impaired root architecture, reduced photosynthetic efficiency, disrupted nutrient acquisition, and the uptake and translocation of nano-sized particles into edible tissues. A central contribution of this review is the explicit coupling of these biophysical impacts to their economic and systemic dimensions, because recent global meta-analyses estimate that MP-induced photosynthetic suppression alone may reduce staple crop production by tens to hundreds of millions of tons annually, translating into substantial revenue losses, quality downgrading, remediation expenditure, and heightened exposure of food supply chains to shocks. Rather than reporting these modelled outputs at face value, we dissect the inferential chain that produces them, from effect size to biomass to harvestable yield to price, and we identify the assumptions at each step that determine whether the resulting figures are decision-grade. We complement the global estimates with farm-level cost-benefit evidence showing that the private returns to plasticulture remain positive while the contamination externality contributes under one percent of the accounted benefits of current management, which explains the persistence of practices that degrade the productive base. Throughout, illustrative case studies from China, Chile, Australia, and Europe are embedded within each thematic section rather than treated in isolation, demonstrating how local contamination patterns propagate into landscape- and market-scale consequences. We further appraise mitigation and remediation options, ranging from source reduction and material substitution to biochar amendment, and we assess emerging governance instruments such as the FAO Voluntary Code of Conduct and circular-economy regulation. Finally, we identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning the calibration of field-realistic dose-response relationships, the construction of decision-grade economic estimates, and the severe geographical imbalance of the evidence base, in which South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America are collectively represented by a small fraction of published field studies, and we outline research priorities to safeguard soil health and food security. The review argues that microplastic contamination should be reframed not merely as an ecotoxicological problem but as a slow-onset stressor with strategic implications for the stability of global food systems.
