#3 [paper] Integrating bioplastics into waste management: barriers and pathways to a circular economy
Authors: Ejaeta Victory Ayodawha, Lukman Shehu Mustapha, Kiyana Fatemi, Justice Tijesuni Alabi, Mustapha Saheed, Peter Olusakin Oladoye, Oluwatobi Victoria Obayomi, Kehinde Shola Obayomi
Venue: Next Materials
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nxmate.2026.103641
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Bioplastics have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional fossil-based plastics because of their potential to reduce dependence on non-renewable resources and support the transition towards a circular economy. However, their environmental sustainability is determined not only by feedstock selection but also by polymer characteristics, product design, and the effectiveness of end-of-life management systems. Despite rapid growth in bioplastic production and application, significant uncertainties remain regarding their integration into existing waste management infrastructure, resulting in variable environmental outcomes and widespread misconceptions about their biodegradability and recyclability. This review critically examines the compatibility of bioplastics with circular waste management systems by synthesizing recent literature on material classification, feedstock pathways, recycling technologies, industrial composting, policy frameworks, economic considerations, consumer behaviour, and regional implementation strategies. The review further evaluates the environmental and economic consequences of mismanaged bioplastics using evidence from life cycle assessment studies and discusses emerging technological, regulatory, and bioeconomy-based solutions for improving circularity. The analysis demonstrates that no single end-of-life pathway is universally optimal for all bioplastic systems; rather, environmental performance depends on polymer chemistry, contamination level, collection and sorting efficiency, treatment effectiveness, energy systems, and regional waste-management infrastructure. Under suitable conditions, recycling, industrial composting, anaerobic digestion, or energy recovery pathways may contribute to improved circularity, whereas inappropriate disposal through landfilling, contamination of conventional recycling streams, or inadequate waste management can negate potential environmental benefits. Future progress will depend on coordinated technological innovation, infrastructure development, evidence-based policy implementation, stakeholder collaboration, and public education to enable the sustainable integration of bioplastics into circular waste management systems.

#4 [paper] A bibliometric analysis of research trends on chitosan-based films for food packaging using Scopus database from 2015 to 2024
Authors: Shalahudin Nur Ayyubi, Aprilina Purbasari, Aji Prasetyaningrum, Ahmad Fauzan, Indrie Ambarsari, Yustina Yustina, Muh Arman, Sarah Fiebrina Heraningsih
Venue: F1000Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.188318.1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
<ns5:p>Background Chitosan-based films have emerged as promising sustainable alternatives to conventional petroleum-based films for food packaging. However, there is a lack of a comprehensive bibliometric review of the academic literature on chitosan-based films for food packaging, particularly studies published over the last ten years. Growing concerns about plastic waste and the demand for sustainable and smart packaging have increased academic interest in this field. This study provides a bibliometric review of the literature published from 2015 to 2024 to map the research landscape and guide future studies. Methods Bibliometric data covering the 2015–2024 period were retrieved from the Scopus database using keywords related to “chitosan-based films” and “food packaging”. A dataset of 1,583 publications was analyzed and visualized using VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) and Biblioshiny in the Bibliometrix R package to evaluate publication trends, influential contributors, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic development, and highly cited articles. Results The analysis showed a progressive increase in publications from 2015 to 2024. The study also identified the leading contributors, including countries, institutions, authors, and journals. Keyword analysis, thematic mapping, and highly cited articles clearly indicate that current research hotspots focus on the development of smart packaging, including active and intelligent packaging, as well as the mechanical reinforcement of films. Conclusions To the best of our knowledge, this is the first bibliometric review to examine research trends in Scopus-indexed publications on chitosan-based films for food packaging from 2015 to 2024. The findings may help researchers, organizations, and policymakers understand the development of this field and identify topics for future research.</ns5:p>

#5 [paper] A Systematic Survey of Molecular Taggants, Distributed Ledger Technology, and Machine Learning for Verifiable Plastic Waste Traceability
Authors: Purva Shinde, Adweta Dengale, Abhiraj Gatmane, Nayan Rathod, Umesh Pawar
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23610052
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is now the dominant regulatory instrument for plastic packaging in India, the European Union and elsewhere. It rests on an assumption that current systems cannot test: that a producer's declaration of recovered and recycled tonnage is true. Compliance evidence is aggregate, self-reported and detached from the material it describes, so the central claim of the regime is cheap to falsify and hard to disprove. This paper is a systematic survey conducted under a PRISMA-style protocol. We screened 312 records from five databases and retained 45 sources published between 2023 and 2026 across four communities that seldom cite one another: molecular marking of polymers, machine-readable identifiers, distributed ledger technology (DLT) for provenance, and machine learning for waste classification, forecasting and anomaly detection. The included studies are quality-appraised, and the four bodies of work are compared against one another using a four-layer analytical framework and six capability criteria derived from the regulatory requirements. Three principal findings emerge. Not one reviewed configuration satisfies all six criteria, and the sharpest — whether an identifier survives mechanical reprocessing — is failed categorically by every approach built on digital identifiers alone. Where one layer is weak another is characteristically strong, yet no reviewed study evaluates the layers in composition. The third finding carries furthest: because no shared dataset, protocol or benchmark permits reported accuracies and throughputs to be compared, the field's apparent maturity cannot be verified, and its limiting constraint proves evaluative rather than technical. We specify what an adequate benchmark requires, and derive a reference framework whose design decisions are each traced to supporting evidence. Implementation and empirical validation are outside the scope of this survey.

#6 [paper] Micro- and nanoplastics across the plant-food-human continuum: Plant uptake, phytotoxicity, food safety, human-health implications, and mitigation strategies
Authors: Huixin Shao, Hongli Cao, Kai Zhang, Huiyi Wang, Shiyi Chen, Qingqing Li, Dingxi Bao, Liyong Luo
Venue: Plant Nano Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plana.2026.100338
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Micro- and nanoplastics (M/NPs) are accumulating in agricultural environments, raising concerns about crop performance, food quality, and dietary exposure. Building on earlier reviews of environmental occurrence, plant uptake, and phytotoxicity, this review critically evaluates evidence relevant to the environment-plant-food-human continuum and organizes it around exposure determinants, plant response pathways, and potential intervention points. We first examine how particle size, surface charge, polymer type, exposure route, and plant traits influence M/NP bioavailability, root and foliar uptake, and vascular transport. We then relate these processes to changes in seed germination, growth, photosynthesis, crop quality, and rhizosphere microbiota, and summarize the associated responses involving redox homeostasis, phenylpropanoid and cell-wall metabolism, carbohydrate and energy metabolism, hormone signaling, amino acid metabolism, nutrient homeostasis, and genomic integrity. Evidence for M/NP occurrence in edible tissues and trophic transfer is critically assessed; however, quantitative measurements of internal polymer burdens and plant-derived dietary exposure remain scarce, and adverse human-health implications are inferred mainly from cell and animal studies. Finally, mitigation approaches are evaluated at two levels: reducing plant exposure through rhizosphere management, soil amendments, nutrient regulation, agricultural source control, and ecological interception; and reducing household exposure through changes in drinking water, food preparation, textiles, and dietary practices. The available evidence remains constrained by non-standardized detection methods, simplified model particles, high exposure concentrations, and limited field and human validation. Future work should prioritize standardized measurements, environmentally realistic chronic exposures, and causal evaluation of transfer and mitigation across the plant-food-human pathway.

#7 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

#8 [paper] Life Cycle Assessment of Virgin and Recycled Polypropylene Kitchenware in the UK: Impacts of Domestic Recycling, International Supply Chains, and Consumer Use
Authors: Caitlin Jaramillo, Janna Aljoubory, Kok Siew Ng, Kun Qi, George Fern, Eleni Iacovidou
Venue: Circular Economy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.55845/t4f1dj13
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study evaluates the cradle-to-grave environmental performance of polypropylene (PP) kitchenware in the United Kingdom (UK), addressing critical gaps in understanding how material choices, global supply chains, domestic recycling, and consumer use-phase practices interact. Four scenarios were assessed using life cycle assessment (LCA) modelling: virgin PP (vPP) manufactured in China and Germany, recycled PP (rPP) produced in the UK, and a 50:50 vPP–rPP blend. Environmental impacts evaluated using the ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) and IPCC 2021 GWP100 showed that under the modelled scenarios, UK-produced rPP reduces global warming potential (GWP) by about 53% compared with imported vPP, and by 22% compared with UK-manufactured vPP from Germany, driven by avoided virgin polymer production, the absence of long-distance shipping and end-of-life recycling. Toxicity-related impacts revealed trade-offs associated with recycling processes. The rPP product reduced terrestrial ecotoxicity and human non-carcinogenic toxicity by approximately 36% and 16% relative to imported vPP, demonstrating rPP’s potential to reduce toxicity-related impacts. Consumer use-phase practices (routine household dishwashing) contributed substantially to lifecycle impacts, becoming the dominant life cycle stage (30-64% of GWP) as material-related impacts were reduced. The study demonstrates that the environmental performance of consumer plastics requires integrated consideration of material systems efficiency, geography, supply-chain arrangements, recycling infrastructure, and consumer behaviour. Such an approach can promote circularity in polymer value chains, with the potential to generate substantial environmental, economic, technical and social benefits.

#9 [paper] Research Trends in Biodegradable Polymers (PLA and PEF) for Sustainable Plastic Waste Management: A Bibliometric Study
Authors: Muhammad Mobin Siddiqi, Maryam Ikram, Muhammad Nihal Naseer
Venue: Research Square

#10 [paper] Exposure States, Environmental Fate, and Functional Effects of Microplastics in Soil: Bibliometric Mapping and Critical Mechanistic Synthesis.
Authors: Li, Yuhe, Yan, Su, Lv, Xinting, Tian, Yuxin, Jin, Mingji, Quan, Yue, Zheng, Yiran
Venue: Polymers
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42884995/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Reported effects of microplastics in soil vary with particle properties, exposure conditions, and measured endpoints. We combined bibliometric mapping with a critical mechanistic synthesis to examine these differences. A 3200-record Web of Science Core Collection corpus was tested against broad (4787) and title-strict (2375) sensitivity corpora. A year-stratified manual relevance audit judged 115 of 120 sampled records (95.8%) to be in scope. An article-only subset of 2756 records retained positive directions for all twelve principal title-concept trends and preserved 112 of 119 primary co-citation nodes. Twelve title concepts increased consistently across corpus definitions and start years, led by plant and crop performance, biodegradable plastics, and aging and weathering. Only co-contamination and nitrogen cycling remained significant under every robust model specification. The mechanistic synthesis indicates that differences in particle state, soil-mediated contact, endpoints, and inferential scope can contribute to apparently contradictory findings. We propose an exposure-to-function framework that integrates exposure descriptors with a bounded sequence linking particle characterization, fate and biological contact, process change, functional consequences, and persistence or recovery. Risk and management claims should remain within the links supported by evidence.

#11 [paper] Technological Innovations for Ocean Plastic Waste Management: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Technologies
Authors: Jehu Roeh C. Rubenial Franklin M. Ganancias
Venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.59543/jidmis.v3.1213
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental challenges worldwide, driving increasing interest in technology-based solutions for monitoring, prevention, mitigation, and sustainable waste management. Despite the rapid growth of research in this field, a comprehensive understanding of its scientific development, collaboration patterns, and emerging technological directions remains limited. This study presents a global bibliometric analysis of technological innovations for ocean plastic waste management using 12,039 English-language publications retrieved from the Scopus database on 09 July 2026. Bibliographic data were analyzed using Bibliometrix (RStudio) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, journals, institutions, countries, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified microplastics, plastic waste, circular economy, recycling, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and remote sensing as dominant research themes. Thematic evolution further revealed a transition from broad marine pollution research toward technology-oriented investigations emphasizing plastic waste management and microplastics. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

#12 [paper] Research Priorities for a Circular Economy for Plastic Sustainability in the Caribbean
Authors: Anne Marie Mozrall, Jessica P. Feliz Garrido, P. Tejada-Tejada, Akeem Mohammed, Brigitte Mildred Roldán Ramírez, Alana Malinde S.N. Lancaster, Iris Odett Atencio, Diego Batista
Venue: Environmental Science & Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c16637
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Caribbean countries bear a disproportionate burden of marine plastic pollution because of their small landmass, high population density, and insufficient waste management infrastructure. Many Caribbean nations depend on informal, unmanaged landfills, underscoring an urgent need for more resilient, sustainable systems. This perspective synthesizes existing data to map the region’s plastic waste landscape and leverages regional expertise to identify key research priorities. This work emerged from interdisciplinary international professionals and members of the CEPlaSt (circular economy for plastic sustainability) network. A major barrier to circularity is the lack of reliable data on waste composition and flows, alongside stark infrastructure disparities across the wider Caribbean region. Addressing these gaps through targeted investment and region-specific planning is essential to modernize waste systems, reduce plastic emissions, and advance a sustainable Caribbean plastic circular economy.

#13 [paper] Sustainable Manufacturing Practices in the Plastic Packaging Industry and Associated Barriers: A Systematic Literature Review
Authors: Anny Jasbleidy Avendaño Avendaño, Fernando Antônio Forcellini
Venue: Circular Economy and Sustainability
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s43615-026-01161-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The plastic packaging industry is a major contributor to environmental impacts due to its intensive use of fossil-based materials and low recycling rates. In this context, Sustainable Manufacturing (SM) has emerged as a strategic approach to mitigate these impacts while balancing environmental, economic, and social dimensions. However, the literature remains fragmented, particularly regarding the integration of practices, barriers, and performance in sustainability. This study aims to systematically identify and analyze SM practices in the plastic packaging industry, examine the barriers to their implementation, and propose an integrated framework that relates practices, barriers, and performance in the dimensions of the Triple Bottom Line (TBL). A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA protocol, searching the Scopus and Web of Science databases without temporal restrictions. A total of 18 peer-reviewed articles were selected for in-depth content analysis. The data were coded and categorized to identify practices, barriers, and their interrelationships. The results indicate a predominance of practices focused on the environmental dimension, such as sustainable design and development, recycling, and resource efficiency, while social practices remain underexplored. Significant barriers include high investment costs, technological limitations, inadequate recycling infrastructure, and regulatory inconsistencies. Based on these findings, this study proposes an integrated framework that captures the relationships among SM practices, barriers to implementation, and performance across TBL dimensions. This study directly addresses the operational need for site-specific and temporally granular forecasts, which are often lacking in coarse numerical ocean models #8. The authors present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a graph–temporal architecture that achieves the lowest 1-hour RMSE and the highest long-horizon residual skill among the tested deep models #8. Crucially, the model demonstrates a 38-hour mean advisory lead time during a regional alert period, proving that it can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal stakeholders #8. While other papers discuss prediction on multi-year timescales #6 or the detection of subsurface events #17, #8 provides a concrete, high-performance solution for the short-to-medium term operational forecasting required to trigger immediate protective actions.

#1 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. #5 [paper] Marine heatwave exposure is changing unevenly across Scottish aquaculture sites

Abstract:
Introduction Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are an increasing climate hazard for coastal aquaculture, yet regional assessments may not resolve how exposure varies across the locations where farms operate. Methods Here, we analysed daily ~5-km OSTIA sea surface temperature data from 1990 to 2025 at the locations of 361 active Scottish finfish and shellfish farms, represented by 218 unique grid cells, and compared satellite temperatures with in situ records from eight farms. We used principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering to describe long-term MHW exposure, and mixed-effects models to assess temporal changes. Results Two broad exposure profiles were identified. Cluster 1 was characterised by higher mean, maximum and cumulative intensity, whereas differences in event duration and frequency between clusters were smaller. Temporal trends, however, differed more strongly. MHW frequency increased at similar rates in both clusters, while event duration, cumulative intensity and severity increased more rapidly in Cluster 2. Between 1990 -2019 and 2020 -2025, estimated event duration increased by 44.6% in Cluster 1 and 89.9% in Cluster 2, while cumulative intensity increased by 50.0% and approximately 127.5%, respectively (cluster × period, p < 0.001). The estimated probability of a Severe or Extreme event rose from 2.2% to 26.2% in Cluster 2, compared with 1.8% to 6.1% in Cluster 1 (cluster × period, p < 0.001). Mean event intensity changed comparatively little. Discussion These findings show that MHW exposure across Scottish aquaculture is multidimensional, spatially uneven and changing at different rates through time. The resulting hazard -exposure landscape helps bridge regional MHW assessments and individual-farm monitoring, providing a foundation for more targeted monitoring and future assessment of aquaculture vulnerability and climate risk.

Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#7 [paper] Understanding ecosystem responses to recurrent marine heatwaves
Authors: Emily Lester, Stanley Mastrantonis, Sharyn M. Hickey, Anna Lafratta, Jessica A. Benthuysen, Eben Afrifa-Yamoah, Arani Chandrapavan, martial depczynski

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. While extensive research has documented the impacts of these events, most studies have examined individual heatwaves or specific taxonomic groups in isolation, limiting our understanding of cumulative and cascading effects across the ecosystem. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. We emphasise that the successful implementation of such strategies hinges upon the accurate and timely prediction of future MHW events.

#8 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le

Abstract:

Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. The PROMOTE Sandpit brought together 54 participants from across ARIA’s Forecasting Tipping Points (FTP) programme to discuss development of a future Early Warning System (EWS) for tipping of North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre (SPG) and Greenland Ice sheet systems. The sandpit marks a significant shift from a focus on detecting climate tipping points towards designing actionable warning systems that support real-world decision making. There was a consensus that the scientific detection of tipping alone is insufficient and that an effective EWS should integrate observations, modelling, impacts, communication and response planning, while being designed around stakeholder needs. Whilst highlighting that FTP has already made significant advances, participants also identified critical gaps in current research efforts. This includes the definition of the SPG tipping events, advocating standardized definitions, benchmarking frameworks and multiple indicators rather than reliance on single metrics such as mixed layer depth. Machine learning and AI were recognized as valuable tools for detecting warning signals and/or estimating proximity to tipping points. However, there were concerns regarding explainability and transferability to real-world systems as well as ground truthing against observations. Other major gaps or concerns were impact translation, attribution, state estimation, systems integration, decision support and stakeholder co-design. Adaption pathways and response capabilities were also found underdeveloped. It was strongly suggested to begin working on these components immediately rather than waiting for scientific uncertainties to be fully resolved. Key recommendations include developing an integrated end-to-end EWS framework with sufficient weighting given to the four EWS pillars of observations, monitoring and forecasting, disaster risk knowledge, preparedness and response capability, and warning, dissemination and communication; strengthening links between observations, models and impacts, and preparing for use of fast developing UK observational infrastructure; retaining multiple indicators, improving the robustness of ML prediction techniques and further developing an SPG state estimation capability; placing more emphasis on attribution studies; establishing demonstration/benchmarking systems or prototypes; using techniques developed within FTP to embed stakeholder co-design within the programme; improving the communication framework; and prioritising decision-making under uncertainty.

These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#19 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#20 [paper] OCEAN-RAD P1: Conceptual Design, Numerical Modelling and Test Protocol for Radiative Cooling of Enclosed Seawater Tanks (v1.1)
Authors: Jakub Slahounek
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23931365
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OCEAN-RAD P1 is a preliminary engineering study investigating radiative sky cooling as a potential means of removing heat from enclosed seawater tanks. The proposed laboratory configuration comprises 2 m² of radiating panels, a closed freshwater circulation loop and a titanium heat exchanger coupled to a 100-litre seawater tank. Initial testing is intended to take place on land, without organisms, primarily under nocturnal conditions. The study provides a thermal model, reproducible Python code, synthetic parameter studies, a proposed experimental protocol, measurement templates and an internal technical review. A second numerical implementation reproduces the steady-state results across 1,008 prescribed parameter combinations. This agreement demonstrates computational consistency under shared assumptions; it does not establish experimental validity. Under one prescribed favourable nocturnal scenario, the model predicts an initial heat extraction rate of approximately 78 W. Performance depends on atmospheric radiation, temperatures, heat-transfer coefficients and component properties. The reported values are conditional numerical results rather than measured or representative coastal performance. Version 1.1 distinguishes heat transported between the heat-exchanger ports from heat extracted from the seawater, accounting for changes in the exchanger’s stored thermal energy during transients. It also strengthens data validation, extends uncertainty accounting and revises the proposed startup procedure. No prototype testing or biological experiments have been conducted. Practical efficiency, durability, economic viability and ecological benefits remain unverified. The work is intended to support laboratory evaluation and possible future applications in small, controlled marine facilities; it does not demonstrate cooling of the open ocean or a net planetary cooling effect. AI tools were used for technical drafting, numerical implementation and internal review. The internal review used the same AI system and does not constitute independent external peer review.

#2 [paper] Comparative analysis of barriers and opportunities for implementation of blue-green infrastructure for enhancing urban flood resilience in Uganda, Rwanda, and Sweden
Authors: Erik Nilsson, Seith N. Mugume, Johanna Sörensen, Marie Leonce Murebwayire, Umaru Garba Wali
Venue: Cities
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cities.2026.107713
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Recent studies have identified a combination of socio-economic, institutional, governance and financing barriers that constrain the adoption of Blue-Green Infrastructure (BGI) for enhancing urban flood resilience and provision of multiple benefits in cities. However, most barrier analysis studies have used literature reviews, semi-structured interviews, or questionnaire surveys in case studies in the Global North; in contrast, there is limited research and uptake of BGI in flood prone cities in Sub-Saharan Africa. This study addresses these gaps by conducting a comparative analysis of barriers and opportunities for BGI implementation in two flood prone Sub Saharan African cities (Kampala, Uganda; and Kigali, Rwanda), and one Global North city (Lund, Sweden), with the aim of supporting strategies for BGI implementation and identifying transferable best practices and learning opportunities. Through a systematic mapping of barriers and opportunities based on a stakeholder co-development process, the study identified policy and regulatory challenges, limited public funding for BGI implementation, and institutional challenges as the main barriers to adoption of BGI in the three cases. The study identified several opportunities to increase BGI uptake, including land availability, using public-private partnerships for BGI implementation, and knowledge of the benefits of BGI. In addition, research on multifunctional effects can facilitate funding and implementation of new funding mechanisms, such as tax breaks or reduced utility fees for property owners. The identified barriers, opportunities, and proposed methodological framework can be used to develop strategies for the uptake of BGI to contribute to resilient and sustainable urban water management.

#3 [paper] Understanding engagement with a deposit return scheme for reusable cups: A qualitative study on barriers and enablers of cup use and return through the COM-B Model
Authors: Isabel Warner, Ayşe Lisa Allison, Paulina M. Schenk
Venue: PLOS Sustainability and Transformation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pstr.0000301
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Single-use plastics are embedded in daily life and contribute heavily to environmental impacts. Circular initiatives such as deposit return schemes aim to curb this problem yet remain under-researched despite their growing popularity. This study explored the barriers and enablers of engagement within a piloted deposit return scheme at University College London (UCL), in which participants paid a £1 deposit on reusable cups, receiving this refund upon return. Nine semi-structured interviews were conducted with UCL students and staff and analysed inductively to identify influences on behaviour, with themes subsequently mapped onto the Capability Opportunity Motivation-Behaviour (COM-B) Model. Thirteen themes were developed and organised under five COM-B constructs: Psychological capability (understanding the scheme; forgetting to return cups), Physical opportunity (cup design; accessibility of drop boxes; posters and instructions), Social opportunity (social interactions regarding the cups), Automatic motivation (habits; positive feelings) and Reflective motivation (perceived ease; perceived usefulness; perceived reliability; perceived hygiene; alternative goals for using the scheme). For example, for the scheme’s uptake, participants reported needing to understand the scheme, as well as perceiving it as hygienic and useful, and having constructive social interactions about it. Accessible drop locations were noted as particularly important for return behaviours, while forgetting cups or using them for other purposes (e.g., mementos) prevented reusable cups from functioning as shared, reusable assets. By applying a behaviour change framework, this study provides recommendations into how circular initiatives can be strengthened, for example, by providing clearer step-by-step instructions, enhancing communication by staff delivering the intervention and offering timely reminders to encourage cup returns. These insights can be used to inform similar schemes aiming to reduce single-use plastic consumption. The work also contributes to the growing body of evidence highlighting the need for strategies to manage packaging items at the sources, such as reducing and reusing cups, beyond recycling initiatives.

#5 [paper] Household-week measurement and cost accounting for community food provisioning: framework specification and partial pilot demonstration
Authors: Craig Steven Wright
Venue: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2026.1813246
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Community food projects commonly report production, expenditure, labour, water, or participation as separate totals. Such records do not show whether a defined service was offered and delivered to an eligible household in a particular service period. This Methods article specifies a household-week framework that joins six established streams—harvest, loss, distribution, labour participation, cost, and water—to a prospectively declared service obligation: recipient × service period × parameter set, with a weekly period as the default. It states the strongest objection to that design—that the join is only a fact-table grain, and that community-supported agriculture pick-up logs, food-bank visit records and humanitarian distribution monitoring already track recipients per cycle—and answers it: an event log cannot record a scheduled delivery that did not happen; demand-driven logs measure use rather than promise-keeping; and humanitarian distribution runs through relief supply chains and is monitored for donors, whereas a multi-year community project must join its own production, loss, labour, cost and water records to the same obligation. The join distinguishes production, offer, and delivery; identifies the first documented break; and calculates cost per eligible or successful obligation on one shared frame. Thresholds and cadence are declared parameters with threshold-response sensitivity, and provisioning reliability is separated from household food security. An 18-week pilot at one tropical site partially demonstrates the production pathway: recorded vegetable harvest totalled 1,421.63 kg, rising from 8.56 to 155.89 kg/week; the late five-week mean was 143.98 kg/week (SD 12.58); routine egg counts exist only for Weeks 43–44. Household delivery, complete loss, labour, full economic cost, and water records are absent, so continuity, cost per successful household-week, governance effects, waste reduction, and transferability are not pilot results. A complete schema, reference implementation and synthetic multi-period demonstration are supplied. This is the first, protocol-setting paper of a programme of five or more years, not a validated intervention.

#6 [paper] Can ‘local public food procurement’ extend to healthcare? – A policy content analysis
Authors: Kathy Faulkner, Jorja Collins, Heather Gilbertson, J. Porter, Alexandra Chung
Venue: Frontiers in Nutrition
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2026.1906366
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction Local public food procurement (LPFP) by hospital foodservice offers governments an opportunity to support local food systems and capitalise on multiple co-benefits. Policy is a potential lever to shift procurement practices. This study aims to identify and analyse food policy documents that promote LPFP, to explore how LPFP is represented, and the extent to which it extends to healthcare. Methods Policies from the World Health Organisation (WHO), Global Database on the Implementation of Food and Nutrition Action (GIFNA) were screened for eligibility, descriptively characterised and qualitatively analysed. Results Forty-two policies relating to LPFP were identified; almost 70% targeted schools, half were from Europe and a third were from Latin America and The Caribbean. Five overarching themes described how LPFP was represented in policies: LPFP benefits nutrition and local food culture, social economic development, and environmental sustainability; a multiplier effect where LPFP offers greater value than its initial investment; and variable policy commitment to LPFP. The representation of LPFP was influenced by regional, cultural and context specific factors. Ten policies (24%) included reference to hospitals, mostly described as one of many public institutions that could potentially support LPFP. Just one policy was specific for hospitals which represented LPFP for its environmental benefit. Conclusion Overall, the extent to which local food procurement was recommended in healthcare was minimal. Findings suggest, that to establish LPFP in healthcare and realise its multiplier effect, it should to be prioritised under a strategic national strategy, to better enable a coordinated collaboration across the food supply.

#7 [paper] Making inequities visible: a call for participatory food system dashboards for SDG monitoring
Authors: Rositsa T. Ilieva, Yvette Ng, Nevin Cohen
Venue: Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsufs.2026.1741924
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Municipal governments lack tailored tools to track food system performance at the level of disaggregation required to address equity gaps, hindering robust, science-based monitoring of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of two prototype food equity dashboards (FEED-NYC and East End of Long Island) using a mixed-methods, practice-based design. The approach integrated traditional administrative datasets with novel data sources (web-scraped grocery prices, online store reviews, anonymized mobility data, a…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two regions in New York State: New York City and the East End of Long Island.
Abstract:
Introduction Cities are at the forefront of addressing interconnected challenges of food insecurity, nutrition inequities, and food system sustainability. The United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development calls for robust, science-based indicators to monitor progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet municipal governments often lack tailored tools to track food system performance at the level of disaggregation required to address equity gaps. Methods This paper documents the development of, and insights from, two prototype food equity dashboards developed in New York State: the Food Environment Equity Dashboard NYC (FEED-NYC) and the East End of Long Island Food Equity Dashboard. Using a mixed-methods, practice-based design, we integrated traditional administrative datasets with novel data sources, including web-scraped grocery prices, consumer sentiment from online store reviews, anonymized mobility data, app-based food pantry reservation data, and community narratives gathered through surveys and interviews with service organizations. Indicators were selected and refined through a participatory co-design process involving community organizations, service providers, and government stakeholders, and were implemented as interactive visualizations. Results The dashboards highlight key insights into disparities in food access and security, including varying school meal participation across schools with comparable student poverty levels, gaps between estimated SNAP eligibility and enrollment across community districts, spatial and temporal gaps in emergency food access, and substantial neighborhood-level variation in grocery prices for basic food items. Community narratives indicated levels of unmet need higher than those represented in publicly available statistics. Retrospective mapping of the indicators to the SDG framework showed alignment with SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, and 17, and identified dimensions of local food equity that the current indicator framework does not fully capture. Discussion The dashboards demonstrate how municipal food systems monitoring can advance beyond static metrics to incorporate community knowledge, provide interactive exploration capabilities, and expand opportunities for evidence-based policymaking. Our findings suggest that cities are well-positioned to lead both in monitoring progress and advancing UN SDGs through the visualization of food system metrics that prioritize equity, community engagement, and systemic understanding of food access.

#10 [paper] Distribution Completion, Targeting Accuracy, And Cost-Effectiveness Of Government Food Reserve Disbursement: A Quasi-Experimental Study Of Indonesia's February-March 2026 Food Assistance Program
Authors: Eko Fajar Setiawan
Venue: AJIRSS Asian Journal of Innovative Research in Social Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.53866/ajirss.v5i2.1567
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study evaluates the operational effectiveness, cost-efficiency, and sustainability risk of Indonesia's Government Food Reserve (Cadangan Pangan Pemerintah/CPP) rice and cooking-oil disbursement during the February-March 2026 cycle, covering all 514 districts/cities and 33.24 million target beneficiaries. Using post-audit administrative data, we classify districts by distribution completion (100% versus incomplete disbursement, n=31/514) and apply propensity score matching (PSM), with covariates drawn from the 2025 national Food Security Index (Indeks Ketahanan Pangan/IKP), to estimate the average treatment effect of complete disbursement on audit-verified targeting accuracy. After matching (30 of 31 incomplete-disbursement districts matched within caliper), the estimated effect on targeting accuracy is small and not statistically significant (ATT = -0.00013, SE = 0.00010, p = 0.199), indicating that incomplete disbursement is not associated with materially worse targeting quality once baseline food-security conditions and administrative risk tier are controlled for. Cost-benefit analysis shows non-transporter operational cost (BOP) of IDR 177.2 billion delivered IDR 10,473.3 billion in commodity value at official reference prices (benefit-cost ratio = 59.1), while cost-effectiveness varies more than two-and-a-half-fold across regional offices (IDR 183-528 per kilogram-equivalent). An illustrative, literature-calibrated Social Return on Investment places social value between IDR 194.9 and 11,517.2 billion. Districts with the lowest disbursement completion are concentrated in Papua's highland districts, which also register the lowest food-security scores nationally, suggesting that operational risk and pre-existing food insecurity compound rather than offset each other. With an official strong El Niño forecast for July-September 2026, we argue that distribution risk management should prioritize the small number of chronically under-served districts rather than uniform national cost controls. The study's main limitation is the absence of household-level welfare outcome data, which restricts causal claims to program delivery rather than beneficiary well-being.

#11 [paper] Assessing the environmental impact of clear aligner therapy: a scoping review
Authors: Sapthami Pai, Dhruv Ahuja, Ashith MV, Haneesh Kiran PT, Amoli Singh
Venue: Frontiers in Dental Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fdmed.2026.1849048
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objective To evaluate the environmental impact and sustainability-related practices of clear aligner therapy (CAT), focusing on environmental impact, economic implications, waste management, recycling practices, manufacturing processes, and aligner materials. It further explores the alignment of clear aligner practices with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG's) 3,9,12 and 13. Methodology A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review was guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. A comprehensive literature search was performed across five electronic databases (PubMed Central, Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost) for studies published between January 2014 and December 2024. Studies evaluating the environmental sustainability of clear aligner therapy, including materials, manufacturing processes, waste management, recycling practices, and carbon emissions, were included. Results Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence indicates that clear aligner therapy contributes to plastic waste, microplastic generation, and greenhouse gas emissions throughout its life cycle. The included studies reported biodegradable materials, direct three-dimensional (3D) printing technologies (SDG-9), recycling initiatives (SDG 12), and circular economy approaches as potential strategies to reduce environmental impacts (SDG 3 & 13). However, the implementation of these strategies remains constrained by limited recycling infrastructure, economic considerations, and insufficient high-quality evidence. Conclusion Available evidence suggests that innovations in material selection, circular economy approaches, optimized manufacturing processes, and enhanced recycling programs may reduce the environmental burden associated with clear aligner therapy. Nevertheless, further high-quality environmental assessment studies are required to support the development of more sustainable orthodontic practices aligned with SDGs 3, 9, 12, and 13.

#12 [paper] Expert insight on the design, implementation, and monitoring of future community benefit funds within the energy transition
Authors: E. Boyle, A. Revez, Aoife Deane, B. Ó. Gallachóir
Venue: Discover Energy
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0255d82aaededef457ac0966198f350485bcdc76
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Increasingly, citizen and public participation are considered central to achieving the energy transition to a low carbon future. Such participation has different dimensions in new energy infrastructure, in terms of both renewable energy installations and additional electricity grid developments. Participation includes active involvement in decision making, the ability to invest in developer-led projects, and capacity for community owned renewable energy projects. This also includes community benefit funding (CBF), whereby a local fund is established by the developer and provided to communities impacted by infrastructural developments. There is a growing body of experience with CBF, but it has not received much attention in the scientific literature. In addition, there is a paucity of analysis of the design, implementation, and evaluation of CBF schemes. This research intervention addresses this gap using a modified Delphi panel approach to explore areas of consensus and divergence on these dimensions of CBF programs. We bring together national and international experts on community benefit funding who work on key areas of relevance such as policy formation, strategy design, fund administration, and community development to deliberate on the role of CBF in supporting future developments towards energy system change. The method implemented draws out lessons learned concerning community benefit funding and insights concerning its future design, implementation, and monitoring from a range of sectors and perspectives. While participant experts within the study are made up of three groups: the public, private and academic sectors, the results have specific application in relation to CBF associated with renewable energy production whereby the financial benefit accrued is long lasting over time. This is critically important in the context of the scale of growth planned and the significant associated levels of CBF that will transfer from private funds to public good. The results highlight where there is consensus and divergence of opinion for the design, delivery, and monitoring of CBF, which can usefully inform policy deliberations as well as advancing knowledge as we see CBF growing in significance both in Ireland and internationally.

#13 [paper] REVISITING THE FUNDING MODELS AND SUSTAINABILITY OF NOT-FOR-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS IN NIGERIA: DIRECTION FROM DONOR FUNDING, GRANTS AND ENDOWMENT
Authors: AGHOGHO H. ERAKPOTOBOR, JOHN K. OBAMIRO, JOSEPH A. DADA, Emmanuel Ehimen Okoh
Venue: International Journal of Management Science and Business Analysis Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.70382/caijmsbar.v13i7.0101
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study examined the relationship between funding models and the sustainability of selected not-for-profit organisations in Lagos State, Nigeria. The study investigated how different funding models influence the sustainability of not-for-profit organisations, with particular focus on donor funding, grants and endowments, social enterprise activities, and partnerships. The study was anchored primarily in Resource Dependence Theory and Organisational Sustainability Theory. An explanatory descriptive survey research design was adopted for the study. The population comprised 89 active not-for-profit organisations operating in Lagos State, Nigeria. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to relevant management and finance personnel of the selected organisations. The data collected were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical techniques, such as frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations were used to determine the relationship between funding models and organisational sustainability. The study concludes that the adoption of appropriate and diversified funding models is critical to enhancing the sustainability of not-for-profit organisations in Lagos State. It therefore recommends that not-for-profit organisations reduce excessive dependence on single sources of funding by exploring a balanced combination of donor funding and grants and endowments to promote financial stability, operational continuity, and long-term organisational sustainability.

#14 [grant] Innovative circular solutions for end-of-life footwear through collection, sorting and recycling
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-05
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

Abstract:
Improved forage production is important for increasing livestock productivity and supporting sustainable mixed crop–livestock systems. This study assessed the sustainability of innovative forage technologies within agroforestry practices Dire Enchini District by assessing local community perceptions, identifying determinants of adoption, and examining community-driven forage resource conservation. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 142 randomly selected households from four kebeles: Nanno Jedue, Bilo Abayi, Arfinjo Daga, and Waldo Hene. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the survey data. Nine major improved forage species were identified, with Desho grass (19.0%), Rhodes grass (16.7%), and Napier grass (14.3%) being the most frequently reported. Tree Lucerne (Tagasaste) and Oat–Vetch mixtures each accounted for 7.1%. The major constraints to improved forage adoption were limited access to improved planting materials (31.0%), inadequate institutional support, limited technical knowledge, poor soil fertility (14.3%), and land shortage (7.1%). Male farmers accounted for 85.7% of reported adopters, compared with 14.3% for female farmers. Most respondents (65%) reported a moderate level of experience with improved forage technologies, while only 10% reported a high level of experience. The findings indicate that improved forage production in the study area is constrained primarily by limited access to planting materials, technical knowledge, and institutional support. Strengthening farmer training, extension services, and local forage seed and planting-material multiplication through farmer training centers could support wider adoption and sustainable production of improved forage species suited to local agroecological conditions.

Abstract:
Abstract Background: Digital tools are increasingly promoted to improve the reach, timeliness and continuity of perinatal mental health screening and referral. However, less is known about how digitally integrated screening pathways are adopted by primary care professionals in routine practice. This study examined the implementation of the Matter digital perinatal mental health screening and referral pathway in primary care in Central Alentejo, Portugal, focusing on barriers and facilitators shaping use among healthcare workers. Methods: This qualitative implementation monitoring evaluation examined the Matter programme. A purposive maximum-variation sample of 14 primary care professionals (10 physicians and four nurses) from eight units was recruited from 29 eligible staff. Participants with at least one recorded digital pathway activation before recruitment were classified as users, whereas those with none were classified as non-users. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted in June and July 2025 by an external behavioural science monitoring team independent of programme delivery. Data were analysed in Portuguese using thematic analysis, combining coding informed by the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation-Behaviour model (COM-B) and the Theoretical Domains Framework with inductive theme development; the Behaviour Change Wheel informed implementation recommendations. Results: Participants in both groups recognised the clinical relevance of perinatal mental health screening and considered the Matter programme's digital pathway useful for earlier identification and referral. Positive perceptions did not, however, ensure routine use. Five themes were identified: time pressure and competing clinical demands; technical and workflow barriers; role clarity and team-based implementation; local champions and organisational support; and equity challenges related to language and communication. Adoption was shaped principally by physical and social opportunity, including staff availability, and by variable psychological capability. Facilitators included intuitive platform design, routines outside consultation time, nurse-physician collaboration, responsive support and evidence-informed recommendations. Conclusions: Uneven adoption of the Matter programme's digital pathway was not primarily explained by rejection of perinatal mental health screening, but by whether the pathway could be embedded in routine workflows and team-based care. Sustainable implementation requires role clarity, protected time, reliable technical infrastructure, local support and equity-oriented adaptations. #19 [paper] Funding mechanisms as incentive systems: a role for science philanthropy
Authors: Lillian Parr, Nadia Sarfraz, Sylvina M. Raver, Nadia M. Penrod
Venue: Frontiers in Systems Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1939099
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Biomedical research is shaped not only by scientific questions, but also by the incentive structures that determine what scientists study, how they approach the work, and how success is defined. Current incentives often prioritize individual achievement as a pathway to career advancement, while undervaluing replication, data sharing, mentorship, collaboration, and shared infrastructure. This can make it challenging for scientists to prioritize these contributions, even when they recognize that they are essential for a strong scientific ecosystem. This article examines how funders and funding mechanisms create implicit incentives and argues that funding design is a powerful lever for shaping both scientific behavior and the broader research ecosystem. Philanthropy is uniquely positioned to experiment with funding design by supporting high-risk research, emerging areas, and investments in people, fields, norms, and shared infrastructure that other funders may be unable or unwilling to pursue, while also dedicating resources to learn from how these investments shape scientific behavior. Here, we highlight questions funders can ask about the incentives embedded in funding mechanisms, including what behaviors they encourage, who participates and benefits, and what persists beyond the award. For scientists, understanding funding goals, participating in evaluations, and making contributions beyond traditional outputs visible can strengthen the feedback between funding design and scientific practice. By treating funding mechanisms as design choices that can be tested and refined, philanthropy can generate evidence that informs future funding approaches and strengthens the scientific ecosystem.

Based on the provided evidence, the three papers most directly relevant to a "Marine heatwave early warning project" are:

1.  **Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture** (#3). This paper explicitly presents a "Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM" architecture designed for "operational marine-heatwave early warning" and demonstrates a "38 h mean advisory lead time" for coastal aquaculture, making it directly applicable to developing actionable early warning systems (#3).
2.  **FOCCUS WP9 D9.1 Application Demonstrator: ESC3 – 3.1.2 - Tracking sub-regional marine heatwaves in the Mediterranean Sea** (#16). This paper describes a web-based application that provides "near real-time detection and short-term forecasting of marine heatwaves" using Copernicus Marine satellite products and high-resolution regional model analysis, which serves as a practical blueprint for operational monitoring and forecasting tools (#16).
3.  **The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)** (#7). While focused on terrestrial heat, this study examines the evolution of a heat early warning system (HEWS) from a single trigger to a tiered system and evaluates how operational, institutional, and scientific factors shape system design, providing critical lessons for the design and implementation of any heat early warning system, including marine ones (#7).

Other papers, such as #1 (focusing on decision-maker interpretation of probabilistic predictions), #2 (proposing a new biological stress framework), #4 (describing a specific rescue intervention), #6 (focusing on reef mortality forecasting), #9 (analyzing exposure trends), #11 (using CMIP6 data for ML training), #12 (detecting MHWs in Indonesia), #13 (mitigating MHWs via cloud brightening), #14 (analyzing the 2023 North Atlantic event), #15 (detecting MHWs in the Adriatic), #17 (a duplicate of #16), #18 (reviewing ecosystem responses), #19 (forecasting emergency department demand), and #20 (analyzing concurrent heatwaves) provide supporting context but are less directly focused on the core operational early warning system design and forecasting methodology than the three selected above.
