Problem (Mycelium's reading): How adding probabilistic information to deterministic machine learning water temperature guidance shapes coastal decision-makers' interpretations, perceptions of event likelihood and certainty, and potential decisions and actions for cold-stunning event management.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Qualitative study using scenario-based interviews with returning and new participants, incorporating two interactive visualization activities: (1) comparing deterministic and probabilistic guidance for two scenarios, and (2) ranking five challenging scenarios using an interactive dashboard and slid…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Coastal decision-makers (natural resource managers, weather forecasting entities, and coastal economic operators) involved in the Texas Marine Coldwater Response Collaborative (TCRC) along the Texas coast.
Abstract:
Overview of Interview Materials This repository contains interview protocols and accompanying elicitation materials from a qualitative study of coastal decision-makers’ interpretation and use of deterministic and probabilistic machine learning water temperature predictions for cold-stunning event management along the Texas coast. Participants included natural resource managers, weather forecasting entities, and coastal economic operators involved in the Texas Marine Coldwater Response Collaborative (TCRC). The study builds upon prior work with TCRC members examining how users assess, interpret, and trust cold-stunning predictive information, including operational deterministic machine learning water temperature forecasts (White et al., 2026). Through scenario-based interviews with returning and new participants, this follow-up study examined how adding probabilistic information to deterministic guidance shaped interpretations, perceptions of event likelihood and certainty in the guidance, and potential decisions and actions. Materials include protocols for new and returning participants, links to two interactive visualization activities, and an accompanying scenario-ranking slide deck. Interview Protocols Two versions of the interview protocol accommodated participants with and without prior participation in the earlier interview study: New participants: Includes introductory questions about professional roles, organizational risks associated with cold-stunning events, information sources, preparedness and response actions, and communication pathways. Returning participants: Omits the introductory background questions and proceeds to the visualization activities following the interview preamble. Both versions include the following two activities and associated discussion questions. Activity 1: Interpretation and Comparison of Deterministic and Probabilistic Information Participants explored two potential cold-stunning event scenarios using an interactive dashboard. Within each scenario, participants first viewed deterministic water temperature guidance (Scenarios 1A and 2A), followed by probabilistic guidance for the same event (Scenarios 1B and 2B). The visualizations displayed observations and predictions, allowing participants to examine water temperature values over time. Interview questions explored participants’ interpretations, perceptions of certainty, potential actions and their timing, and the forecast features informing those assessments. Additional questions addressed interpretations of the shaded uncertainty ranges, strengths and weaknesses of each presentation format, forecast preferences, and perceived decision-making challenges. Access Activity 1: Deterministic and Probabilistic Scenario Comparisons Activity 2: Ranking Challenging Cold-Stunning Event Scenarios Participants compared probabilistic water temperature guidance across five potential cold-stunning event scenarios: the two scenarios examined in Activity 1 and three additional scenarios. Participants explored the forecasts using an interactive dashboard and used the accompanying PowerPoint slide deck to rank the scenarios from least to most challenging for decision-making. They were encouraged to think aloud while exploring and ranking the scenarios. Follow-up questions examined which forecast characteristics influenced their rankings and what made particular scenarios more or less challenging. Access Activity 2: Five-Scenario Exploration This material is based upon work supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation under Grant No. RISE-2019758 and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Adminstration, Office of Education Educational Partnership Program award (NA21SEC4810004).

#2 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#3 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#6 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection

Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#7 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

This is Stage 1 (OCEAN-001) of a research programme on conservative transport diagnostics of marine heatwaves (MHWs) and cold spells (MCSs) in the East Sea (Japan Sea), 1993–2022, based on the GLORYS12V1 reanalysis and ERA5 surface fluxes. What the record contains. (1) The analysis code (01_Scripts/): a cubical 2-complex on the Arakawa C-grid, a first-order upwind (donor-cell) transport operator for two positive thermal masses (a temperature-variance mass, Track A, and a positively truncated excess-heat mass, Track B), the exact four-face compression identity, the discrete chain-rule (variance-mixing) correction, the discrete Hodge decomposition of the internal heat current (sparse LU), Schnakenberg entropy production and cycle affinity, and a retrospective, event-conditioned regression with year-block hold-out and cross-validation, surrogate nulls (face-transport permutation, node-mass permutation, other-year velocity with slot-matched baselines, fixed-coefficient velocity reversal) and paired year-block bootstraps. (2) Derived data for 672 offshore events (42,888 event-days): per-object peak files, daily diagnostics (daily_hodge_672.parquet), event features, statistics, and all regression/null summary tables. (3) The accumulated normal-equation sums of the real design matrices and of all surrogates (second archive), from which every regression result of the paper can be refitted without the original fields. (4) The LaTeX sources with the auto-generated macro file that carries every number in the paper, the figures and the PDF. (5) The SHA-256 manifest of all input files and the two independent audit reports with the author's responses. Reproducibility. All tables, figures and numbers of the paper regenerate from this record alone (c03–c06, c04 --fit). Regeneration from the raw fields requires the public GLORYS12V1 (GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_PHY_001_030, accessed 7 April 2025) and ERA5 (accessed 10 April 2025) products and the preprocessing of the population network study (10.5281/zenodo.23362418); see README.md. Main results. With all four faces of a cell counted, the compression term is about one fifth of the conservative tendency magnitude near the peak (MHW 0.21, MCS 0.23) and the three-quarter “compression” of an internal-only graph is an open-boundary artefact; the discrete variance-mixing term is of the same order. The Hodge curl fraction is larger in MCSs and the signed plaquette circulation reproduces the vorticity polarity of the host flow (anticyclonic in MHWs, cyclonic in MCSs; ρ = 0.97 with ζ/f). A formal entropy production is larger in MHWs per unit mean speed. In the regression, the downstream-drift part of the upwind operator carries almost all of the skill of advection, the compression and base-exchange coefficients are strongly attenuated, and a quarter to two fifths of the mean-square target is a change of the event mean beyond any zero-sum redistribution. Software environment: Python 3.10; numpy 2.2, scipy 1.15, pandas 2.3, pyarrow 25, matplotlib 3.10, h5py 3.16, netCDF4 1.7; TeX Live. License: MIT (code), CC BY 4.0 (data, figures, documents). The analysis pipeline was written with the assistance of large-language-model tools (Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI Codex, November 2026); the author specified the methods, reviewed and ran the code, and the key results were re-computed independently in the included audits.

Abstract:

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. While extensive research has documented the impacts of these events, most studies have examined individual heatwaves or specific taxonomic groups in isolation, limiting our understanding of cumulative and cascading effects across the ecosystem. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. Abstract Marine (MHWs) and atmospheric heatwaves (AHWs) are intensifying with climate change, but their co-occurrence as concurrent heatwaves (CHWs) poses an even greater threat to marine ecosystems. Based on the provided evidence, the current status of marine heatwave early warning efforts involves the development and validation of several new, advanced systems and frameworks across different regions and timescales:

*   **Mediterranean Reefs:** A new explainable, policy-aware early-warning system has been developed to forecast site-level risk in Mediterranean coralligenous reefs using historical mass mortality data from 1986 to 2020 #1. This model has been validated on independent prospective test data from 2019 to 2020 and achieves an average precision of 0.75 #1. The system is currently available as an open-access interactive decision-support platform to support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning #1.
*   **South Korean Aquaculture:** A new Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM model has been benchmarked for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture, achieving the lowest 1-hour RMSE of 0.057 °C among tested models #5. This system demonstrated a mean advisory lead time of 38 hours during the 2024 regional high water temperature alert period #5.
*   **Coral Reef Regions:** Research has confirmed that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity in 12 vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales, with anthropogenic warming identified as the dominant source of this long-term forecast skill #6.
*   **Dutch Heat Warning System:** The Dutch heat early warning system has evolved from a single trigger into a tiered warning system, although a misalignment remains between the warning levels and the linked Heat-Health Action Plan #2. Current projections indicate that the frequency of heat warnings will increase substantially, rising from approximately 2 per year currently to between 3.9 and 7 by 2050, and up to 29 by 2100 #2.
*   **Subsurface and Regional Detection:** New frameworks are being established to better detect and characterize marine heatwaves, including the use of high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling Systems (ROMS) with eddy diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea #3. Additionally, glider observations in the North Sea are being used to improve the analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies, which satellite data alone cannot fully capture #10.
*   **Upwelling Collapse:** Seasonal forecasting systems have demonstrated the capability to provide early warning of upwelling collapse, such as the extreme event in the Gulf of Panama in 2025, which was accurately predicted a season in advance #14.
*   **Methodological Advances:** New probabilistic frameworks, such as the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW), are being proposed to shift focus from statistical temperature anomalies to biologically relevant thermal exposure #16. Furthermore, studies are evaluating whether localized interventions, such as marine cloud brightening, can effectively mitigate the impacts of predicted marine heatwaves #17.

Abstract. This study presents cSINGV v1.0, a high-resolution (1.5 km) regional coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling system developed for the Western Maritime Continent (WMC). The system integrates a convection-permitting atmospheric model (SINGV) with newly configured ocean (NEMO) and wave (WAVEWATCH III) components within a unified coupling framework based on the Regional Coupled Suite and OASIS3-MCT coupler. The primary contribution of this work lies in the development of a fully coupled system enabling two-way interactions between atmosphere, ocean, and waves at kilometre scale. The influence of coupling is assessed by comparing the coupled and uncoupled atmospheric configurations. Overall, cSINGV provides a physically consistent framework for representing coupled processes in the WMC and offers a useful platform for investigating air–sea–wave interactions at convection-permitting scales.

Abstract Marine heatwaves (MHWs) in the Gulf of Mexico (GoM) have become more frequent and intense, yet the mechanisms governing basin‐scale events remain incompletely understood. #3 [paper] Breaking barriers: advancing strategies to foster a circular economy through additive manufacturing – a case study in the plastics industry
Authors: Alexander Bade, Rebecca Kißner, Jacob Lohmer, Rainer Lasch
Venue: Journal of Business Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11573-026-01283-w
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The manufacturing industry faces the challenge of using resources more efficiently and implementing circular practices. A promising pathway is to establish a circular economy (CE) through additive manufacturing (AM), enabling on-demand production with low material input and allowing the use of recycled materials. Despite this potential, practical barriers hinder its adoption and are insufficiently understood from a multi-stakeholder perspective. This paper combines stakeholder theory with the circular supply chain management concept in a qualitative multiple-case study to examine the perspectives and interactions of the actors involved. The findings separate the general technical adoption barriers of AM from the socioeconomic and relational barriers of circularity, which arise from power asymmetries, information asymmetries, and coordination failures among interdependent actors of differing salience. These barriers vary substantially with firms’ initial conditions, including their AM technology maturity, their engagement in closed-loop practices, and the managerial relevance they assign to circularity. The study develops five propositions based on the cross-case analysis and identifies three distinct pathways from barrier to solution for firms at different stages of circular supply chain development. Trust-based partnerships between manufacturing and recycling companies can close material loops locally, but they remain fragile amid price competition from virgin materials. Durable circularity therefore requires governance safeguards, including guaranteed-offtake contracts, verifiable production information, and consolidated reverse logistics, all supported by regulatory intervention. The study contributes to the CE and operations management literature by providing a deeper understanding of these barriers and proposing actionable measures for stakeholders to promote circularity in the specific AM domain.

This study aimed to explore the communication barriers faced by the waste picker community in reducing plastic waste in Maros Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia.A qualitative case study design was conducted from March to May 2025.Seven informants, comprising five active waste pickers, one waste collector, and one official of the Maros Regency Environmental Agency, were selected purposively.Data were collected through participant observation and in-depth interviews and analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña.Trustworthiness was established through source and method triangulation and member checking.Five barriers were identified: (1) varied and generally low environmental literacy; (2) a mismatch between the communication channels used and the community's access and habits, as digital media were rarely accessible; (3) overly technical messages that were difficult to understand and apply; (4) low community participation; and (5) inadequate waste-handling infrastructure.These findings indicate that communication barriers occur at the levels of the message, the channel, and the receiver, and are reinforced by structural constraints.Plastic waste reduction programs should therefore use interpersonal and participatory communication through trusted intermediaries such as waste collectors, deliver simple and visual messages, and be accompanied by improved sorting facilities.

#5 [paper] A transdisciplinary approach to food systems communication: a community case study at a science museum
Authors: Rebekah Schulz, Jennifer Schmitt, John Gordon, Len Marquart, Hikaru Peterson
Venue: Frontiers in Communication
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2026.1755194

Abstract:
Since the global food system faces complex crises including the compounding cycles of climate change, resource degradation, and inadequate food and nutrient provision, transdisciplinary approaches hold promise for effectively addressing these challenges. One effective strategy to engage consumers as agents of change within the food system is to empower individuals with the knowledge to make informed choices. However, as food systems involve complex topics, designing effective communication remains a challenge. We posit that a transdisciplinary approach is crucial to reflect the complexity of our food systems and to leverage behavior change. This project documents the 1.5-year transdisciplinary collaboration between scientists and developers from the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment and Food Science and Nutrition department as well as the Science Museum of Minnesota. The project was focused on creating exhibit prototypes for the Museum’s upcoming Future of Food exhibition. By overlaying a transdisciplinary framework over the project, we use this project as a case study for examining the notion that a transdisciplinary approach can better communicate the complexity of our food system to consumers. The project team created five exhibit prototypes and tested them with museum visitors following the structure of the transdisciplinary framework. Qualitative data included notes from bimonthly team meetings, first-hand accounts of visitor interactions while testing prototypes, and formal ex-post evaluation with the project team. Based on this feedback, the transdisciplinary collaboration resulted in richer food systems prototypes due to the integration of diverse collaborator perspectives and knowledge. This case study adds to the body of literature advocating for transdisciplinary collaborations to transform food systems, specifically through generating the hypothesis that transdisciplinary food systems communication can aid in engaging consumers with their food systems, ultimately leading to food literacy and behavior change.

#6 [paper] Towards family-friendly conferences: results from a first survey in the geosciences
Authors: Elena Päffgen, Lisa Schielicke, Leonie Esters
Venue: Geoscience Communication
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/gc-9-345-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Building an academic career requires a high level of dedication to research, frequent publishing, and maintaining visibility within the academic community. Scientific conferences are the central platforms for networking and knowledge exchange, making them keystones of an academic career. However, the early stages of an academic career often coincide with family planning considerations. Many young researchers face the challenge of balancing professional responsibilities with family obligations. A balancing act that becomes particularly difficult during non-routine work events such as conferences. Such occasions tend to pose significant organizational challenges for families. As mothers still provide most of the care, they are disproportionately affected. This conflict is an important factor contributing to the “leaky pipeline” by inhibiting the progression of women through academic ranks. Increasing the family-friendliness of conferences has the potential to diversify the scientific community, allowing more parents to participate, while reducing the tension between academic work and family obligations. Here, we present the results of an online survey among researchers in the geoscientific field, primarily based in Europe. The required support of parents at scientific conferences is analyzed and the acceptance for the implementation of new support offered by researchers without children is examined. Our key findings are that (1) parents wish for more support at conferences, (2) the majority of non-parents welcome family-friendly measures, and (3) conference organizers can accomplish a lot in this respect, even with small adjustments. The responses we received from parents paint a qualitative picture of measures that can be considered to create a family-friendly conference experience, ranging from increased transparency and awareness for the challenges of parents to tangible offers such as childcare and financial support. Our findings are distilled into guidelines for conference organizers, allowing them to better address the work-family conflict and transform their conferences towards more equity, diversity, and inclusion.

#7 [paper] Navigating the practice of co-produced convergence research: Lessons from projects funded by NSF's Coastlines and People (CoPe) program.
Authors: Tilt, Jenna H, Behl, Mona V, Moore, Laura J, Mosier, Samantha L, Auermuller, Lisa, Zarger, Rebecca
Venue: Cambridge prisms. Coastal futures

Abstract:
Convergent, co-produced coastal research engages researchers across disciplines and brings together researchers, practitioners and community representatives to co-create new knowledge and understanding to support community resilience while advancing scientific understanding. This type of research is increasingly required by funding agencies and yet it is relatively new. Given this, along with the expansive range of scholarly and lived expertise required to carry out this type of research, there are many epistemological, relational, temporal and institutional challenges for successful projects to overcome. Here we describe these challenges, along with strategies employed to overcome them, based on the work of multiple convergent, co-production research projects focused on coastal communities and environments, funded by the National Science Foundation's Coastlines and People (CoPe) Program. Our experience leads us to recommend that project leaders use inclusive communication practices; incorporate boundary spanners; build shared understanding; select the style and depth of co-production intentionally; focus on earning trust; tailor co-production approaches to the communities involved; equalize power dynamics; embrace and acknowledge the expanded timeline required; plan for delays; embrace flexibility; and build and sustain partnerships for the long haul. Additionally, supporting this type of work requires academic institutions to reward and value the best research practices and research products that emerge from convergent, community-engaged research, including revision of promotion and tenure guidelines to accommodate the expanded timelines required, and the different types of outcomes and products arising from these types of efforts. Further, we recommend that funders consider offering staged, progressive funding opportunities and longer funding timeframes, in recognition of the time it takes to build and sustain meaningful, trusting community partnerships and to plan research projects in a deeply collaborative way with community partners.

Year: 2026

Abstract:
This paper examines how volumetric reasoning permeates everyday practices in Bangkok’s circular economies. While circular economies calculate, value, and contain plastic waste, mobile waste flows are hidden from view and often evade regulation. As a result, circular economy initiatives struggle to account for low-value waste, microplastics, and chemicals that proliferate through land, water, air, and blood in bodies. In these instances, waste travels and transforms volumetrically without a traceable latitude and longitude. Similarly, the actual dimensions of plastic objects impact their ability to be valued in the circular economy. Drawing on seventeen months of ethnographic fieldwork in Bangkok, Thailand, this paper documents how circular economy practitioners manage waste that takes on new materialities as it moves through plastic circularity loops. Nonstate waste practitioners invoke volumetric reasoning as they grapple with circular economy solutions (e.g., recovering, repurposing, and upcycling plastics). My argument is twofold: first, I argue that practitioners’ everyday volumetric practices expose the limits of formal circular economy policy. Second, I argue that volumetric reasoning gives practitioners a set of techniques for reclaiming agency over the everyday management of waste. By attending to commonplace yet novel spatial dimensions of plastic circularity, this paper contributes to emerging scholarship at the intersection of political ecology and volumetric analyses of plastic pollution in Asia.

Yes, the provided evidence contains multiple studies detailing the mechanisms, modeling, and observation of how marine litter is transported and beached.

Several studies utilize Lagrangian particle-tracking models to simulate the transport and coastal deposition of floating debris. For instance, a study on the Mediterranean Sea presents a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded observations from shipboard surveys as initial conditions to predict transport and coastal deposition #2. Similarly, research on the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire employed a Lagrangian particle-tracking model forced by high-resolution ocean circulation data to assess seasonal beaching dynamics, finding that regional hydrodynamics play a dominant role in shaping debris distribution #5. Another study focused on the East/Japan Sea evaluated near-surface forcing combinations, such as geostrophic currents, wind-driven currents, and wave-induced drift, to improve the accuracy of floating debris transport modeling #20.

Field-based observations and specific physical mechanisms are also documented in the feed. A campaign in the Dutch Wadden Sea tracked shallow surface drifters to characterize the transport and coastal interaction dynamics of floating macroplastic in intertidal regions, noting that wind towards the coast increases the frequency of interactions #6. Additionally, a laboratory investigation explored the mechanism of particle pickup in wave–swash interactions, finding that the interaction between consecutive waves produces the vertical forces required to suspend negatively buoyant debris on natural beaches #16.

The evidence also includes specific tools and guidelines related to these processes. A code repository was shared for a tide-resolving beaching kernel developed for particle-tracking experiments, which was applied to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea #15. Furthermore, guidelines for marine monitoring and assessment of beach litter were updated by the OSPAR Beach Litter Expert Group #4. While some studies focus on the resulting accumulation rather than the transport process itself, such as those on the Norwegian coast #19, Trindade Island #1, and tropical small islands #8, the feed explicitly covers the dynamics of how litter moves to and settles on beaches.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#2 [paper] Marine litter in the Mediterranean: observation-based Lagrangian particle tracking
Authors: Santiago Bravo, Eugenia Pasanisi, Svitlana Liubartseva, Giovanni Coppini, Alice Madonia, Igor Atake, Marta Azzolin, Lara Carosso

Method (Mycelium's reading): A data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework using Parcels, initialized with monthly gridded FMML observations from shipboard surveys and forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusio…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean Sea, specifically areas surveyed via the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries from August 2023 to December 2024.
Abstract:
Introduction The Mediterranean is a major hotspot for floating marine macro-litter (FMML) accumulation, yet spatially explicit, observation-grounded predictions of its transport and coastal deposition remain scarce. We present a data-driven stochastic Lagrangian framework that uses monthly gridded FMML observations from systematic shipboard surveys as simulation initial conditions complementing existing source-based modelling approaches. Methods Observations were collected from August 2023 to December 2024 within the LIFE Conceptu Maris Project using ferries as monitoring platforms under a standardised protocol. A total of 158 surveys detected 4,801 FMML items across approximately 6,200 km² of surveyed sea surface, of which more than 62% were artificial polymers. Observed monthly FMML item counts at 5 × 5 km resolution initialised ensemble Lagrangian simulations (18 members per target month; 17.2–32.5 million virtual particles per seeding window, 5,000 particles per observed item) using Parcels, forced by Copernicus Marine Service Mediterranean reanalysis currents and ERA5 wind fields with a 1% windage coefficient and a 2D random-walk turbulent diffusion scheme. Monthly frequency-of-occurrence maps were computed at the sea surface and on coastlines. Results The Southern Tyrrhenian and Northern Ligurian seas, including the Pelagos Sanctuary, exhibited in 2024 near-persistent high sea surface FMML occurrence, peaking in late summer–autumn and reaching a seasonal minimum in winter–early spring. The Balearic Sea showed elevated occurrence from late spring through summer (May–September), declining through autumn. The Adriatic displayed intense sub-basin-scale spreading from January to June and again in December, with summer leakage into the Northern Ionian Sea. Coastal deposition frequencies were highest on Corsica, western Sardinia and northern Tunisia, then the south-eastern Tyrrhenian and Ligurian–Tuscan margins, with Valencia–Barcelona largely confined to summer. Integration with loggerhead turtle nesting records illustrates how coastal frequency-of-occurrence maps can support conservation applications. Discussion A web-based Particle Analysis Dashboard translates these outputs into an interactive tool with Marine Protected and Conserved Area overlays for scientists and decision-makers. The framework provides a scalable, observation-anchored foundation for MSFD Descriptor 10 monitoring, transferable to other semi-enclosed sea basins. Priority future work includes complementary validation against independent beach-litter monitoring data, integration of land-based source inventories, and linkage with species distribution models.

Abstract:
Beach management practices are widely implemented in coastal environments, yet their association with litter size structure remains poorly understood. We evaluated macro- and meso-litter across vegetated (unmanaged) and non-vegetated (managed) beach areas along the northwestern Adriatic coast (Italy) through seasonal stratified surveys comprising 448 plot-level sampling events across 112 plots. Meso-litter accounted for approximately 84% of all recorded items. Negative binomial generalized linear mixed models revealed a significant interaction between litter size class and area type (p < 0.001). Macro-litter abundance was 53% lower in non-vegetated areas (p < 0.001), whereas meso-litter abundance did not differ significantly between area types (p = 0.539). Binomial mixed models further indicated a higher predicted proportion of meso-litter within the combined meso- plus macro-litter total in non-vegetated areas (OR = 2.70, p < 0.001), revealing a compositional shift toward smaller debris fractions in managed beach sectors. These findings suggest that beach management is associated with changes in litter size structure and that monitoring approaches based exclusively on macro-litter may not fully capture variation in coastal litter composition. Incorporating meso-litter into monitoring programs could therefore improve assessments of coastal litter dynamics and support more comprehensive management strategies.

Abstract:

The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). #1 [paper] Barriers to living walls implementation in Saudi Arabian sustainable construction projects: A PLS-SEM approach
Authors: Naif Sultan Alaboud
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-76473-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
To maximize financial benefits and sustainability throughout a project’s lifecycle, the construction industry must move beyond the partial implementation of living wall (LW). While the existing literature has focused on LW drivers, there is a lack of comprehensive evidence regarding implementation barriers. This study prioritizes and assesses the LW implementation barriers in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) building industry. Data were collected via an expert survey and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The model demonstrated robust internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability meeting the required thresholds, and average variance extracted values exceeding the 0.50 (50%) requirement. Based on the second-order analysis, the identified LW barriers were found to be formative, but collinearity was assessed and found to be within the acceptable thresholds (VIF < 3.5), ensuring the distinct contribution of each formative indicator. The path model results showed that awareness and economic barriers ( β = 0.278), integration and complexity barriers (β = 0.303), operational and behavioral barriers (β = 0.380), and resource and structural barriers (β = 0.372) significantly impede LW implementation (all p ≤ 0.001). Conversely, maintenance and technical barriers (β = 0.097) were not significant ( p = 0.227), indicating their minimal impact compared with the other model constructs. These findings provide policy guidance concerning LW adoption in the KSA and other Gulf nations, facilitating the completion of projects by removing the barriers to LW implementation and enhancing their overall success.

#2 [paper] The mPFC-reuniens-hippocampus pathway links brain circuitry and neural plasticity in antidepressant response
Authors: Maxime Veleanu, Louise E. Schuberth, Antje Kilias, Jakob Weber, Jan Warneke, Lovis Würz, Tim Schwär, Rebecca Heck
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-77248-y
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The pathophysiology of depression involves multiple biological processes, including circuit dysfunction and impaired neuroplasticity, yet an integrative view linking these processes remains elusive. Here, we identify a convergent circuit for antidepressant response and plasticity modulation. We demonstrate that chemogenetic activation of the infralimbic cortex (IL) exerts rapid antidepressant-like effects across multiple behavioral domains in a mouse model of stress-induced depression. IL stimulation exerts top-down control over the hippocampus, enhancing structural plasticity, restoring long-term potentiation deficits and improving state-dependent network dynamics in the ventral hippocampus (vHIPP). We identify the thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) as a necessary mediator of these effects. Notably, direct inhibition of RE, its inputs from IL or projections to vHIPP, blocks both IL stimulation-induced antidepressant response and the therapeutic and neuroplastic effects of ketamine. Our findings demonstrate that the functional IL → RE→vHIPP circuit plays a central role in the antidepressant response, linking circuit activity, hippocampal plasticity, and depressive-like behaviors.

#3 [paper] BARRIERS TO PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS IN THE CONSTRUCTION SECTOR IN IRAQ
Authors: Ruaa Mahdi, Özge Alboga, Ahmad Reshad Noorı, Serkan Aydınlı
Venue: Konya Journal of Engineering Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.36306/konjes.1789018
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
During the management of public-private partnerships (PPPs), numerous barriers may arise that could negatively affect the implementation of partnerships in investment projects. For developing economies such as Iraq, where the PPP project delivery system has a high potential to offer significant benefits, it is important to identify the barriers to the system in a hierarchical manner. This study aims to identify the barriers that prevent the adoption of PPPs in Iraq's construction sector. First, potential barriers were identified through a literature review. Subsequently, a survey focusing on four main categories of barriers (legal, technical, implementation, and political) was administered to sector professionals in Iraq. The analytic hierarchy process method was used to determine the importance of the barrier groups. The findings indicate that legal barriers were found to have the highest impact on the PPPs in Iraq, technical barriers and implementation barriers have equally impact, and political barriers were found to be the least influential barrier group. Additionally, it was determined that most of the barriers contributing to the failure of PPPs projects stem from misguidance by consultants in decision-making processes. The study suggests that identifying potential challenges related to public-private partnership legislation could be beneficial in helping Iraq become a country with a high standard of living at all levels.

#4 [paper] The Fragmentation of Material Flows: Mapping Barriers to Circular Economy Adoption in Bangladesh's Ready‐Made Garment Sector
Authors: Sutapa Chowdhury, Saniyat Islam, Caroline Swee Lin Tan, Rebecca Van Amber, Mustafijur Rahman
Venue: Business Strategy and the Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/bse.71711
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT This paper provides an empirical diagnosis of the systemic challenges preventing the transition to a circular economy (CE) in Bangladesh's ready‐made garment (RMG) sector. Drawing on in‐depth interviews ( n = 13) with key industry stakeholders, the study characterises current waste flows and analyses the barriers to circularity. Findings reveal a predominantly linear material flow dominated by informal networks and constrained by a lack of traceability, limited recycling infrastructure and weak policy support. The study identifies power asymmetry between global brands and local manufacturers as one of four interacting ‘lock‐in’ mechanisms, alongside institutional voids, infrastructural and technological constraints and traceability failure, that together prevent the industry from moving beyond fragmented, linear practices. This structural governance failure actively inhibits progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 12, particularly Targets 12.5 and 12.6. Based on the multilevel perspective, supplemented by institutional theory and the resource‐based view, the analysis argues that the current linear production regime is maintained by institutional voids and internal resource constraints that must be addressed before prescriptive solutions can be operationalised. The empirical scope centres on postproduction and preconsumer waste governance; postconsumer textile waste is examined specifically as an import‐ and feedstock‐classification barrier rather than as an empirically traced material flow.

#5 [paper] Breaking barriers: advancing strategies to foster a circular economy through additive manufacturing – a case study in the plastics industry
Authors: Alexander Bade, Rebecca Kißner, Jacob Lohmer, Rainer Lasch
Venue: Journal of Business Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11573-026-01283-w
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The manufacturing industry faces the challenge of using resources more efficiently and implementing circular practices. A promising pathway is to establish a circular economy (CE) through additive manufacturing (AM), enabling on-demand production with low material input and allowing the use of recycled materials. Despite this potential, practical barriers hinder its adoption and are insufficiently understood from a multi-stakeholder perspective. This paper combines stakeholder theory with the circular supply chain management concept in a qualitative multiple-case study to examine the perspectives and interactions of the actors involved. The findings separate the general technical adoption barriers of AM from the socioeconomic and relational barriers of circularity, which arise from power asymmetries, information asymmetries, and coordination failures among interdependent actors of differing salience. These barriers vary substantially with firms’ initial conditions, including their AM technology maturity, their engagement in closed-loop practices, and the managerial relevance they assign to circularity. The study develops five propositions based on the cross-case analysis and identifies three distinct pathways from barrier to solution for firms at different stages of circular supply chain development. Trust-based partnerships between manufacturing and recycling companies can close material loops locally, but they remain fragile amid price competition from virgin materials. Durable circularity therefore requires governance safeguards, including guaranteed-offtake contracts, verifiable production information, and consolidated reverse logistics, all supported by regulatory intervention. The study contributes to the CE and operations management literature by providing a deeper understanding of these barriers and proposing actionable measures for stakeholders to promote circularity in the specific AM domain.

#6 [paper] Sustainable Manufacturing Practices in the Plastic Packaging Industry and Associated Barriers: A Systematic Literature Review
Authors: Anny Jasbleidy Avendaño Avendaño, Fernando Antônio Forcellini
Venue: Circular Economy and Sustainability
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s43615-026-01161-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The plastic packaging industry is a major contributor to environmental impacts due to its intensive use of fossil-based materials and low recycling rates. In this context, Sustainable Manufacturing (SM) has emerged as a strategic approach to mitigate these impacts while balancing environmental, economic, and social dimensions. However, the literature remains fragmented, particularly regarding the integration of practices, barriers, and performance in sustainability. This study aims to systematically identify and analyze SM practices in the plastic packaging industry, examine the barriers to their implementation, and propose an integrated framework that relates practices, barriers, and performance in the dimensions of the Triple Bottom Line (TBL). A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA protocol, searching the Scopus and Web of Science databases without temporal restrictions. A total of 18 peer-reviewed articles were selected for in-depth content analysis. The data were coded and categorized to identify practices, barriers, and their interrelationships. The results indicate a predominance of practices focused on the environmental dimension, such as sustainable design and development, recycling, and resource efficiency, while social practices remain underexplored. Significant barriers include high investment costs, technological limitations, inadequate recycling infrastructure, and regulatory inconsistencies. Based on these findings, this study proposes an integrated framework that captures the relationships among SM practices, barriers to implementation, and performance across TBL dimensions. This framework contributes to advancing theoretical understanding and provides practical support for managers and policymakers in promoting a more systemic and sustainable transition in the plastic packaging industry.

#7 [paper] From total volume control to governance logic: a legal review and institutional solution for the production cap rules in global plastics agreements
Authors: Pan Zhang, Shuai Zhang, Yuxian Zheng, W Chen, Pengyuan Fu
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1969913
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The issue of global plastic pollution has become a pressing environmental concern that requires a unified response from the international community. Ongoing negotiations for the “Global Plastics Convention” are positioning upstream production controls as the primary strategy for combating plastic pollution. Among these provisions, the debate over whether to impose an upper limit on the total volume of virgin plastic production stands out as the most contentious. This study employed normative analysis, textual analysis, and comparative legal methods, using various draft negotiation texts from the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee as the basis for analysis. It also draws upon the rules of treaty interpretation under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), along with fundamental principles of international environmental law, such as the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and the principle of state sovereignty. The evolution of negotiations concerning the upstream control clauses of the Global Plastics Convention was traced systematically through the multi-layered approach. The findings reveal that the disputes surrounding upstream controls are not merely a result of political bargaining; rather, they arise from the interaction of various normative conflicts. These conflicts primarily reflect deep-rooted tensions between interpretations of treaty authorization and the principles governing responsibility allocation. Building on this analysis, the study further explored how barriers—including reliance on end-of-pipe solutions, jurisdictional fragmentation, and insufficient institutional provisions—have triggered and intensified these legal conflicts. This study argues that relying solely on rigid “total volume control” clauses is insufficient for reconciling the differing interests of stakeholders. Instead, a shift is necessary towards a reconfigured governance logic that emphasizes risk classification, tiered responsibility allocation, and the effective integration of soft and stringent governance measures. Based on this framework, the study proposes an alternative upstream governance mechanism that includes hierarchical classification-based controls, a two-tier collaborative governance model, a differentiated CBDR(Common but Differentiated Responsibilities) mechanism, and an accompanying supporting safeguard system. The contributions of this study are twofold: theoretically, it clarifies the legal conflicts underlying the debates over production limits and advances the academic discourse on the transition from rigid law to soft law within international environmental law; practically, it offers a compromise solution aimed at enhancing the institutional design of upstream control provisions within the Global Plastics Convention, thereby balancing juridical legitimacy with operational feasibility.

#8 [paper] China’s approach to tackling marine plastic pollution: an institutional analysis centered on the ecological and environmental code
Authors: Yangyi Wu, Tianzi Yu, Yuxian Zheng, Wen Kuang
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1998994
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The governance of marine plastic pollution has long been hindered by two significant challenges: the fragmentation of international norms and the disconnect between domestic legislation. The first challenge arises from the lack of alignment among international agreements—such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the London Convention, and the Basel Convention—regarding their scope and regulatory subjects. The second challenge is reflected in the dispersed nature of relevant regulations across various statutes and the inadequacy of the land-sea separation approach, which fails to effectively address the predominantly land-based origins of plastic pollution. The enactment of the 2026 Ecological and Environmental Code presents a new normative foundation aimed at alleviating these contradictions. This paper focuses on the Ecological and Environmental Code and employs three methodological approaches—normative analysis, comparative law, and legal hermeneutics—to explore its institutional framework. The analysis centers on two fundamental principles: integrated land-sea management and whole-life-cycle governance. It examines the Code’s provisions across three critical stages: source reduction, process control, and end-of-pipe disposal. The paper compares this Code with relevant extraterritorial legislative examples from the European Union, Japan, and South Korea. The study reveals that the Code effectively connects its General Provisions, the Pollution Prevention and Control Chapter, the Green and Low-Carbon Development Chapter, and the Legal Liability Chapter through internal coordination. This integrated land-sea management approach spans the regulatory chain from production to ocean discharge. The Code’s “multi-chapter synergy” structure offers distinct systemic advantages for comprehensive governance of marine plastic pollution across its life cycle, partially overcoming limitations in existing environmental law, which often neglects whole-life-cycle governance. Nonetheless, in comparison to standalone extraterritorial legislation, the Code shows institutional gaps in areas such as source-based total quantity control, specific operational rules for the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regime, dynamic management of new pollutant lists, and alignment with international conventions. This paper suggests recommendations for improvement in three key areas: governance philosophy, institutional specifics, and performance mechanisms. These recommendations aim to serve as a theoretical reference for future revisions of the Code and for negotiations related to the Global Plastics Treaty, while also facilitating the effective alignment of domestic regulations with upcoming international frameworks.

#9 [paper] Profiles of Structural Exclusion in the Twin Transition: Ideal Types, Political Disaffection, and Participatory Governance
Authors: Andrés Arias Astray, Melisa Campana, David Alonso González, Juan Iglesias
Venue: Politics and Governance
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17645/pag.12501
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The simultaneous pursuit of green decarbonisation and digital transformation (the twin transition) generates disproportionate structural burdens on marginalised social groups.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Max Weber’s ideal-type methodology (Idealtypus) and comparative analysis of recurring exclusion mechanisms.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Spanish statistical evidence across sectors including urban mobility, platform/gig economy, rural energy, digital public infrastructure, digital agriculture, and urban renovation.
Abstract:
This article analyses how the simultaneous pursuit of green decarbonisation and digital transformation—the twin transition—generates disproportionate structural burdens on marginalised social groups. Drawing on Max Weber’s ideal‐type methodology (Idealtypus) and Spanish statistical evidence, it develops six prototypical profiles of structural exclusion across key twin‐transition sectors: urban mobility and transport, the platform and gig economy, rural energy and depopulation, digital public infrastructure and smart cities, digital agriculture, and urban renovation. Each profile identifies the mechanisms through which green and digital policies impose unequal costs on vulnerable groups, examining the resulting dynamics of institutional disaffection, potential political radicalisation, and common structural patterns. Comparative analysis identifies four recurring exclusion mechanisms—the upfront cost barrier, the digital literacy gateway, the geographic penalty, and knowledge disqualification—tracing a common pathway from structural exclusion to political disaffection. The article concludes by proposing five governance principles grounded in community work and participatory governance, offering a framework transferable to comparable EU contexts.

#10 [paper] Assessing the environmental impact of clear aligner therapy: a scoping review
Authors: Sapthami Pai, Dhruv Ahuja, Ashith MV, Haneesh Kiran PT, Amoli Singh
Venue: Frontiers in Dental Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fdmed.2026.1849048

Abstract:
Objective To evaluate the environmental impact and sustainability-related practices of clear aligner therapy (CAT), focusing on environmental impact, economic implications, waste management, recycling practices, manufacturing processes, and aligner materials. It further explores the alignment of clear aligner practices with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG's) 3,9,12 and 13. Methodology A scoping review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review was guided by the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. A comprehensive literature search was performed across five electronic databases (PubMed Central, Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost) for studies published between January 2014 and December 2024. Studies evaluating the environmental sustainability of clear aligner therapy, including materials, manufacturing processes, waste management, recycling practices, and carbon emissions, were included. Results Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence indicates that clear aligner therapy contributes to plastic waste, microplastic generation, and greenhouse gas emissions throughout its life cycle. The included studies reported biodegradable materials, direct three-dimensional (3D) printing technologies (SDG-9), recycling initiatives (SDG 12), and circular economy approaches as potential strategies to reduce environmental impacts (SDG 3 & 13). However, the implementation of these strategies remains constrained by limited recycling infrastructure, economic considerations, and insufficient high-quality evidence. Conclusion Available evidence suggests that innovations in material selection, circular economy approaches, optimized manufacturing processes, and enhanced recycling programs may reduce the environmental burden associated with clear aligner therapy. Nevertheless, further high-quality environmental assessment studies are required to support the development of more sustainable orthodontic practices aligned with SDGs 3, 9, 12, and 13.

#11 [paper] Systemic barriers to circular economy adoption in UAE construction: Bayesian network evidence and a transition framework
Authors: Sabreen Dar Amer, Sara Abdulmaksoud, Zied Bahroun, Ghassan Abu–Lebdeh, Serter Atabay
Venue: Frontiers in Built Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fbuil.2026.1979368
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Circular economy (CE) adoption in construction is increasingly promoted as a pathway for reducing construction and demolition waste (CDW), preserving material value, and improving resource efficiency. Yet CE implementation remains difficult because the barriers constraining circular construction are rarely isolated. They interact through procurement practices, stakeholder fragmentation, regulatory conditions, digital readiness, secondary-material markets, and investment behavior. Unlike conventional barrier-ranking studies that treat implementation barriers as independent obstacles, this study examines their probabilistic interdependencies in the UAE construction industry using a Bayesian Belief Network (BBN). A literature-based index of 25 barriers was developed across six dimensions: technological, economic, regulatory, organizational, infrastructure, and behavioral barriers. The index was validated by eight experts and assessed through survey responses from 60 UAE construction professionals. The analysis compares conventional independence-based ranking with an interdependence-based Network Propagation Impact (NPI) ranking. The findings show that complexity in shifting to CE (NPI = 0.1245), fragmentation of the building construction industry (NPI = 0.1212), and prioritization of cost and time (NPI = 0.1071) are the most systemically influential barriers. The results demonstrate that perceived severity and systemic influence are not equivalent, as barriers ranked moderately under direct assessment can become critical when their network propagation effects are considered. Building on these findings, the study develops an integrated CE transition framework linking foundational barrier domains, dominant propagation barriers, intervention levers, and expected outcomes. The study contributes by reframing CE implementation as a socio-technical transition challenge and by showing how BBN-based analysis can support more strategic prioritization of circular construction interventions in the UAE.

#12 [paper] Who is governing the global plastics crisis? Mapping the global plastics governance landscape
Authors: Babet de Groot
Venue: International Environmental Agreements Politics Law and Economics
Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract As plastic pollution intensifies, questions arise about whether the global plastics crisis (GPC) is being governed, and by whom. While an array of international institutions is often assumed to address this issue, the scholarship has yet to systematically examine who governs plastics and plastic pollution in practice. This article provides an empirical mapping of the GPC governance landscape, finding that multilevel public, civil society, and hybrid institutions incidentally facilitate governance through information dissemination, operational activities, and standard-setting. It identifies focal points that shape the global agenda and powerbrokers that disseminate it, with the United Nations Environment Programme and the Basel Convention emerging as influential. Meanwhile, private actor involvement is limited to multistakeholder partnerships that enable business and industry to feign environmental action while pursuing expansive business-as-usual practices. This article thereby establishes an empirical baseline for understanding GPC governance in the absence of a global plastics treaty, demonstrating that legal and regime-based classifications of institutional relevance offer an incomplete account.

#13 [paper] International legal regulation of marine plastic pollution: basic theories, specific issues, and China’s responses

Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution (MPP) is among the gravest environmental issues of the international community and is directly linked with the shared interests of humanity. The current international legal frameworks that regulate MPP primarily involve the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and other international conventions and other soft-law instruments. Nevertheless, there is still no fully developed international legal regulatory framework of MPP. According to the basic theories of the international regulation of MPP, this paper identifies the unresolved problems in the current process of governance, including the limitations of existing international conventions, the difficulty in negotiating the Global Plastics Treaty, the insufficient compliance capacity of relevant States, and the inadequate oversight mechanisms. #15 [paper] Mainstreaming recycled fertilisers: An integrated SWOT, barrier, policy roadmap, and design-thinking governance framework
Authors: Anthony Imoudu Oyeogbe
Venue: Sustainable Futures
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sftr.2026.102075
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Recycled fertilisers are a critical lever for transitioning to a circular nutrient economy, yet their mainstreaming is hindered by complex, interconnected barriers that require a proactive policy framework. While several studies have examined specific barriers, from technical uncertainties and economic disincentives to regulatory fragmentation and social perceptions, no coherent framework systematically integrates these diverse challenges with actionable policy pathways and adaptive governance mechanisms. This paper offers a novel integrated framework that combines analytical (SWOT and barrier assessment), strategic (phased policy roadmaps), and process-oriented (design thinking) components to examine the complexities and interventions required to move recycled fertiliser products from niche innovation to mainstream practice. Findings reveal that recycled fertilisers offer substantial strengths, including closing nutrient loops and decarbonising production, yet remain constrained by weaknesses, including contamination risks and regulatory fragmentation. These interconnected barriers require a phased policy roadmap strategy involving short-term regulatory harmonisation and financial incentives, medium-term digital traceability and market-pull mechanisms, and long-term fiscal reform and certification. Design-thinking shifts policymaking from siloed, top-down implementation to iterative, empathy-driven co-creation. This ensures policies reflect stakeholder needs, enabling adaptive refinement through prototyping and testing to build trust essential for successful implementation. Systematically linking analytical, strategic, and process-oriented components, prioritising interventions by impact and feasibility, and embedding stakeholder co-creation as core governance, this framework offers policymakers a practical, adaptive blueprint for accelerating circular nutrient transitions.

#16 [paper] Environmental Impacts and Life Cycle Assessment of Recycled Plastic Bricks
Authors: Sirri Neba Nforsoh, Kayla Kurtz, Marlene Prien, Jitka Bečanová, Šimon Vojta, Rui Wang, Rakesh Paswan, Karla Pozo
Venue: ACS Omega
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.6c04677
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract This study evaluated the mechanical performance, contaminant release, and life-cycle impacts of recycled plastic blocks manufactured from beach-collected and facility-sourced plastic waste. Four formulations combining polyethylene terephthalate, high-density polyethylene, low-density polyethylene, sand, and glass were evaluated. Unweathered blocks had compressive strengths between 20.6–24.3 N/mm2, suitable for paving applications; however, higher plastic fractions led to lower strength and higher porosity. UV weathering reduced strength by 6–12% and increased metal leaching by up to ∼400%. Per- and polyfluorinated concentrations peaked at 13.8 ng/L; concentrations decreased slightly after weathering due to polymer photo-oxidation and embrittlement that enhanced sorption capacity and retention. Formulations with lower plastic content (∼33%) had higher strength and lower leaching. Life-cycle assessment identified extrusion and waste-plastic processing as dominant contributors to climate change (0.12 kg CO2-eq/kg block) and particulate matter (0.42 x 10–3 kg PM10-eq/kg block), driven by fossil-based energy use and process emissions. Blocks with higher plastic ratios exhibited greater environmental burdens, matching leaching trends. These findings revealed that incorporating waste plastics into construction materials can support waste management and infrastructure, but durability, contaminant release, and processing emissions are sensitive to the formulation. Optimizing plastic-to-aggregate ratios and improving processing efficiency can improve durability while reducing environmental and health risks.

Abstract:
Background: Foamed polystyrene, widely known by the colloquial name Styrofoam, is a lightweight, low-cost material whose physical properties make it unusually prone to fragmentation, wind and water transport, and poor recovery once it escapes waste systems. #1 [paper] Framing tinnitus-correlated distress as a brain disorder may contribute to the very distress it seeks to explain
Authors: Benjamin Boecking, Kurt Steinmetzger, Matthias Rose, Petra Brueggemann, Birgit Mazurek

Year: 2026
