Abstract:
Abstract Marine (MHWs) and atmospheric heatwaves (AHWs) are intensifying with climate change, but their co-occurrence as concurrent heatwaves (CHWs) poses an even greater threat to marine ecosystems. This study examines the spatiotemporal variability, physical drivers, and ecological impacts of CHWs across the marginal seas of the Arabian Peninsula from 1982 to 2021. CHWs are most frequent in the northern Red Sea, Arabian Gulf, and western Arabian Sea, and least common in the southern Red Sea. Their frequency and duration have increased significantly, by up to 7.5 days per decade in the northern Red Sea. CHWs extend the duration of MHWs and AHWs by an average of 6 and 2.2 days, respectively, compounding ecological stress. Our findings show that CHWs are the dominant drivers of coral bleaching and productivity loss in the region, with 80–85% of severe bleaching events linked to CHWs. They also triggered more than 20% decline in chlorophyll-a concentrations – nearly 1.4 times that of standalone MHWs. These results underscore the critical role of atmospheric heat in marine impacts. Case studies from 1998 and 2010 highlight the influence of high-pressure anomalies and weakened winds in shaping the widespread CHWs. The study calls for integrating CHW risks into conservation strategies to build ecosystem resilience in a warming climate.

#10 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science

Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350

Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#11 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

This study aims to investigate the impacts of heatwaves towards sea level and sea surface temperature using multi-mission satellite altimetry. #14 [paper] Marine heatwave exposure is changing unevenly across Scottish aquaculture sites
Authors: Camila Toledo-Jaime, Jennifer A. Graham, Ben Hudson, David Andrew Moffat, Bryony L. Townhill, Steven J. Palmer
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science

Abstract:
Introduction Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are an increasing climate hazard for coastal aquaculture, yet regional assessments may not resolve how exposure varies across the locations where farms operate. Methods Here, we analysed daily ~5-km OSTIA sea surface temperature data from 1990 to 2025 at the locations of 361 active Scottish finfish and shellfish farms, represented by 218 unique grid cells, and compared satellite temperatures with in situ records from eight farms. We used principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering to describe long-term MHW exposure, and mixed-effects models to assess temporal changes. Results Two broad exposure profiles were identified. Cluster 1 was characterised by higher mean, maximum and cumulative intensity, whereas differences in event duration and frequency between clusters were smaller. Temporal trends, however, differed more strongly. MHW frequency increased at similar rates in both clusters, while event duration, cumulative intensity and severity increased more rapidly in Cluster 2. Between 1990 -2019 and 2020 -2025, estimated event duration increased by 44.6% in Cluster 1 and 89.9% in Cluster 2, while cumulative intensity increased by 50.0% and approximately 127.5%, respectively (cluster × period, p < 0.001). The estimated probability of a Severe or Extreme event rose from 2.2% to 26.2% in Cluster 2, compared with 1.8% to 6.1% in Cluster 1 (cluster × period, p < 0.001). Mean event intensity changed comparatively little. Discussion These findings show that MHW exposure across Scottish aquaculture is multidimensional, spatially uneven and changing at different rates through time. The resulting hazard -exposure landscape helps bridge regional MHW assessments and individual-farm monitoring, providing a foundation for more targeted monitoring and future assessment of aquaculture vulnerability and climate risk.

#17 [paper] Day-to-day atmospheric circulation modulated the impact of marine heatwaves on heatstroke risk in Hokkaido in August 2023
Authors: Takehiro Morioka, Tomonori Sato
Venue: SOLA
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44393-026-00038-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Extreme high temperature and humidity threaten high-latitude regions that are less adapted to such conditions. While marine heatwaves (MHWs) can contribute to hot and humid conditions over land, the modulation of these impacts by the day-to-day atmospheric circulation remains poorly understood. This study focused on Hokkaido, the northernmost prefecture in Japan, to investigate how the daily atmospheric circulation regulated the distribution and intensity of MHW-related heatstroke risk during August 2023. Regional atmospheric model simulations indicated that the MHWs that developed south of Hokkaido increased the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) by approximately 2°C in southern coastal areas. Backward trajectory analysis showed that the intensity of MHW-induced heatstroke risk was governed by the daily atmospheric circulation. On days when MHWs substantially impacted the WBGT in the southeastern coastal region, air parcels passed over regions with high sea surface temperatures (SSTs). Conversely, when trajectories bypassed these MHW areas, the impact remained low. These results demonstrate that the daily atmospheric circulation can determine the magnitude of heatstroke risk over land. Our findings suggest that the relative positioning of airflow pathways and the SST distribution should be considered to improve heatstroke risk prediction in coastal regions.

#18 [paper] From hazard-based to impact-based warnings: using social sensing to refine coastal flood thresholds in Maricá – RJ, Brazil
Authors: Camila Américo dos Santos, Fábio Ferreira Dias
Venue: Anthropocene Coasts

Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44218-026-00151-y
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Conventional coastal warning systems issue alerts based on regional oceanographic thresholds calibrated for navigation safety, generating a recurrent disconnection between physical hazard and documented urban impact. This study addresses that disconnection on the coast of Maricá (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), a microtidal urban shoreline of reflective beaches exposed to South Atlantic swells. Hourly significant wave height ( Hs ) from the ERA5 reanalysis (2022–2025) was validated against the SiMCosta buoy CDRJ-1 ( R = 0.90; RMSE = 0.32 m under extreme conditions) and cross-referenced with 645 documentary records of storm surge episodes, compiled from institutional sources (Brazilian Navy, Maricá Civil Defense), local news portals, and citizen-generated Instagram content, consolidating 113 distinct events. Forecast skill metrics (POD, FAR, CSI) revealed contrasting source profiles: institutional alerts operate with FAR between 5.0% and 16.1% under a hazard-based threshold ( Hs ≥ 2.5 m), while citizen-generated records reached POD = 85.5% with FAR = 31.5%, capturing impacts that institutional logic excludes. In 2024, Maricá Civil Defense replaced the Brazilian Navy as the primary alert issuer. The analysis identified Hs ≥ 3.5 m as the critical threshold above which structural damage to urban infrastructure becomes recurrent, with damage frequency rising from 6.2% below 3.0 m to 50.0% above 3.5 m. Furthermore, 42.5% of documented events occurred below the operational threshold of 2.5 m, exposing the limitation of purely hazard-based warning logic. These results support the recalibration of local warning systems and the transition from hazard-based to impact-based logics on urbanised coasts.

#19 [paper] Environmental controls on the detectability of hydrodynamic changes induced by offshore wind farm structures
Authors: Michela De Dominicis, Rory O’Hara Murray, Alejandro Gallego, Charlotte Anne June Williams, Beth E. Scott
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-71585-0

Abstract:
Abstract A combination of model simulations and field observations collected in 2023 and 2024 near Seagreen, Scotland’s largest Offshore Wind Farm (OWF), is used to assess when, where and by how much (physical) changes induced by OWFs structures become detectable and environmentally relevant. Seagreen has the deepest (> 55 m) fixed bottom foundations of any OWF in the world (in 2026), and in offshore deep (> 50 m) waters there is the potential for OWFs structures to perturb natural ocean mixing and modify seasonal stratification. We found that OWF impacts on local hydrodynamics are highly sensitive to environmental conditions, with the strongest effects occurring under weakly stratified conditions, in frontal/transitional zones, when the water column is most responsive to small increases in mixing. Summer average sea surface temperature decreases are generally between -0.1 and -0.3 $$^{\circ }$$ C within the farm and in its wake, but with cooling exceeding -0.5 $$^{\circ }$$ C during the 2023 marine heatwave. Due to high seasonal and monthly variability, OWF impact assessments based on limited observational periods may underestimate or overestimate the range of hydrodynamic changes. This work highlights the value of combining numerical models with observations: model simulations identified the periods and locations of detectable OWF-induced changes, while observations supported the modelled response.

The provided evidence does not contain information regarding a specific "next step" for a single, unified "Marine heatwave early warning project." The evidence consists of distinct, independent studies and data repositories, each with its own specific findings, limitations, or future directions.

However, the evidence suggests several potential next steps or future research directions for the *field* of marine heatwave early warning, derived from the specific conclusions of individual studies:

*   **Integration of Biological Context:** One study proposes the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework as a complementary approach to existing definitions to better assess biological consequences, suggesting a next step toward integrating biological thresholds into warning systems #17.
*   **Improved Prediction of Precursors:** Research in the Adriatic Sea highlights the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to understand MHW precursors, indicating a next step to strengthen early-warning capabilities by anticipating hazards through better understanding of drivers #5.
*   **Operational Implementation of Rescue Strategies:** For the red handfish, the study highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation, implying a next step in strengthening capacity for pre-emptive rescues during environmental extremes #4.
*   **Adaptive Management in Western Australia:** A review of Western Australia suggests next steps include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs, noting that success hinges on accurate and timely prediction #11.
*   **Expansion of Climate Intervention Studies:** A study on marine cloud brightening motivates further study to determine if localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs #9.
*   **Addressing Data Limitations:** A study on the South China Sea suggests that leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from CMIP6 to construct extensive training datasets for machine learning models is a viable next step to address limited observational data #18.
*   **Utilizing Subsurface Information:** A study on the Gulf of Panama suggests exploiting subsurface information for improved early-warning and description of upwelling events, which are linked to marine heat stress #20.
*   **Transferability of Frameworks:** The Adriatic Sea study notes that its framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, suggesting a next step to apply this detection and predictive understanding to other regions #5.
*   **Long-term Forecasting for Coral Reefs:** A study on coral reefs identifies where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness and conservation, implying a next step in operationalizing these multi-year forecasts for specific vulnerable regions #10.

The evidence does not identify a single overarching project with a defined "next step."

#1 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#4 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#5 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#6 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. #2 [paper] From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry.
Authors: Baniahmad, Abdelraheem, Bani-Ahmad, Sulieman
Venue: Molecules (Basel, Switzerland)
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42943689/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.

#4 [paper] Developing and evaluating an AI-assisted chatbot for promotion and tenure guidance in an academic medical center
Authors: May May Yeo, Deborah D. Navedo, Patrick J. Casey, Bernard C. Y. Tan
Venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1919009
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The SingHealth Duke–NUS Academic Medical Center manages over 2,800 clinical faculty members and processes over 400 appointments and promotions annually. The current Promotion and Tenure documentation includes over 30 documents, making it difficult and time-consuming for the faculty to locate specific appointment information. We developed “AskADD” in response to requests for clearer academic career development guidance. This study reports initial alpha testing and subsequent beta testing with 35 faculty members using AskADD. AskADD aids the faculty—physician-educators, physician-scientists, physician-innovators, and physician-leaders—in navigating academic career paths while increasing transparency and trust in appointment, promotion, and tenure processes. Our AI-integrated systems, initially tested using low or no-code Microsoft platforms and later developed with a custom GPT, deliver contextualized responses to promotion and tenure queries. The faculty and staff participated in user testing, providing feedback for improvements. Alpha and beta testing conducted with the same group of users indicated that a substantial portion of participants found the tool beneficial; suggestions were given for further refinement. Our experience contributes to the limited literature on AI-driven faculty advancement in academic medical centers and offers a novel paradigm for academic career support.

#5 [paper] AI Call Center Supervisor in a Live Company: A Three-Week Case Study of an Autonomous AI Agent Supervising a Phone Team
Authors: Evgeny V. Arsentyev
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23926850
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This technical report shows how the figures in the article "An AI Supervisor Ran a Call Center Team for Three Weeks. Then Someone Checked Its Weekly Report" were calculated. An AI supervisor is a software agent that does a team lead's daily work: it watches the team's numbers, reviews calls, flags problems, answers the team's questions and reports up. The subject is an autonomous Claude agent that supervised the small remote phone team of a US-facing telemedicine company for three weeks, with a human team supervisor, a department head and company leadership kept in the loop. In 16 days the agent was started 459 times, about 280 of them to answer people in the team chat. In week three the team's talk time with partners was 33% to 80% above its best week before the agent, depending on whether the human supervisor's own calls are counted; the first two weeks with the agent were worse. Both main operational defects of the period (a call-screening setting on a caller's phone and the dialer connection order) were found by people, not by the agent. The agent decided nothing about people and recommended no dismissals. Of the nine checkable claims in its own weekly report, one held exactly as written, three held only under one way of counting, two were misleading and three could not be reproduced from the raw call records. The report gives the formulas, assumptions, confounders and limitations (no control group, one team, call classification available for week three only). The company operates under a non-disclosure agreement: the report contains only the published figures and how they were calculated; the underlying data is not published.

#6 [paper] A Cloud-Enabled LIMS-QMS Platform With Large Language Model-Assisted Standard Operating Procedure Generation for GLP/GMP-Aligned Theranostics Laboratory Operations.
Authors: Durmaz, F Aytac
Venue: SLAS technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42901382/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Theranostic development centers operate under stringent good laboratory practice (GLP) and good manufacturing practice (GMP) requirements that fragmented, paper-based workflows cannot adequately support. This paper presents the design, regulatory compliance mapping, and pilot deployment of the Laboratory Tracking Software (LTS) platform, a cloud-ready, web-based system that unifies laboratory information management system (LIMS) and quality management system (QMS) functions under a risk-based Computer Software Assurance (CSA) framework aligned with U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 21 CFR Part 11 and ISO/IEC 17025. The platform operationalizes a 6×6 deterministic request-and-service lifecycle across nine governance modules and embeds a large language model (LLM)-assisted module that, from a single service-name input, generates structured standard operating procedures (SOPs), identifies required consumables and instruments, performs operational risk assessment, and proposes an executable workflow. Pilot deployment across 187 laboratory requests is reported descriptively (23-day mean turnaround time, 1,456 quality-control checkpoints, and 43 deviation-handling episodes); because no comparable pre-deployment dataset could be reconstructed, these values are not interpreted as efficiency or error-reduction gains. A 21 CFR Part 11-aligned control matrix and a CSA-based verification package document authenticated electronic approvals, activity records, two-factor authentication (2FA), and role-based access control (RBAC); a consolidated high-risk user-acceptance campaign executed 31 of 31 scripted scenarios successfully, with independent reviewer and approver sign-off still pending. Beyond the original single BRAF droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) illustrative case, a document-level evaluation was performed across a locked corpus of 20 laboratory services (10 analysis and 10 synthesis workflows). All 280 mandatory template elements were present (100.0% template adherence), and none of the 80 predefined automated document-control checks was flagged (0.0%). Expert-adjudicated error rate, human edit distance, and time saving were not measured and are deferred to a prospective follow-up study. Comparative analysis against QT9 ERP/QMS, RAMS®, and SENAITE LIMS positions the platform as a governance-first, theranostic-specific informatics system with native LLM-assisted documentation generation, a capability absent from existing commercial and open-source alternatives. The results indicate that integrating LLM-assisted document generation into a regulated laboratory informatics platform is technically feasible; however, given the hallucination risk documented in the medical LLM literature, systematic human-in-the-loop validation of generated content remains a prerequisite for unsupervised deployment in GLP/GMP settings. The revised design description additionally specifies a template-constrained prompting strategy, a generation-record schema supporting prompt and output reconstruction, a model-change-control procedure, an explicit LLM data-privacy boundary, and alignment with the January 2026 FDA/EMA guiding principles of good artificial intelligence (AI) practice in drug development.

#7 [paper] Guidance for laboratory implementation, governance and continuous assurance of artificial intelligence in histopathology
Authors: Emad A. Rakha, Jelle Wesseling, Anikó Kovács, Aleš Ryška, Elena Provenzano, Gábor Cserni, Zsuzsanna Varga, Zsuzsanna Bagó-Horváth
Venue: Archiv für Pathologische Anatomie und Physiologie und für Klinische Medicin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00428-026-04684-y
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming histopathology, with applications ranging from workflow optimisation and quality assurance to tumour diagnosis, grading, biomarker assessment and estimation of prognosis. While numerous AI algorithms have demonstrated promising analytical and clinical performance, pathology laboratories are increasingly adopting commercially available AI systems with regulatory-approval rather than developing their own algorithms. Existing guidance largely focuses on AI development, validation and regulatory approval, with comparatively little practical direction on the local verification, governance and ongoing assurance required for safe routine clinical implementation. This paper proposes a practical framework for the clinical implementation of AI specifically within pathology laboratories. Rather than addressing AI development, it focuses on the responsibilities of laboratories adopting established AI systems into clinical practice. The framework distinguishes AI applications according to their intended clinical function, recognising that diagnostic applications, biomarker evaluation, workflow optimisation and generative AI applications require different implementation, verification, governance and quality assurance strategies. It further distinguishes algorithm validation, local verification and continuous assurance as complementary stages of implementation and advocates a function-based, risk-proportionate approach integrated within existing laboratory quality management systems. Practical recommendations are provided for workflow integration, interoperability, human oversight, user competency, performance monitoring, incident management, software updates and proportionate re-verification throughout the AI operational lifecycle. By extending implementation beyond regulatory approval, this guidance complements existing AI development and regulatory frameworks rather than replacing them. It provides a practical governance framework for pathology laboratories, professional organisations, accreditation bodies, and healthcare providers to support the safe, standardised, and sustainable integration of AI into routine histopathology while maintaining diagnostic quality, patient safety, and clinical governance.

#9 [paper] AI agents in clinical medicine: delegation, supervision, and the problem of correlated failure
Authors: Ethan Waisberg, Joseph W. Guarnieri
Venue: Irish Journal of Medical Science (1971 -)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11845-026-04584-9
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Clinical artificial intelligence has to date generated outputs upon which a clinician then acted. Agentic systems execute the task itself, completing a sequence of steps and returning finished work. Adoption has proceeded rapidly across other sectors while clinical uptake has remained confined largely to pilots, an interval that affords medicine an a opportunity to govern the technology deliberately rather than retrospectively. The governing question is thereby transformed from whether a prediction is accurate to whether a task may be entrusted, a question medicine has addressed throughout its history of training juniors under supervision. We argue that the appropriate frame for agentic systems is consequently delegation rather than prediction, and that the entrustment frameworks developed within postgraduate education furnish a serviceable structure of graded autonomy, task-level scope, and named supervisory responsibility. We then identify the point at which the correspondence ceases to hold. Supervision of human colleagues presupposes that errors are independent and idiosyncratic, such that mistakes arise individually and are detected individually. A single agent deployed across an institution generates one error process reproduced at scale. The consequence is that agentic systems cannot be adequately supervised through case-level review, and require instead the population-level surveillance characteristic of quality improvement.

Background: Laboratory test turnaround time (TAT) is a critical quality indicator in healthcare It has a direct impact on patient safety, emergency department productivity, clinical decision-making, and general healthcare quality.Delays in laboratory testing often arise from communication failures, incomplete documentation, inefficient specimen management, and fragmented interdisciplinary collaboration.Objective: This review explores how structured collaboration among secretary nurses, laboratory specialists, and medical records professionals can significantly improve laboratory turnaround time while enhancing patient safety and workflow efficiency.Methods: A narrative review of current healthcare quality improvement literature was conducted.Evidence regarding laboratory workflow optimization, health information management, interdisciplinary teamwork, electronic medical records (EMRs), and laboratory information systems (LIS) was synthesized to identify collaborative strategies that reduce delays throughout the laboratory testing cycle.Results: Successful collaboration improves every phase of laboratory testing, including order entry, specimen collection, transportation, analysis, result reporting, and documentation.Digital integration, standardized communication, and clearly defined professional responsibilities significantly reduce turnaround time and decrease laboratory errors.Conclusion: Improving laboratory performance can be achieved through the establishment of cooperative multidisciplinary workflows backed by electronic information systems, increasing patient satisfaction, and promoting healthcare quality.

#13 [paper] Clinical-priority task orchestration and verified safety supervision for a physician-directed ward-rounding robot: a simulation-based feasibility study
Authors: Cheng Hang, Safaa Najah Saud Al-Humairi, Ahgalya Subbiah
Venue: Frontiers in Robotics and AI
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/frobt.2026.1996839
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction A ward-rounding robot that accepts orders at the level of clinical intent becomes a shared clinical resource: several clinicians may hold outstanding requests of differing urgency, and execution is punctuated by confirmation gates at which the robot waits on a human and by engagement steps that cannot safely be interrupted. This paper formalizes the resulting scheduling problem together with the safety layer that it necessitates. Methods We present (i) a task model in which an intent-level order expands into primitives carrying resource locks, physician confirmation gates, and an explicit interruptibility partition; (ii) the Clinical-Priority Scheduler (CP-Sched), which combines urgency weighting, aging, travel awareness, and class-relative escalation and preempts only at safe interruption points; and (iii) a safety supervisor specified as a network of timed automata and verified exhaustively for a single robot serving one order at a time, with independent reproduction in the TLA+ model checker TLC. All task timings in the 1,590 discrete-event simulation runs are modeling assumptions, not hardware measurements. Results Across 1,080 runs spanning two ward sizes and three utilization levels, CP-Sched reduced the 95th-percentile time for urgent orders to bedside from 347 s to 215 s at moderate utilization, a 38% reduction relative to the strongest of four baselines; all comparisons survived Holm’s correction at p < 0.0001 under both the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank and unpaired Mann–Whitney tests (rank-biserial effect sizes: 0.93–1.00 paired, 0.66–0.93 unpaired). A further 510 runs showed that aging alone cannot bound the waiting time and that escalation at a fixed absolute horizon restores a guarantee only by inflating the urgent tail at saturation. All five clinical invariants hold under the supervisor and each is violable without it, so none is vacuous. Runtime enforcement eliminated all 757 unsafe interruptions observed in the unshielded ablation at a cost of 2.1–35.4 s in the median urgent tail. Discussion The enforcement cost is small but systematic at light and moderate loads and undetectable at saturation, which supports keeping the safety layer independent of the scheduling policy. The formal guarantee covers a single-order model, and absolute timings require calibration on a physical platform.

#14 [paper] Responsibility without a map: defining oversight of automated result release in the medical laboratory.
Authors: Said İncir, Kerim Erhan Palaoğlu, Osman Oğuz
Venue: Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (CCLM)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1515/cclm-2026-1371
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Laboratory specialists have been assigned responsibility for algorithmically assisted reporting without an operational definition of what responsible oversight means. Results pass largely through rule-based approval systems, and increasingly through probabilistic models, yet the obligation attached to the specialist's name on the report has never been restated. Taking the position of the specialist who signs rather than the regulator who writes, and starting from requirements the discipline already accepts, we derive four capacities on which approving a result depends: designing the release logic and making it legible, anticipating where it will fail, correcting it when it does, and detecting that it has failed. These are not properties of a technology. Every system sits on a gradient whose position depends less on whether it uses machine learning than on what the laboratory has recorded about it. The oversight problem therefore did not arrive with machine learning but with automation, and most of what is now asked of laboratories in respect of artificial intelligence was already owed in respect of autoverification. Mapped against the four capacities, current frameworks require documentation and change control, address detection only in general terms, and nowhere require a laboratory to state in advance which results may be released without human review. Where laboratories have been asked, they report holding few of the records by which compliance could be shown. We propose a set of such records, identify what a single laboratory can and cannot reasonably do, and set out the questions the profession has not yet answered.

#15 [paper] Assigned roles change how clinical AI agents allocate shared resources
Authors: A. Gorenshtein, M. Omar, Y. Barash, J. B. Kruskal, M. Ahmed, O. Brook, E. Klang
Venue: medRxiv
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/2e795227d001fc2dbe836d8700e35fc3bfdd8760
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Clinical AI agents may be assigned to individual patients, but hospital resources are shared across many patients. We tested what agents do when helping their assigned patient would violate the hospital's rule for a scarce resource. We analyzed 22,916 simulated cases comprising 274,992 logged agent actions across 20 AI models. In each scenario, the agent could claim a scarce resource for its patient even though the hospital rule gave another patient priority. We varied only the agent's assigned role, from responsibility for the whole ward to strong advocacy for one patient. Violations of the hospital rule rose from 32.5% under whole-ward responsibility to 69.4% under strong patient advocacy, a 36.9-point increase (95% CI, 25.7-48.0). Agents correctly identified which patient should receive the resource in 95.7% of tests, yet still took it for their own patient in 65.9% of those episodes. Asking the agent to apply its own allocation judgment immediately before acting reduced violations to 0-2% in a three-model follow-up experiment. Assigned roles can shape how clinical AI agents use shared hospital resources, even when they identify the correct priority patient. Patient-focused agents should not independently control shared resources without an allocation check.

Abstract:
Clinical biochemistry generates approximately 70% of the objective data used in medical decision-making, yet the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and large language models (LLMs) into laboratory operations remains fragmented. Existing digital-health maturity constructs (HIMSS EMRAM, HITI, CAMM) do not jointly address analytical metrology, algorithmic lifecycle governance, and clinical outcome accountability, leaving laboratories without a structured roadmap for AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. Face validity was assessed with five laboratory directors, and structural comparisons were performed against four precedent maturity models. A chain of custody aggregation rule prevents high analytical scores from masking governance or equity deficits. Alignment with TRIPOD + AI, DECIDE-AI, and TRIPOD-LLM reporting standards is embedded at tiers 3–5. BASM provides laboratories, health systems, and regulators with an actionable, standards-aligned instrument to plan, benchmark, and audit AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. A multi-institutional modified-Delphi validation is the priority next step.

Abstract:
ObjectiveSince the majority of errors in the medical laboratorytesting process occur in the pre-analytical phase andunnecessary test ordering adversely affects patientsafety and healthcare system costs, this study aimedto assess the knowledge and awareness levels ofsixth-year medical students (medical interns) regard-ing the laboratory pre-analytical phase and rationaltest ordering, and to contribute to the developmentof pre-internship training programs based on the findings.Material and MethodThis cross-sectional survey study included 167 med-ical interns from the 2024–2025 (n = 57) and 2025–2026 (n = 110) academic years. Data were collectedusing an online questionnaire. Descriptive statisticsare expressed as frequencies, percentages, andmean ± standard deviation. Pearson’s chi-square testwas used to compare categorical variables betweencohorts. Total pre-analytical knowledge scores andtotal rational test ordering scores were calculated bysumming the correct responses to the relevant items.Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.ResultsNo statistically significant differences were observedbetween the 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 cohortsacross all knowledge domains (Cramer’s V: 0.01–0.05). Although nearly all participants reported phle-botomy experience, formal education about pre-an-alytical processes and rational laboratory use waslimited, and awareness of national policies was low.Significant deficiencies were identified for technicalpre-analytical topics, including order of draw, diur-nal variation, tube handling, and coagulation sampleanalysis time limits. Knowledge of minimum test rep-etition intervals was generally insufficient, with higheraccuracy for HbA1c and lower accuracy for common-ly requested tests such as AST, ALT, TSH, and CRP.Overall knowledge scores indicated low competency,with no differences between cohorts.ConclusionPractical experience alone does not ensure standard-ized knowledge. #5 [paper] Artificial Intelligence Can Direct Patients Toward a Complaint-specific Musculoskeletal Provider
Authors: Ethan C. Gazan, Colin Emrich, Alexander Baur, Zachary C. Lum, Jenna Bernstein, David C. Landy
Venue: PubMed Central
Year: 2026
Link: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13406377/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Patients with musculoskeletal complaints often search online to identify an appropriate healthcare provider. With the increasing availability of large language models (LLMs), these artificial intelligence (AI) tools can direct patients to providers. This study evaluated the ability of LLMs to recommend appropriate providers based on representative patient musculoskeletal queries. METHODS: Three LLMs (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini) were prompted with standardized musculoskeletal queries for two US cities (Lynchburg, VA, and Trumbull, CT). Provider recommendations were considered appropriate if the physician was currently practicing in the requested location and specialized in the relevant area. Listed phone numbers were checked for accuracy. Descriptive statistics and Fisher exact tests were used to summarize findings. RESULTS: The appropriateness of recommended providers differed across models with ChatGPT being most often appropriate (17/17, 100%) compared with Gemini (9/21, 43%) and DeepSeek (4/10, 40%), (P < 0.001). Of the 18 inappropriate recommendations, 13 (72%) were real providers in unrelated specialties and 5 (28%) were hallucinations, all from DeepSeek. Phone number accuracy differed significantly across models with Gemini being most accurate (5/6, 83%), outperforming both ChatGPT (6/9, 67%; P = 0.60) and DeepSeek (2/10, 20%; P = 0.04). DISCUSSION: LLMs showed potential to direct patients to local, specialized musculoskeletal providers based on their report, although the specific contact information was at times inaccurate. As these tools evolve, providers should be aware of AI's ability to make provider recommendations and work to ensure the presentation of their contact information is accessible by these models as best possible.

#7 [paper] Workplace Learning in Clinical Laboratories: Health Professionals’ Perceptions and Practices of Training Students
Authors: Henriette Lorenzen, Diana Mejlstrup Barrett Momsen, Lene Gredal, Marianne Ellegaard
Venue: Medical Science Educator
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40670-026-02930-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Introduction Clinical placements, where students learn through participation in everyday work, are a central component of many health education programs, including biomedical laboratory science (BLS). While research has primarily focused on students’ experiences, less is known about how participating staff perceive their role. This study explores how BLS staff perceive and enact clinical training. Materials and methods A qualitative study was conducted comprising four focus groups with BLS staff from two hospital settings, including both experienced and newly employed staff. Interviews were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Activity theory guided a subsequent analysis of workplace learning tensions. Results Six themes were identified, reflecting staff perceptions related to student training: (1) professional pride and ambassador for the field, (2) organisational aspects, (3) interpretations and perceptions of student motivation and engagement, (4) aspects of own motivation and engagement, (5) responses to perceived student engagement and methods to engage students, and (6) confidence in students, students as helpers. Staff expressed a positive commitment to supporting students and fostering professional identity. However, an Activity Theory analysis identified five interconnected tensions related to production, laboratory quality, onboarding of newly hired, division of responsibility, and pedagogical resources. These tensions shaped staffs’ opportunities to involve and support students in clinical work. Discussion Side-by-side training is an integrated and often implicit part of everyday work. Strengthening clinical education requires recognising training as a shared organisational responsibility and creating conditions that support student participation.

#8 [paper] From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry.
Authors: Baniahmad, Abdelraheem, Bani-Ahmad, Sulieman
Venue: Molecules (Basel, Switzerland)
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42943689/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.

#12 [paper] Perception of Medical Laboratory Professionals on the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Advancing Hematology Diagnostics.
Authors: Qadah, Talal
Venue: Clinical laboratory
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42570674/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has grown quickly in healthcare and has had a big effect on medical laboratory diagnostics, especially when it comes to diagnosing blood disorders. To figure out the pros and cons of using AI in hematology diagnostics, it is important to understand the perspective of medical laboratory workers instead of specialists toward AI use in hematology laboratory diagnostics. The goal of this study was to investigate what medical lab workers now know about AI and how they think it affects the accuracy of diagnostic hematology and patient outcomes. METHODS: Methods involved 113 participants, mostly laboratory technologists who filled out a standardized questionnaire as part of a quantitative exploratory research design. The data collection phase lasted 6 months, during which time-informed consent was sought and reminders were provided to boost response rates. Statistical tests were used including t-tests and regression analysis to determine the links between demographic factors and workers opinions on AI in hematological diagnoses. RESULTS: The primary findings of this study dwell within the role of job skill and gender influence on "attitude", specifically, the study found that most of the participants believe that their professional attitude to adoption of AI in diagnoses could make their job more accurate and faster. However, there were several concerns about the quality of data, how easy it will be to understand the model, and the moral implications. There were positive relationships between knowledge, attitudes, and practices linked to AI. The secondary outcomes showed that most of the participants were young, with 45.1% being between the ages of 30 and 39. In addition, 65.5% of them had bachelor's degree, which suggests that they were comfortable with technology. Some of the participants had less than ten years of work experience, while others had more than ten years. Statistical tests demonstrated that demographic characteristics are quite important in how medical laboratory workers think about AI. CONCLUSIONS: Medical laboratory workers believe that the use of AI in hematology diagnostics has its benefits, but they need more training and assistance to deal with their fears and create a space where human expertise and AI technologies can work together. By taking these views into account, healthcare organizations may better educate their staff for the changing role of AI in diagnostics, which will lead to improved patient outcomes and satisfaction.

#13 [paper] Assigned roles change how clinical AI agents allocate shared resources
Authors: A. Gorenshtein, M. Omar, Y. Barash, J. B. Kruskal, M. Ahmed, O. Brook, E. Klang
Venue: medRxiv
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/2e795227d001fc2dbe836d8700e35fc3bfdd8760
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Clinical AI agents may be assigned to individual patients, but hospital resources are shared across many patients. We tested what agents do when helping their assigned patient would violate the hospital's rule for a scarce resource. We analyzed 22,916 simulated cases comprising 274,992 logged agent actions across 20 AI models. In each scenario, the agent could claim a scarce resource for its patient even though the hospital rule gave another patient priority. We varied only the agent's assigned role, from responsibility for the whole ward to strong advocacy for one patient. Violations of the hospital rule rose from 32.5% under whole-ward responsibility to 69.4% under strong patient advocacy, a 36.9-point increase (95% CI, 25.7-48.0). Agents correctly identified which patient should receive the resource in 95.7% of tests, yet still took it for their own patient in 65.9% of those episodes. Asking the agent to apply its own allocation judgment immediately before acting reduced violations to 0-2% in a three-model follow-up experiment. Assigned roles can shape how clinical AI agents use shared hospital resources, even when they identify the correct priority patient. Patient-focused agents should not independently control shared resources without an allocation check.

#14 [paper] Knowledge and self-reported practice of laboratory biosafety among medical laboratory professionals in selected public and private hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia: a cross-sectional study
Authors: Omar Sidow Zubair, Ahmed Abdi Yonis, Bashir Abukar Mohamud, Mohamed Hassan Mohamud
Venue: Frontiers in Public Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1916020
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Laboratory biosafety protects healthcare workers, patients and the environment, yet evidence from fragile and resource-limited settings remains scarce. In Somalia, previous work has assessed infection prevention and control at the facility level, but the biosafety knowledge and practice of laboratory professionals themselves, and the relationship between the two, have not been characterized. This study assessed knowledge and self-reported practice of laboratory biosafety, and factors associated with good practice, among medical laboratory professionals in public and private hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 164 eligible medical laboratory professionals in 12 hospitals selected by stratified random sampling from the public and private hospital sectors in Mogadishu. All eligible professionals within the selected hospitals were enumerated; the study is therefore a complete enumeration within sampled facilities rather than a census of all laboratory professionals in Mogadishu. Data were collected with a structured, self-administered questionnaire adapted from the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual and previously validated knowledge–practice instruments. Knowledge was measured with 8 dichotomously scored items (range 0–8; KR-20 = 0.60) and self-reported practice with 9 dichotomous items (range 0–9; KR-20 = 0.52), both classified using pre-specified modified Bloom’s cut-off points. Distributions were assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test. Associations were examined using the Pearson chi-square test and Spearman’s rank correlation, and factors associated with good practice using univariable and multivariable binary logistic regression. Results The median knowledge score was 7 (IQR 5–7) of 8 and the median practice score 9 (IQR 8–9) of 9; both departed significantly from normality. Knowledge was high for hand hygiene (89.0%) and personal protective equipment (86.6%) but low for infectious waste colour-coding (53.7%). Overall, 83 participants (50.6%) had good knowledge, 51 (31.1%) moderate and 30 (18.3%) poor. Self-reported practice was high for lab coat use (98.2%), hand hygiene (98.2%) and glove use (97.6%), and lower for equipment inspection (78.7%) and accident reporting (81.7%); 134 participants (81.7%) were classified as having good practice. A statistically significant positive association was observed between knowledge level and practice level ( χ 2 = 19.58, df = 2, p < 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.35; Spearman’s ρ = 0.296, p < 0.001), with good practice reported by 94.0, 74.5 and 60.0% of those with good, moderate and poor knowledge, respectively. In multivariable analysis, each additional correct knowledge answer independently increased the odds of good practice (aOR 1.73, 95% CI 1.33–2.24, p < 0.001), as did participation in a safety drill in the preceding year (aOR 2.80, 95% CI 1.09–7.15, p = 0.032). Only 64.6% of participants had taken part in such a drill. Conclusion Medical laboratory professionals in Mogadishu hospitals demonstrated moderate biosafety knowledge and high self-reported biosafety practice, although there were gaps in knowledge of infectious waste colour-coding. Knowledge scores were positively associated with self-reported practice, while recent participation in a safety drill was independently associated with reported participants’ practice. These findings suggest that regular safety drills and targeted reinforcement of infectious waste-management procedures may be useful areas for strengthening biosafety practices. However, the high reported practice scores and their potential effect underscore the need for future studies to assess biosafety practices through direct observation.

#17 [paper] ExpertTwins: Auditable Long Horizon Scientific Panels through Grounded Expertise
Authors: Ali Foroughi pour, Abbas Shirinifard
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.06.757114
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Multi-agent language-model systems increasingly assign roles to agents and let them deliberate. A role label, however, does not specify which evidence an agent can bring or which standard it applies before accepting a conclusion. Agents that read one another's outputs tend to converge. We present ExpertTwins, a framework in which each seat of a scientific panel is defined by an inspectable evidence policy. Discipline seats retrieve under field-specific queries, and scientist-associated seats retrieve from attributed publications and a citation-derived scholarly neighborhood. Private initial packets, structured exchange, cited-source disclosure, deterministic quotation checks, and peer source review turn deliberation into an auditable record, which we also render as interactive idea-flow maps. Scientist associations denote publication-grounded perspectives, not replicas or endorsements of named researchers. In a nine-seat, four-turn neuroblastoma panel, 438 of 439 claims passed all attached quotation checks, and seats withdrew or defended positions when challenged on their evidence. A ten-turn panel sustained evidence acquisition and differentiated recommendations without conversational collapse. Across six base models given byte-identical initial packets, four sustained 97.9-99.8% quotation grounding, and at least 91% on every turn, whereas Haiku 4.5 failed by paraphrase and GPT-5 mini by silence. Agreement among strong models fell from 31% of claims at turn one to 5% at turn four. With follow-up questions held fixed, it stayed at 28-33% through turn three and fell to 20% only at the closing turn. Stress runs showed the collapse guardrail escalating through its full intervention ladder when consensus was forced, but missing deference to one unusually strong seat. On idea-flow maps, the forced consensus appeared as parallel lanes of identical ideas, although quotation grounding and participation balance stayed at their maxima. We also reimplemented two close published systems and ran them on matched models, seats, and questions. A multi-persona debate cited only real records, yet none of its cited sentences carried a checkable quotation and it had no way to abstain. An author-memory fusion system ran only after its fact checker was split by seat to fit in context. Its fused answer kept about two-thirds of the fact-checked specialist claims, answered 36 of 60 question parts on which our seats had abstained, and showed the reader 19% of its agents' disagreements. In a computational pathology case study, six scientist-associated agents built distinct pipelines to predict MYCN amplification from whole-slide images. Across six base models, seat-by-model interaction explained 57% of internal variance, and internal rank poorly predicted external rank (r = 0.18 across 36 nominees). These results establish differentiated, source-traceable scientific reasoning as an operational capability and identify the base model as a parameter that must be reported with the protocol.

#18 [paper] Developing and evaluating an AI-assisted chatbot for promotion and tenure guidance in an academic medical center
Authors: May May Yeo, Deborah D. Navedo, Patrick J. Casey, Bernard C. Y. Tan
Venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/frai.2026.1919009
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The SingHealth Duke–NUS Academic Medical Center manages over 2,800 clinical faculty members and processes over 400 appointments and promotions annually. The current Promotion and Tenure documentation includes over 30 documents, making it difficult and time-consuming for the faculty to locate specific appointment information. We developed “AskADD” in response to requests for clearer academic career development guidance. This study reports initial alpha testing and subsequent beta testing with 35 faculty members using AskADD. AskADD aids the faculty—physician-educators, physician-scientists, physician-innovators, and physician-leaders—in navigating academic career paths while increasing transparency and trust in appointment, promotion, and tenure processes. Our AI-integrated systems, initially tested using low or no-code Microsoft platforms and later developed with a custom GPT, deliver contextualized responses to promotion and tenure queries. The faculty and staff participated in user testing, providing feedback for improvements. Alpha and beta testing conducted with the same group of users indicated that a substantial portion of participants found the tool beneficial; suggestions were given for further refinement. Our experience contributes to the limited literature on AI-driven faculty advancement in academic medical centers and offers a novel paradigm for academic career support.

#21 [paper] Perceptions of ChatGPT- and veterinarian-generated responses to pet owners’ medical questions
Authors: Aïnoha Griot, Rob Ward
Venue: Frontiers in Veterinary Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fvets.2026.1939644
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly significant in veterinary medicine, particularly in answering pet owners’ medical questions. AI’s integration could reduce veterinary professionals’ workload while improving access to medical advice. However, the reliability and quality of AI-generated responses compared to veterinarians’ remain unexplored. The objective was to determine whether AI-generated responses were perceived as comparable to veterinarian-generated responses. Methods This cross-sectional study analysed the answers to a sample of pet owners’ medical questions. Both a veterinarian and ChatGPT (GPT-4o, May 2024) provided answers, which were anonymised and presented in a survey distributed through mailing lists and public Facebook groups. Participants were asked to assess each response based on structure, quality, and empathy, using a five-point Likert scale. They then had to indicate whether they trusted the response, and which response they preferred. Results Over two-thirds of the 201 participants (68%) preferred the ChatGPT-generated answers ( p < 0.05), which were rated higher in structure, quality, and empathy. Limitations This study has several limitations, including a small sample size, reliance on a single veterinarian, and use of only two Reddit-derived scenarios. Response accuracy was not assessed, and word count restrictions may have affected perceived response quality. Additionally, prior research suggests that irrelevant patient details can impact ChatGPT’s accuracy, raising questions about user trust if clinical inaccuracies were present. Conclusion AI-generated responses received higher participant ratings in structure, quality and empathy, suggesting AI may enhance veterinary client communication when used under appropriate professional supervision.

Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming histopathology, with applications ranging from workflow optimisation and quality assurance to tumour diagnosis, grading, biomarker assessment and estimation of prognosis. While numerous AI algorithms have demonstrated promising analytical and clinical performance, pathology laboratories are increasingly adopting commercially available AI systems with regulatory-approval rather than developing their own algorithms. Existing guidance largely focuses on AI development, validation and regulatory approval, with comparatively little practical direction on the local verification, governance and ongoing assurance required for safe routine clinical implementation. This paper proposes a practical framework for the clinical implementation of AI specifically within pathology laboratories. Rather than addressing AI development, it focuses on the responsibilities of laboratories adopting established AI systems into clinical practice. The framework distinguishes AI applications according to their intended clinical function, recognising that diagnostic applications, biomarker evaluation, workflow optimisation and generative AI applications require different implementation, verification, governance and quality assurance strategies. It further distinguishes algorithm validation, local verification and continuous assurance as complementary stages of implementation and advocates a function-based, risk-proportionate approach integrated within existing laboratory quality management systems. Practical recommendations are provided for workflow integration, interoperability, human oversight, user competency, performance monitoring, incident management, software updates and proportionate re-verification throughout the AI operational lifecycle. By extending implementation beyond regulatory approval, this guidance complements existing AI development and regulatory frameworks rather than replacing them. It provides a practical governance framework for pathology laboratories, professional organisations, accreditation bodies, and healthcare providers to support the safe, standardised, and sustainable integration of AI into routine histopathology while maintaining diagnostic quality, patient safety, and clinical governance.

#2 [paper] Responsibility without a map: defining oversight of automated result release in the medical laboratory.
Authors: Said İncir, Kerim Erhan Palaoğlu, Osman Oğuz
Venue: Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (CCLM)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1515/cclm-2026-1371
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Laboratory specialists have been assigned responsibility for algorithmically assisted reporting without an operational definition of what responsible oversight means. Results pass largely through rule-based approval systems, and increasingly through probabilistic models, yet the obligation attached to the specialist's name on the report has never been restated. Taking the position of the specialist who signs rather than the regulator who writes, and starting from requirements the discipline already accepts, we derive four capacities on which approving a result depends: designing the release logic and making it legible, anticipating where it will fail, correcting it when it does, and detecting that it has failed. These are not properties of a technology. Every system sits on a gradient whose position depends less on whether it uses machine learning than on what the laboratory has recorded about it. The oversight problem therefore did not arrive with machine learning but with automation, and most of what is now asked of laboratories in respect of artificial intelligence was already owed in respect of autoverification. Mapped against the four capacities, current frameworks require documentation and change control, address detection only in general terms, and nowhere require a laboratory to state in advance which results may be released without human review. Where laboratories have been asked, they report holding few of the records by which compliance could be shown. We propose a set of such records, identify what a single laboratory can and cannot reasonably do, and set out the questions the profession has not yet answered.
