Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Navigating the more than 550 inborn errors of immunity (IEI) requires efficient diagnostic reasoning. Information theory suggests questions should be prioritized by their capacity to reduce diagnostic uncertainty (entropy); yet whether experts or large language models (LLMs) optimize for information gain remains unquantified. OBJECTIVE: We compared expert clinician and LLM diagnostic prioritization strategies using an information-theoretic framework. METHODS: Fifteen immunologists and six LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, and Llama) ranked 35 diagnostic questions by efficiency. Shannon's entropy was used to estimate expected information gain (EIG) for each question. Agreement was assessed via Spearman correlations, consensus ranking, and principal components analysis (PCA). RESULTS: Clinician consensus rankings strongly correlated with estimated information gain (Spearman ρ = -0.71, p < 0.001). "Age at onset?" ranked first by clinicians, provided the highest information gain (2.29 bits), reducing diagnostic uncertainty by 80%. Clinicians and LLMs showed strong agreement on top-tier discriminators (Spearman ρ = 0.73, p < 0.001). However, PCA revealed a distinct LLM cluster; clinicians prioritized bedside/history questions, whereas LLMs favored syndromic and laboratory features. Optimal questioning reached diagnostic confidence in 4-5 steps, approaching the theoretical minimum. CONCLUSIONS: Expert clinicians implicitly approximate information-theoretic optimization in IEI diagnostics. While LLMs share a core heuristic for high-yield questions, divergence in mid-sequence reasoning suggests a shift from experiential heuristics to probabilistic data-matching. #4 [paper] LabFactory: Building and Evaluating Executable AI Labs

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty of realizing scientific tasks that require building custom computational systems (data acquisition, model training, tool implementation) into a single, executable, and evaluatable unit.
Method (Mycelium's reading): LabFactory, a framework where an AI builder transforms a scientific brief into an 'executable AI lab'—a task-specific solver integrating models, knowledge, and tools—which is then executed by a separate host on held-out inputs for objective scoring.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 28 constructions across seven scientific task categories, including molecular/genomic prediction, physiological signals, clinical decision support, and biomedical text.
Abstract:
Scientific tasks specify a desired capability, but realizing it often requires building a computational system tailored to the task---acquiring data, designing representations, training models, implementing tools, and deciding how they are used at inference. We present LabFactory, a framework in which an AI builder turns a scientific brief into an executable AI lab: a task-specific solver that integrates models, knowledge resources, tools, and a controller behind a fixed interface. The builder develops and packages the lab in a metered workspace; a separate host then executes the delivered artifact on held-out inputs, with reference labels kept outside the solver's input interface, and scores its outputs under the task's protocol. This makes the delivered system, rather than the builder's account of its progress, the object of evaluation. We document 28 selected constructions across seven scientific task categories---from molecular and genomic prediction to physiological signals, clinical decision support, and biomedical text---whose delivered labs exceeded their configured reference values on all 33 subtests under host-side execution. Ten contain predictive models fitted during construction; the others assemble retrieval systems, executable analysis environments, and tool-driven workflows around a fixed platform LLM. Together they show that an AI agent can carry a scientific brief all the way to a working lab that can still be invoked, inspected, and checked after construction ends.

#5 [paper] AI agents in clinical medicine: delegation, supervision, and the problem of correlated failure.
Authors: Waisberg, Ethan, Guarnieri, Joseph W
Venue: Irish journal of medical science
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42667591/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Clinical artificial intelligence has to date generated outputs upon which a clinician then acted. Agentic systems execute the task itself, completing a sequence of steps and returning finished work. Adoption has proceeded rapidly across other sectors while clinical uptake has remained confined largely to pilots, an interval that affords medicine an a opportunity to govern the technology deliberately rather than retrospectively. The governing question is thereby transformed from whether a prediction is accurate to whether a task may be entrusted, a question medicine has addressed throughout its history of training juniors under supervision. We argue that the appropriate frame for agentic systems is consequently delegation rather than prediction, and that the entrustment frameworks developed within postgraduate education furnish a serviceable structure of graded autonomy, task-level scope, and named supervisory responsibility. We then identify the point at which the correspondence ceases to hold. Supervision of human colleagues presupposes that errors are independent and idiosyncratic, such that mistakes arise individually and are detected individually. A single agent deployed across an institution generates one error process reproduced at scale. The consequence is that agentic systems cannot be adequately supervised through case-level review, and require instead the population-level surveillance characteristic of quality improvement.

Venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series
Year: 2026

Abstract:

Authors: Ethan C. Gazan, Colin Emrich, Alexander Baur, Zachary C. Lum, Jenna Bernstein, David C. Landy

Abstract:

#10 [paper] From Prompt to Provenance: BloClaw, a Capability-Gated AI4S Workstation for Auditable Computational Biology
Authors: Qin Yao, Jinhua Pang, Xiaoming Zhang
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.26.747436
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Scientific agents can produce plausible answers while remaining unable to establish whether the computation behind an answer is executable, recoverable, or reproducible. We present BloClaw, an AI4S workstation built around a simple principle: a scientific agent should know what it can do, show how it did it, and state what remains unvalidated. Each capability declares an execution state, input constraints, dependencies, expected outputs, and scientific limitations. Natural-language requests are translated into structured tasks, validated against this registry, executed through scientific tools, and recorded in a provenance-aware Living Lab Notebook. The system is designed to detect invalid inputs, failed tool calls, missing dependencies, and remote timeouts, and to route them to repair, retry, or escalation. The implemented and tested scope comprises RDKit-based molecular property and rule screening, protein structure analysis, docking-pose inspection, 3D visualization, and structured reporting. We demonstrate the workflow on a PubChem-retrieved osimertinib structure and a supplied 6LU7 docking artifact: the former yields deterministic descriptors (molecular weight 499.619 Da, cLogP 4.5098, TPSA 87.55 A^2), while the latter contains 2,387 protein ATOM records, 309 residues, and nine pose records. These examples are workflow demonstrations, not efficacy or affinity studies. Beyond retrospective prediction, the manuscript specifies a prior-minimized constructive mode in which a desired function is compiled into explicit physical, chemical, and systems constraints, candidate mechanisms are simulated, and observations are reintroduced for calibration and falsification; this is a proposed extension rather than a result of the present case studies. We describe an evaluation protocol that compares BloClaw with a standard single-agent workflow and fixed-script execution using task completion, scientific correctness, recovery success, provenance completeness, reproducibility, human review time, latency, and cost. This manuscript reports the system design, verified capability boundary, deterministic software artifacts, and a reproducible evaluation protocol; it does not claim benchmark improvements before those experiments are run. BloClaw is an execution and accountability layer for AI-assisted research, complementing expert review and experimental validation rather than replacing them.

Abstract:

Distinguishing Decision Coverage, Adjudication Accuracy, and Orchestration Efficiency in Agentic Gene Annotation Review of: Sinha, A. AI Models Excel at Orchestration but Falter at Biological Judgment: Findings from an Agentic Gene Annotation Study. bioRxiv (2026). https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.23.753765 Overall assessment This preprint addresses an increasingly important question in scientific AI: whether competence in coordinating analytical workflows should be taken as evidence of competence in interpreting their biological outputs. By separating deterministic sequence analysis, LLM-guided evidence acquisition, and final adjudication, Genome Skeptic offers a useful experimental framework for examining these capabilities independently. The prospectively locked comparisons, explicit scoring rules, and publicly available computational artifacts are notable strengths. Independent recalculation from the available case-level records reproduced the principal paired results, including the decrease from 18/20 to 11/20 correct classifications (exact two-sided McNemar P = 0.015625). I found no numerical inconsistency in this comparison. My principal concerns therefore concern interpretation rather than numerical correctness. In particular, the findings invite a more explicit distinction between decision coverage, correctness conditional on making a decision, and the incremental value of LLM-guided evidence acquisition. Clarifying these dimensions would strengthen the study's implications for scientific agent design. Major comment 1. Distinguishing abstention from incorrect biological adjudication The reduction in overall accuracy when Sol assumes final decision authority is statistically supported. However, its mechanism deserves greater emphasis. Independent examination of the locked case-level outputs confirms that all nine disagreements between the deterministic and LLM adjudicators involve transitions from ABSENT to UNRESOLVED, rather than incorrect definitive positive calls. Under a secondary selective-classification interpretation that treats UNRESOLVED as abstention, the LLM provides definitive classifications for 11/20 cases, all of which are correct. Thus, decision coverage is 55%, whereas accuracy conditional on a definitive classification is 100%. These secondary figures do not replace the prespecified accuracy endpoint. Problem (Mycelium's reading): The risk that clinical AI systems reduce clinicians to procedural validators rather than active judges, particularly when agreeing with AI recommendations requires less effort than disagreeing.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Mixed-method study involving eleven practising radiologists interacting with two prototypes: an oracular system (single diagnosis) and an evaluative system (multiple differentials with reference exemplars).

Abstract:
We propose productive friction as a design principle for clinical AI: the deliberate, graded introduction of interaction cost when accepting machine recommendations, calibrated to case uncertainty so that analytical reasoning is activated without disrupting workflow. We ground this principle in a mixed-method study with eleven practising radiologists interacting with two contrasting prototypes, an oracular system delivering a single diagnosis and an evaluative system presenting multiple differentials with reference exemplars. We argue that productive friction carries direct ethical significance: when agreeing with an AI recommendation requires less effort than disagreeing, the clinician's role risks becoming procedural rather than a genuine locus of judgement. We operationalise this principle along four dimensions, temporal delay, option cardinality, evidence depth, and commitment structure, and translate it into implementable design mechanisms for adaptive clinical AI.

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fgwh.2026.1881840

Abstract:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) affects approximately 9-13% of women of reproductive age worldwide, an estimated 170 million individuals, depending on which diagnostic criteria are applied [1,2]. It is one of the most common endocrine disorders in this population. Even though it is so common, PCOS has often been underdiagnosed, care has been fragmented, and research funding has been limited [3,4]. Part of the problem comes from its name, which can be misleading [3,4]. The term 'polycystic ovary' suggests that the disorder involves abnormal ovarian cysts, but this is not actually the case. Instead, ultrasound usually shows arrested follicular development caused by neuroendocrine and metabolic problems, which is a different issue [5].In May 2026, Teede et al. published the outcome of an unprecedented global consensus process involving 56 organisations, 14,360 survey responses from patients and health professionals across all world regions, modified Delphi surveys, nominal group workshops, and marketing analysis [5]. The resulting new name, polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), omits the misleading cyst reference and explicitly captures the condition's endocrine, metabolic, and ovarian dimensions. This opinion article evaluates the evidence base underpinning this rename, examines its clinical and psychosocial implications, and identifies the implementation priorities essential to converting a nomenclature change into genuine improvement in patient outcomes (Figure 1). The historical framing of PCOS as a primarily gynecological or ovarian disorder has led to its broader effects being treated as separate issues. However, international guidelines have tried to address this. The 2018 and 2023 International Evidence-Based Guidelines recognize a range of metabolic, reproductive, psychological, and skin-related features and note that gaps in practice and delays in diagnosis persist even with these guidelines [3,4]. The 2023 update added anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) as another option for adult diagnosis, highlighted the importance of metabolic and cardiovascular risks, and placed greater emphasis on psychological health [4]. Yet clinicians continue to show variable awareness of diagnostic criteria and the breadth of PMOS features [6].PMOS involves multiple interacting endocrine axes. Elevated gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulse frequency drives excess luteinizing hormone secretion, augmenting ovarian androgen production. Insulin resistance is present in approximately 85% of affected individuals, including 75% of lean women, and acts synergistically to amplify androgen excess and disrupt steroid hormone balance [5,7,8]. Abnormal AMH signaling, altered adipokine profiles, and excess adrenal androgens further compound endocrine dysregulation [5,7]. Cardiometabolic sequelae are well-documented: type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), hypertension, and elevated cardiovascular disease risk represent the downstream morbidity that the old name systematically obscured [3,4,7]. Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#5 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science

Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. OCEAN-RAD P1 is a preliminary engineering study investigating radiative sky cooling as a potential means of removing heat from enclosed seawater tanks. Initial testing is intended to take place on land, without organisms, primarily under nocturnal conditions. The study provides a thermal model, reproducible Python code, synthetic parameter studies, a proposed experimental protocol, measurement templates and an internal technical review. Performance depends on atmospheric radiation, temperatures, heat-transfer coefficients and component properties. The reported values are conditional numerical results rather than measured or representative coastal performance. Version 1.1 distinguishes heat transported between the heat-exchanger ports from heat extracted from the seawater, accounting for changes in the exchanger’s stored thermal energy during transients. It also strengthens data validation, extends uncertainty accounting and revises the proposed startup procedure. No prototype testing or biological experiments have been conducted. Practical efficiency, durability, economic viability and ecological benefits remain unverified. The work is intended to support laboratory evaluation and possible future applications in small, controlled marine facilities; it does not demonstrate cooling of the open ocean or a net planetary cooling effect. Interview Protocols Two versions of the interview protocol accommodated participants with and without prior participation in the earlier interview study: New participants: Includes introductory questions about professional roles, organizational risks associated with cold-stunning events, information sources, preparedness and response actions, and communication pathways. Returning participants: Omits the introductory background questions and proceeds to the visualization activities following the interview preamble. Both versions include the following two activities and associated discussion questions. Activity 1: Interpretation and Comparison of Deterministic and Probabilistic Information Participants explored two potential cold-stunning event scenarios using an interactive dashboard. Within each scenario, participants first viewed deterministic water temperature guidance (Scenarios 1A and 2A), followed by probabilistic guidance for the same event (Scenarios 1B and 2B). The visualizations displayed observations and predictions, allowing participants to examine water temperature values over time. Interview questions explored participants’ interpretations, perceptions of certainty, potential actions and their timing, and the forecast features informing those assessments. Additional questions addressed interpretations of the shaded uncertainty ranges, strengths and weaknesses of each presentation format, forecast preferences, and perceived decision-making challenges. Access Activity 1: Deterministic and Probabilistic Scenario Comparisons Activity 2: Ranking Challenging Cold-Stunning Event Scenarios Participants compared probabilistic water temperature guidance across five potential cold-stunning event scenarios: the two scenarios examined in Activity 1 and three additional scenarios. They were encouraged to think aloud while exploring and ranking the scenarios. #1 [paper] Governing The Accelerator: The Case for National Collaboration in AI‐Enabled Materials Discovery
Authors: Richard Harry, Shanshan Mei, DEAN BALL
Venue: Advanced Materials Technologies
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.71315
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping materials discovery into a more integrated pipeline by combining data generation, surrogate prediction, and, in selected settings, closed‐loop experimentation at an unprecedented rate. However, the institutional mechanisms needed to govern reproducibility, interoperability, and oversight across these workflows remain underdeveloped. This perspective examines how federally funded research and development centers (FFRDCs) can close that gap across three domains: data and infrastructure, algorithmic intelligence, and autonomous experimentation. In each, absent a national coordinating body, these decisions default to institutions not built for coordination, accountability, or mission persistence. We propose a two‐tier leadership model in which science and technology (S&T) laboratories drive technical capability, while study and analysis (S&A) centers provide policy integration, cost‐benefit analysis, and governance frameworks to translate scientific output into national strategy. Without a coordinating framework, the United States risks advancing a technology faster than it can govern it. Meanwhile, foreign competitors pursue centralized national materials programs of their own.

#5 [paper] Funding mechanisms as incentive systems: a role for science philanthropy
Authors: Lillian Parr, Nadia Sarfraz, Sylvina M. Raver, Nadia M. Penrod
Venue: Frontiers in Systems Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1939099
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Biomedical research is shaped not only by scientific questions, but also by the incentive structures that determine what scientists study, how they approach the work, and how success is defined. Current incentives often prioritize individual achievement as a pathway to career advancement, while undervaluing replication, data sharing, mentorship, collaboration, and shared infrastructure. This can make it challenging for scientists to prioritize these contributions, even when they recognize that they are essential for a strong scientific ecosystem. This article examines how funders and funding mechanisms create implicit incentives and argues that funding design is a powerful lever for shaping both scientific behavior and the broader research ecosystem. Philanthropy is uniquely positioned to experiment with funding design by supporting high-risk research, emerging areas, and investments in people, fields, norms, and shared infrastructure that other funders may be unable or unwilling to pursue, while also dedicating resources to learn from how these investments shape scientific behavior. Here, we highlight questions funders can ask about the incentives embedded in funding mechanisms, including what behaviors they encourage, who participates and benefits, and what persists beyond the award. For scientists, understanding funding goals, participating in evaluations, and making contributions beyond traditional outputs visible can strengthen the feedback between funding design and scientific practice. By treating funding mechanisms as design choices that can be tested and refined, philanthropy can generate evidence that informs future funding approaches and strengthens the scientific ecosystem.

#6 [paper] A GAITS-driven gap-to-deliverable accelerator for early-stage neurotechnology: design and early outcomes of the blueprint MedTech seedling program
Authors: Evaristus A. Nwulia, Hasan Ali, Maria Mananita S Hipolito, Narayan Rai, Santosh Venkatesha, John Collins, Penny Ford Carleton
Venue: Frontiers in Medical Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmedt.2026.1925746
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Early-stage neurotechnology teams face a persistent structural barrier between scientific proof-of-concept and clinical/commercial viability. Traditional funding mechanisms, including investigator-initiated grants and early-stage SBIR/STTR awards, prioritize scientific novelty but may not address regulatory, clinical, market, and business challenges required for translation. Programs such as I-Corps and C3i improve commercialization literacy but primarily function as educational interventions. The NIH Blueprint MedTech (BPMT) Seedling Program addresses this gap by converting reviewer-identified commercialization weaknesses into structured, time-bounded work packages aligned with the Guidance and Impact Tracking System (GAITS), a commercialization maturity framework, and supported by experienced mentors. Objective To describe the GAITS-driven Gap-to-Deliverable (G2G) acceleration model and characterize early program outcomes among neurotechnology teams participating in the BPMT Seedling Program. Methods The six-month, mentor-centered Seedling Program operates within two NIH-funded neurotechnology incubator hubs: the Center for Innovative NeuroTech Advancement (CINTA) and NeuroTech Harbor ( N TH). Each selected team receives $50,000 to address reviewer-identified commercialization gaps. Following multidisciplinary review, weaknesses are mapped to GAITS maturity indicators across Technology, Regulatory, Market/Business, and Clinical domains and converted into evidence-generating Work Packages. This descriptive program evaluation analyzed gap distributions across three cohorts ( N = 58) and Deep Dive progression outcomes for two completed cohorts ( N = 39). Results GAITS-based review identified frequent commercialization gaps at program entry. Across all 58 teams, gaps were identified in team composition for 48/58 (82.8%), commercialization strategy for 47/58 (81.0%), work planning for 38/58 (65.5%), and regulatory strategy for 33/58 (56.9%). Among the two completed cohorts, 13/17 teams (76.5%; exact 95% CI, 50.1%–93.2%) in Cohort 1 and 18/22 teams (81.8%; 95% CI, 59.7%-94.8%) in Cohort 2 advanced to Blueprint MedTech Deep Dive evaluation; the combined progression rate was 31/39 (79.5%; 95% CI, 63.5%–90.7%). Cohort-specific rates did not differ statistically (Fisher exact p = 0.709). Conclusion Among pre-screened teams with scientific or technical merit and addressable commercialization gaps, most advanced to internal Deep Dive evaluation after completing GAITS-aligned Work Packages. However, this uncontrolled evaluation of a selected cohort and program-specific endpoint does not establish causality or improved translational readiness. Prospective studies should incorporate standardized pre/post maturity measures, external downstream outcomes, and appropriate comparison groups to evaluate program effectiveness.

#7 [paper] FUNDING AS RESEARCH: DEVELOPING OPEN AI ACCOUNTABILITY RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE
Authors: Erkan Yazargan

Abstract:
This publication introduces Funding as Research, a methodological framework for treating research funding opportunities, calls for proposals, and RFPs as external research-development specifications rather than solely as sources of financial support.The framework proposes a structured process through which an emerging research infrastructure can examine a funding opportunity, decompose its objectives and evaluation criteria, compare them with existing capabilities, identify methodological and technical gaps, define a new development phase, and document the resulting analysis as an independent open research object.The proposed workflow is:FUNDING SIGNAL → RFP ANALYSIS → FIT MATRIX → GAP ANALYSIS → PHASE DEVELOPMENT → OPEN PUBLICATION → APPLICATION / NON-APPLICATION → LEARNThe methodology is particularly relevant to emerging research areas involving AI accountability, agentic AI, AI safety, research provenance, institutional observation, digital evidence, citizen auditing, open science, interoperability, verification, and reproducible research infrastructure.The publication develops the concept of Funding as Research as an extension of Research Infrastructure Evolution. Under this approach, a funding call can function as an external maturity signal: its requirements may reveal existing capabilities, missing infrastructure components, implementation challenges, measurable development objectives, and potential future research questions.The framework does not require researchers to reshape their work artificially around a particular funder. Instead, funding criteria are treated as an external analytical reference. The resulting fit analysis may lead to a formal application, further research and infrastructure development before application, or a documented decision not to apply. All three outcomes can generate methodological learning.The approach also proposes that funding-analysis records can become persistent research objects containing the relevant RFP version, analytical criteria, fit matrix, identified gaps, proposed development roadmap, application decision, external response, and subsequent methodological learning. Repeated application of the methodology could therefore support the development of a longitudinal Funding & Research Infrastructure Alignment Corpus.In the context of AI accountability, the framework further explores how funding-driven research development can contribute to open infrastructure for AI identity, authorization, observation, evidence preservation, verification, cross-checking, and research provenance.References to external funding organizations, programs, or RFPs are used solely as analytical inputs. Their inclusion does not imply endorsement, partnership, eligibility, institutional validation, or funding commitment.The primary contribution of this publication is therefore methodological: it proposes that funding environments themselves can become observable components of research infrastructure evolution, providing structured signals for identifying where a research infrastructure currently stands, what it needs to develop next, and what evidence supports that development.

#8 [paper] Bridging the Computational-Experimental Gap: A Supply Chain Management Framework for Just-in-Time Synthesis in Advanced Materials Discovery
Authors: Khalid Zaman Mumit, MD Rayhan Hasan Shakib, Irtiza Asmar Riad, Foisal Mahmud, Tanzim Hasan
Venue: Supply Chain Insider
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23310723
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The fast pace of development of high-performance computing, density functional theory, and machine learning has reduced the process of screening new materials through theory from years to days. But the same pace has not been achieved in the physical supply chain of laboratory materials, thus causing a major hindrance in the pipeline of discovery of new materials. This paper focuses on the supply chain problems in advanced materials science and engineering laboratories and suggests a model for eliminating this hindrance. The three major gaps that have been identified from a structured review of literature involving 50 papers and thematic analysis of eight stakeholders including Principal Investigators, Post-Doctoral Researchers, Lab Managers, Computational Scientists, Procurement Officers, Facility Engineers, Industry R&D Managers, and Sustainability Officers are: (1) disconnect between computational screening and procurement process, (2) lack of predictive lead-time models for laboratory chemicals, and (3) lack of closed-loop approach for R&D at circular economy. The quantitative results show that the average score for predictability of procurement lead-time is 2.0/5, whereas the average score for severity of delays is 4.4/5. The average recovery of precursors' mass is 26%. There are four main qualitative themes: "Wait-and-see Trap", "Customs and Bureaucracy Black Box", "Cost vs. Purity Dilemma", and "Desperately Predictive Need". SynchroLabs' SCM Framework consists of four components: Predictive Procurement Engine, Lead-Time Intelligence Dashboard, Closed-Loop Recovery Engine, and Integrated Smart Inventory. Readiness for adoption was reported to be 4.4/5 on average, demonstrating high potential for implementation. Contribution to the theory of supply chain is that it applies the theory of closed-loop to laboratories and offers recommendations for laboratory managers, institution administrators, and developers of the technologies of synthesis and computational discovery.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Living labs working on nature restoration[1] are better connected, they are better involved in policy developments, and they benefit from existing knowledge and experience, leading to scale up of solutions for nature restoration and to address bottlenecks to implementation in particular through strengthened ownership including by local communities, private actors and public authorities;

- the cooperation between research, practice and policy on nature restoration is increased, with attention to practitioners involved in nature restoration (farmers, foresters, fishers and/or other businesses depending on ecosystem services) and rural/local communities and authorities as well as traditional and local knowledge holders;

- public authorities, land owners and/or managers, water related stakeholders, food and bioeconomy actors and practitioners have access to shared, validated deployment and governance frameworks that support the scale up of nature restoration actions as well as estimates for demand for certified environmental outcomes supporting restoration objectives (certified carbon farming credits[2] and, once methodologies are available, nature credits).

Scope:

The EU biodiversity strategy for 2030 defines nature restoration objectives in line with target 2 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The EU Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR) provides that Member States shall put in place effective and area-based restoration measures.

Support to nature restoration living labs has been granted under Horizon Europe and more living labs are expected to be settled, making coordination and transfer of implementation frameworks increasingly important. including to capture recurring implementation bottlenecks. The Soil Mission has gathered experience on living labs for soil restoration notably through the project SOILL[3].

The Commission announced in the Bioeconomy Strategy the creation of a Buyers’ Club for carbon farming; its aim is to bring together potential buyers of carbon farming credits certified under the Carbon Removal and Carbon Farming (CRCF) Regulation, for instance by facilitating alliances between land managers and potential financiers. The Commission has adopted a roadmap towards nature credits[4].

Proposals should:

- organise a European network of living labs and lighthouses dedicated to nature restoration to ensure a cohesive development and the effective uptake of validated deployment frameworks. It should notably facilitate the development of common methodologies, standards, impact frameworks and capacity-building activities for living labs across Europe, ensuring strong involvement of national and regional living lab networks and fostering cross-border collaboration. #14 [paper] Selecting Materials Outreach Topics from Community Repair Demand: Organizational Weighting, Temporal Transfer and Local Fit
Authors: Chahn Yong Jung
Venue: Journal of Materials Education (Electronic)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.71448/jme2026346
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Community repair events bring materials science into contact with familiar products, but outreach teams must decide which objects deserve limited preparation time. This study evaluates topic selection under two representation rules: equal influence for each recorded repair attempt and equal influence for each repair group. The Open Repair Alliance collection contains 48,669 attempts. Selection used 17,805 attempts from 95 groups, followed by evaluation on 18,802 attempts from 126 groups. The four topics selected by attempt weighting were laptops, lamps, separate audio equipment and coffee makers. Group weighting replaced the latter two with mobile phones and small kitchen appliances. Its selection-period advantage in average group coverage contracted from 3.09 to 0.43 percentage points in the following year. Network-stratified group resampling gave a 95% interval of −1.29 to 2.28 points for that contrast, while attempt coverage decreased by 3.27 points. Local differences had opposing signs: 58 groups gained coverage, 63 lost coverage and five were unchanged. Resampling the selection groups recovered the complete topic sets in only 19.28% and 35.84% of draws. Increasing the kit to eight topics made the two rules select identical categories; ten topics were needed to exceed one-half of average group demand. These results establish the consequences of representation choices without attributing learning gains to category matching. A shared materials kit therefore requires an explicit intended beneficiary, host-specific preparation and an educational assessment independent of repair completion.

Abstract:
Modern microbiological research generates vast quantities of data, particularly from high-throughput "omics" technologies. These datasets promise unprecedented insights into microbial diversity, function, and interactions, yet they are often deposited in unstructured formats with inadequate metadata, significantly hampering their discoverability, interoperability, and long-term reusability. Community engagement remains vital: we will strengthen collaboration with existing stakeholders while actively reaching out to previously underrepresented groups, specifically researchers working on eukaryotic microbes such as fungi and protists, and we will work more closely with data-generating facilities to capture rich metadata early on. These enhancements will support a more comprehensive and inclusive data infrastructure for microbiological research. #20 [paper] Researcher profiles, proposal submission, and project approval: an exploratory case study at a Brazilian Federal Institute
Authors: Woska Pires da Costa, Cristhian Chagas Ribeiro, Marcos de Moraes Sousa, Cleiton Mateus Sousa, Priscilla Rayanne e Silva, Kodhandaraman Chinnathambi, Manuel Monfort-Pañego, Mark A. Noll
Venue: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/frma.2026.1888607
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction Decisions to enter funding competitions and subsequent funding outcomes are connected components of a broader process. However, evidence on how researcher-profile characteristics relate to these stages remains limited in public research institutions outside the research-intensive university sector, particularly in emerging-economy research systems. Objective This exploratory case study analyzed the associations between researcher-profile characteristics and two respondent-level outcomes among researchers at a Brazilian Federal Institute: proposal submission and, among submitters, self-reported approval of at least one project. Methods An online cross-sectional survey was completed by 83 of 327 eligible researchers (response rate 25.4%) in 2023. Data from this self-selected, single-institution sample were analyzed using bivariate contingency-table tests, exact tests for sparse tables, and Cramér's V as a descriptive effect-size measure. Findings were treated as hypothesis-generating. Results Proposal submission was associated with education level ( p = 0.020; V = 0.285) and teaching in a master's or doctoral degree program ( p < 0.001; V = 0.409). Among respondents who submitted proposals, reporting at least one approved project was associated with age group ( p = 0.011; V = 0.403) and CNPq productivity fellowship ( PQ ) status ( p = 0.047; V = 0.284). The approval outcome was measured at the respondent level and did not represent a proposal-level success rate. Conclusion By distinguishing submission from approval, this study contributes to research evaluation by indicating that proposal submission and reporting at least one approved project among submitters were associated with different researcher-profile characteristics. These exploratory findings do not establish barriers or causal mechanisms. Multicenter, proposal-level, and longitudinal studies using explicit, context-sensitive definitions of career stage should test whether these patterns vary across institutions, fields, and career trajectories.

#3 [grant] Innovative circular solutions for end-of-life footwear through collection, sorting and recycling
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-05
Still open/current: yes

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

Abstract:

This topic aims at supporting activities that are enabling or contributing to one or several expected impacts of destination “Developing and using new tools, technologies and digital solutions for a healthy society”. To that end, proposals under this topic should aim to deliver results that are directed at, tailored towards and contributing to most of the following expected outcomes:

- Individual patients will benefit from a personalised approach to their respective medical condition thanks to the bio-printed regenerative medicine solution.

Scope:

Tissue-specific functional 3D bio-printing of living cells has made significant progress as a new approach for transplantation applications in regenerative medicine. There are currently several types of bio-printing technologies under development for the repair of different targeted tissues or organs. To fully unleash the potential of bio-printed cell constructs for regenerative medicine several bottlenecks still need to be overcome. Various studies in pre-clinical models have shown that bio-printed cell constructs or tissues hold great promise for regenerative medicine, by allowing autologous tissue grafts being printed thus avoiding adverse graft-host reactions. However, translation of such approaches into clinical settings (i.e. humans) and their application to internal organs still needs to be investigated and demonstrated. Dependant on the actual target site (i.e. the defect tissue or organ in the human body) different bio-printing approaches may be preferable. For printing complex tissues and especially entire organs an in-vitro approach followed by transplantation is the preferred way. “In-situ” bio-printing, sometimes also referred to as “in-vivo”, or as “intraoperative”, reflects a bioprinting process performed on a live subject in a surgical setting and has in certain instances (e.g. tissue repair) advantages over an in-vitro bio-printing technique followed by transplantation. In-situ bio-printing involves direct patterning of bio-inks onto a patient’s body at the target site, allowing for precise construction of a site-matching tissue-structure within the actual physiological location where regeneration or repair is needed. As such, in-situ bio-printing allows for high adaptability, reduced risk of contamination, improved cell viability, function and host integration. The high cell densities present in the human vital organs underscore the importance of bio-inks which contain less additional biomaterials as matrix. Hence the bio-printing of cell constructs that comprise native tissue-like cell densities may facilitate repair and/or regeneration of defective complex tissues or internal organs. For such approaches meticulous engineering of the bio-printing equipment is necessary, involving sophisticated micro-surgical instrumentation and medical imaging platforms. To achieve the desired function and to mimic the natural cues in native tissues for in-vitro printed bio-constructs, the use of additional stimuli is needed, whereas in-situ approaches normally rely on the body as natural bioreactor providing the necessary extracellular cues. Recently, combinations of in-situ bio-printing with real-time stimuli have been investigated, even for the repair of internal organs. However, there remain bottlenecks that need to be overcome, like the integration with existing imaging modalities and surgical procedures or the long-time stability and functionality of the created bio-constructs.

#16 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

#1 [paper] Alternative futures for laboratory medicine in 2050: scenarios and signposts for diagnostic capability contraction.
Authors: Yuji, Koichiro, Yuji, Wakako, Ohnishi, Hiroaki
Venue: Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42723619/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Laboratory medicine has begun to describe its own future, and the images it produces are almost uniformly expansionary. What they rarely contain is a collapse scenario: a future in which the field delivers less than today. A profession planning for 2050 needs one. CONTENT: We summarise what structured foresight offers a clinical readership, entering through the threats quadrant of a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis, and treat the standard taxonomy of futures as a lens, not a required method. We define diagnostic capability contraction as progressive degradation rather than catastrophic disappearance, distinct from retiring tests that add nothing. Six drivers are specified: loss of laboratory-developed tests, reduced test availability, workforce attrition, supplier dependency, geographical access and payment. Evidence comes from three jurisdictions, including Japan, where one regulatory driver produced different outcomes in the same period. We set out four scenarios for 2050, one per generic image, and propose signposts as early-warning indicators, with action thresholds, for the contraction scenario. Estimates of likelihood attach to the indicators, not the futures. SUMMARY: The evidence base is uneven across drivers, and informatively so: what is not anticipated is not measured. The argument applies to our own prior work, expansionary in the same way. OUTLOOK: A set containing a contraction branch gives laboratory leadership what an expansionary set cannot: what to watch for, and when to act. A preferred future chosen without it comes from a shorter list than the field faces. Building a balanced set is work that no small group of authors can do alone.

#2 [paper] Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
Authors: Haining Wang, Jing Su
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.10.758253
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

#3 [paper] Bridging laboratory and clinical practice: timelines and challenges in wet lab research
Authors: Nisreen Mohammed Al-Namnam, Steph Collishaw, Melanie Wheeldon
Venue: Bone and Joint Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1302/2046-3758.1511.bjr-2026-0221.r1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
For surgical trainees embarking on a period of laboratory research, the transition from operating theatre to bench science can be both rewarding and disorienting. This annotation is written specifically for clinicians entering a wet laboratory environment, typically on an out-of-programme research placement, who may be unfamiliar with the realities of experimental science. Drawing on the first-hand experiences of a multidisciplinary orthopaedic research team, it explains why laboratory timelines are often longer than expected, and offers practical guidance for working effectively alongside PhD-level scientists, postdoctoral researchers, research technicians, and their trainees - collaborators whose technical expertise is indispensable to experimental success. Wet lab work involves complex protocols, tissue handling, assay optimization, and regulatory approvals, all of which can significantly extend project timelines. Effective communication, realistic planning, and mutual respect are crucial to manage unforeseen challenges and ensure that experiments are reliable, reproducible, and clinically meaningful.

#4 [paper] Which AI Should Pick Grid Batteries? Forecasting Storage Project Completion in US Interconnection Queues with Language Models, Survival Models and Investor Agents
Authors: Eliseo Curcio
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23693081
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Most US grid interconnection requests are never built; storage is nearly half of active requests. We ask which AI system best forecasts, when a storage project enters the queue, whether it will be built by a fixed date. On Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Queued Up 2026 data (38,201 projects) we compare a Bayesian competing-risks survival model and a neural survival ensemble, fitted on entries to 2016 with outcomes read at end-2025, with a decision-specialised model (TypeSafe Jev) and four frontier large language models (LLMs) given the same entry-time features. Each gave the probability that a 2017–2020 storage entry is operating by 31 December 2025. On resolved projects (registered analysis) anonymised LLMs led: Brier 0.066 (Claude), 0.068 (Grok) and 0.073 (GPT) against 0.080 (neural) and 0.104 (Bayesian). A dated amendment rescored all 2,322 projects, counting pending ones as non-events: Claude remained best (0.0531), GPT (0.0660) no longer beat the neural ensemble (0.0659), and no forecaster beat a constant forecast at the realised 5.6% rate (0.0529). Jev came close to the best LLM at under 1% of its cost, but non-inferiority was not established. Better probabilities did not reliably yield more simulated megawatts per dollar. All of this is retrospective: survival models learned from outcomes through 2025, and LLM training data post-date the test outcomes. We have therefore frozen forecasts from Claude, GPT, Jev, gpt-oss-120b and both survival models for all 4,222 storage projects still queued at end-2025 (SHA-256 382de703… and 24ae373d…, 26 October 2026), to be scored only on later events.

#5 [paper] Contemporary Research: Trends, Challenges and Future Perspectives
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.68801/vsg.978-81-181493-1-6
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Research is essential for advancing knowledge, promoting innovation, and addressing contemporary challenges. Rapid technological development, environmental concerns, globalization, and socio-economic changes have increased the need for multidisciplinary collaboration. Integrating science, engineering, mathematics, artificial intelligence (AI), social sciences, humanities, education, arts, and management can generate innovative solutions and support sustainable development. Advances in chemistry, physics, biotechnology, environmental science, and materials science contribute to healthcare, renewable energy, and environmental protection. Engineering transforms scientific discoveries into practical applications, while mathematics supports modelling, statistical analysis, and computational problem-solving. AI and digital technologies further enhance research through machine learning, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation. However, ethical concerns involving data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and research integrity require responsible technological applications. Social sciences and humanities provide insights into human behaviour, cultural diversity, economic development, governance, and social change. Educational research explores digital learning, inclusive education, curriculum development, and AI-assisted teaching. Similarly, arts promote creativity, cultural preservation, and innovative expression, while management research strengthens entrepreneurship, leadership, strategic planning, and organizational efficiency. Despite significant opportunities, research faces challenges such as inadequate funding, limited infrastructure, insufficient training, and difficulties in interdisciplinary collaboration. Ethical issues concerning plagiarism, authorship, data protection, and research reliability also require attention. Institutional support, adequate resources, transparent policies, and academic integrity are essential to overcoming these barriers. Future research will increasingly focus on digital innovation, sustainable development, open science, and collaborative partnerships. Emerging fields such as biotechnology, renewable energy, advanced materials, digital humanities, AI-supported education, and data-driven management offer promising opportunities. Collaboration among universities, industries, governments, and communities can translate research findings into practical solutions while respecting indigenous knowledge and cultural diversity. The present study encourages interdisciplinary collaboration, promotes responsible innovation, strengthens knowledge exchange, identifies future research priorities, and contributes to inclusive and sustainable development.

#6 [paper] The impact of personalized deadline reminders via Microsoft Teams and Moodle calendar on assignment submission and completion rates
Authors: Ahmad Alfailakawi, Abdulaziz Alenizi
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943550
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives This study investigated the effectiveness of two digital deadline reminder strategies—a researcher-authored, friendly-toned announcement delivered through Microsoft Teams and a standard automated calendar/email notification generated by Moodle—compared with a control condition receiving no additional reminders. The study examined differences in on-time assignment submission rates and average submission delays among higher education students. Methodology An A/B/C comparative design with random assignment was employed involving 138 male and female students enrolled in the Introduction to Educational Technology course at the College of Basic Education in Kuwait during the second semester of the 2024–2025 academic year. Participants were allocated equally to three groups: a researcher-authored Microsoft Teams reminder group, an automated Moodle reminder group, and a control group. Five assignments were monitored over a ten-week intervention period, and submission data were obtained from Moodle activity logs. Results Statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups. Students receiving researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminders through Microsoft Teams demonstrated the highest mean on-time submission rate (94.22%) and the shortest mean submission delay (5.18 h). Students receiving automated Moodle reminders recorded an on-time submission rate of 85.65% and an average delay of 15.45 h, while the control group recorded 75.22% and 30.89 h, respectively. The effect sizes were substantial ( η 2 = 0.289 for on-time submission and η 2 = 0.639 for submission delay), although the latter estimate requires cautious interpretation because of the distributional characteristics of the delay variable. Conclusion The findings suggest that proactive digital reminder strategies can support students’ adherence to assignment deadlines. The researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminder strategy delivered through Microsoft Teams was associated with more favorable submission outcomes than the default automated Moodle reminder strategy. However, because the interventions differed simultaneously in communication platform, message content, authorship, and delivery format, the observed differences cannot be attributed to platform characteristics alone. The findings highlight the potential importance of reminder design and delivery practices while emphasizing the need for future research that independently examines the contributions of individual reminder components.

#7 [paper] AI Forecasting of Medical Technologies: Nine Predictions for 2026–2031
Authors: Момыналиев Куват Темиргалиевич

Abstract:
This exploratory prospective pilot study examines the ability of three large language models (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude) to forecast verifiable developments in medical technology research. Nine probability forecasts were collected on October 26, 2026, covering three predefined research events: Q1. Publication of a randomized clinical trial comparing FLASH radiotherapy with conventional radiotherapy (≥100 patients). Q2. #8 [paper] DESIGN AND SIMULATION OF A TASK REMINDER WITH SPACED REVIEW AND DEADLINE PRESSURE DETECTION
Authors: Hizba Muhammad Falah, Anggi Rizky Windra Putri, Tasiu Abdullahi Yusuf
Venue: International Journal of Cyber Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.68404/ijce.v2i1.26
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Describe Task reminders commonly indicate when an assignment is due, but deadline counts alone do not describe the effort required before each due date. Moreover, repeated notifications are not equivalent to retrieval-based spaced review. This study develops an explicit scheduling specification for an existing task-reminder prototype and evaluates a separate executable reference engine. The design combines a recall-dependent review rule, a cumulative deadline-pressure calculation, and an event resolver that distinguishes review prompts from deadline checks. Evaluation comprises 23 functional checks, three scripted review sequences, and 300 synthetic workload scenarios containing 1,150 task records. All functional checks passed. At an assumed capacity of two hours per day and a 72-hour horizon, count-based, aggregate-load, and cumulative deadline-pressure rules flagged 100, 100, and 150 scenarios, respectively. In 50 deliberately constructed early-bottleneck scenarios, only the cumulative rule flagged insufficient capacity before the earliest deadline. Conversely, all 50 light clustered workloads triggered the count rule without exceeding the assumed capacity. An independent exhaustive scheduling oracle agreed with the cumulative rule in all 300 scenarios; agreement was 50.0% for the count rule and 83.3% for the aggregate rule. These results verify logic under the stated capacity model. They do not establish improved retention, productivity, or student well-being. The contribution is a reproducible prototype extension with transparent assumptions and an evidence-based separation of reminder functionality from educational effectiveness.

#9 [paper] Infrastructure Bottlenecks and Data Scarcity: Challenges for AI and Machine Learning Engineering Students in Pakistan
Authors: Hafs Khalil Ur Rehman
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23812094
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Pakistan has recently adopted a National Artificial Intelligence Policy and is expanding AI-related education, yet students who train as AI and machine learning (ML) engineers still work in conditions that differ sharply from those assumed by most published curricula and tutorials. This perspective article examines two interlinked constraints: (i) infrastructure bottlenecks, namely limited access to GPU compute, slow and unevenly distributed connectivity, and power and cost barriers; and (ii) data scarcity, particularly for Urdu and other Pakistani languages and for locally relevant domains such as agriculture, health and flood monitoring. Drawing on policy documents, published research on low-resource language processing, and publicly reported connectivity benchmarks, the article argues that these constraints compound one another and shape what students can learn, build and publish. It then outlines practical mitigation strategies at the level of the student, the institution and national policy. The article is a structured synthesis rather than an empirical study; it does not report a new survey, and its claims about student experience are framed as hypotheses for future empirical work.

#10 [paper] Governing The Accelerator: The Case for National Collaboration in AI‐Enabled Materials Discovery
Authors: Richard Harry, Shanshan Mei, DEAN BALL
Venue: Advanced Materials Technologies
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.71315
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping materials discovery into a more integrated pipeline by combining data generation, surrogate prediction, and, in selected settings, closed‐loop experimentation at an unprecedented rate. However, the institutional mechanisms needed to govern reproducibility, interoperability, and oversight across these workflows remain underdeveloped. This perspective examines how federally funded research and development centers (FFRDCs) can close that gap across three domains: data and infrastructure, algorithmic intelligence, and autonomous experimentation. In each, absent a national coordinating body, these decisions default to institutions not built for coordination, accountability, or mission persistence. We propose a two‐tier leadership model in which science and technology (S&T) laboratories drive technical capability, while study and analysis (S&A) centers provide policy integration, cost‐benefit analysis, and governance frameworks to translate scientific output into national strategy. Without a coordinating framework, the United States risks advancing a technology faster than it can govern it. Meanwhile, foreign competitors pursue centralized national materials programs of their own.

#11 [paper] Predictive Computational Graph Preparation: Forecasting Future Workflows and Precomputing Reusable Intermediate Results
Authors: Jincheng Zhang
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24026457
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Reducing redundant computation in complex AI, scientific, and data analytics workflows by anticipating future computational requirements and precomputing reusable intermediate results, rather than relying solely on caching or memoization of previously executed tasks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Predictive Computational Graph Preparation (PCGP), a conceptual framework that integrates future workflow prediction, computational graph construction, shared subgraph identification, node-level demand forecasting, dependency-aware speculative execution, intermediate result preservation, compatibil…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A proposed experimental methodology for evaluating the framework across data analytics, scientific computing, machine learning pipelines, and AI agent systems; no specific dataset or cohort is identified in the text.
Abstract:
The increasing complexity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, scientific computing environments, data analytics platforms, and automated computational workflows has created substantial opportunities for reducing redundant computation through the anticipation of future computational requirements. Modern computational tasks are frequently organized as interconnected workflows consisting of multiple dependent operations, including data acquisition, preprocessing, transformation, feature extraction, model execution, intermediate result generation, and final output production. Although existing workflow optimization techniques investigate caching, memoization, intermediate result reuse, and dependency-aware scheduling, computational preparation is predominantly associated with previously executed workflows or workloads that have already been submitted. This paper introduces Predictive Computational Graph Preparation (PCGP), a conceptual framework that investigates whether future computational workflows can be forecast and their reusable intermediate computational nodes selectively executed before actual workflow requests materialize. Unlike predictive inference preparation, which primarily anticipates future questions or responses, PCGP focuses on predicting the computational structures underlying future tasks. Its architecture integrates future workflow prediction, computational graph construction, shared subgraph identification, node-level demand forecasting, dependency-aware speculative execution, intermediate result preservation, compatibility verification, and adaptive workflow reconstruction. A central objective is to identify computational nodes that are likely to participate in multiple future workflows and prepare their outputs in advance, thereby reducing repeated execution across different workflows rather than merely accelerating repeated instances of an identical task. The framework further investigates economic-aware node preparation, allowing eligible computations to be scheduled during periods of relatively low GPU utilization, favorable electricity prices, or lower-cost cloud resource availability. A unified optimization formulation is developed to evaluate the expected benefit of precomputing individual nodes and shared subgraphs while accounting for prediction uncertainty, dependency constraints, execution expenditure, storage requirements, data freshness, result compatibility, and resource availability. Importantly, the framework distinguishes between historical intermediate result caching, predictive node execution, and predictive subgraph preparation, recognizing that these mechanisms provide different forms of computational reuse. An experimental methodology is proposed to evaluate workflow prediction accuracy, node reuse rates, avoided computational expenditure, execution latency, GPU utilization, energy consumption, and total system cost. The proposed framework does not assume that every predicted node should be executed in advance; its effectiveness depends on the availability of valid inputs, workflow predictability, cross-workflow reuse opportunities, preparation expenditure, and the compatibility of prepared results with subsequently submitted workflows. #3 [paper] The clinical utility of carrier screening.
Authors: Gruzin, Mia J, Burnett, Leslie
Venue: NPJ genomic medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42547507/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Carrier screening aims to identify couples at risk of having children with serious genetic disorders. However, screening panels vary markedly in size, gene content and price, with little guidance to assess clinical utility or value. We analysed 89 carrier screening panels from 30 global providers, modelling test performance using pathogenic variants from gnomAD v4.1.0 and ClinVar across ten ancestry groups and two synthetic populations (representing the United States and Australia). We evaluated how panel size, content, price and clinical utility interrelate. We also compared value per dollar spent to guide clinical decision-making and fair pricing. Clinical utility showed no consistent relationship with panel size or price. Instead, mid-sized, pan-ancestry "Goldilocks" panels delivered the greatest utility, outperforming both smaller and larger panels, while delivering more equitable outcomes. We developed a visual "clinical utility meter" to compare relative test performance and an "efficiency frontier" framework to identify the best value tests for a given price. This data-driven framework and visual tool can support rational test design and selection for value-based laboratory medicine.

#4 [paper] Multi-agent AI for liver disease guideline development and maintenance: a proof-of-concept study
